This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground-state eigenfunction of the $d$-dimensional time-independent Schrödinger equation with a given potential function. To estimate the generalization error, we derive a upper bound based on the norm of the gradient of the loss function and the complexity of the target function, and demonstrate that it can be expressed as a multiple of the training error with a coefficient related to the input domain and the target function's smoothness. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the generalization error, which approaches the training error as the input dimension $d$ increases. These findings are verified by numerical experiments in two-dimensional space. This research was initially presented at the $38^{th}$ International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2021). The main result presents the asymptotic form of the number of fixed points with a specified degree in a open subset of the complex plane and relates it to a volume of a convex body. Additionally, the degree distribution of these fixed points is determined and found to follow a specific probability measure, denoted as P_n, whose normalization yields a probability distribution that scales as P_n(x)_1 + P_n(x)_2 = x^(n-1) - x^{-n}, with P_n(x)_1 and P_n(x)_2 being non-negative. This general result encompasses multiple cases, including a particular iteration of the Laplace operator and regular perturbations thereof. The case of the standard n-dimensional space was examined under the sole assumption that a certain convex body remains bounded as it is scaled. However, for certain space transformations, known as diagonal matrices, the nature of the convex body was explicitly defined as a scaled version of a standard convex body, such as a sphere or box. The findings were validated through explicit calculations for order 2 and 3. When subjected to this pressure, both types of ice transform into a high-density amorphous ice (HDA) in a sudden, drastic phase transition. An innovative measure, based on the arrangement of oxygen atoms in the ice structure, allowed the researchers to confirm that LDA and HDA do not contain separate, distinct ice domains. While the resulting HDA ice still exhibits certain characteristics similar to those of ice IV, the arrangement of hydrogen bonds differs significantly. Interestingly, the transition from either LDA or HDA to high-density amorphous ice (HDA) displays similar structural patterns, suggesting that a continuous, gradual breakdown of ice crystals occurs in this process. An initial state of high-density amorphous ice with a short-range structural order very similar to ice IV arises temporarily. However, this state has a very short lifespan. Within 10-80 million oscillations, the molecules reach a state of local structural equilibrium. An average compression of molecules in HDA of about 20% is observed at this point. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of products that can be accessed in an orderly manner. Our objective is to delve into the Isabelle Archive's internal workings, assessing its layout and exploring ways to enhance it in the process. Our investigation involves examining the existing layout, evaluating methods to gauge the magnitude and intricacy of individual sections, and proposing a set of general principles and tools aimed at facilitating the enhancement of the Isabelle Archive's structure. Our primary goal is to create a more accessible and readable platform, making it simpler for users to discover and engage with specific areas within the Isabelle Archive. Ultimately, a refined structure has been demonstrated to have a positive effect on the community's overall productivity and should, in turn, foster continued growth in the Isabelle Archive's content and user base. Our work has been applied in a concrete manner to the Formal Methods USA 2019 Workshop. Our methodology and methods have been thoroughly documented in a separate technical report, and the corresponding code is openly available for review and adaptation on the CoLoR platform. Our work has garnered community involvement, and corresponding input and feedback have been solicited in the Formal Methods USA 2019 Workshop to chart the next course of action for the Isabelle Archive's structure. A subsequent step would involve the creation of an automated system to maintain, refine, and update the Isabelle Archive's structure in an effort to preserve and pass down valuable knowledge and knowledge pathways for future generations. This initiative is set to take place in the near future, and details can be accessed at the CoQIsa archive. A crucial next stage would involve integrating the Isabelle Archive's content with an xTex-based document preparation system as initially proposed at the 2018 FMUX conference. This approach is designed to enhance the flow of formal mathematics on the web through a dynamic network of interconnected, refined, and edited articles, theses, and books. A suitable platform to serve as a platform to hold the Isabelle Archive's structure and disseminate the community's work and knowledge in a dynamic and interactive manner would be a TeX-based web search engine, crucial for searching and accessing the Isabelle Archive's content. This approach is set to facilitate the creation of a dynamic, adaptive index, and a refined Isabelle Archive structure, and is an initial step towards a formal mathematics web. This vision is an initial step towards a broader goal of creating a dynamic, interactive platform for searching and accessing formal mathematical documents

In situ data from space, particularly magnetic field measurements, is often represented in complex plots that require specialized knowledge to interpret. While useful for experts in the field, these plots can be inaccessible to those just starting in space research. To bridge this gap, our study examines the audible generation of ULF waves through the creation of low-frequency waves within electronic signals. By applying principles from audio wave manipulation, we aim to develop novel methods for visualizing and listening to ULF waves in their time-frequency domain, similar to how sound waves are represented in frequency spectra. Furthermore, we seek to establish conditions under which an audio frequency component can be extracted from the original time-series magnetic field data, and we outline the technical steps involved in converting magnetometer data into a listenable audio format. Ultimately, we test our proposed methods using data from the MMS spacecraft and conduct a listening exercise to identify features of the observed waves. The successful generation of audible signals not only facilitates the sharing of space research among a broader audience but could also enhance in situ analysis by leveraging the unique listening capabilities of humans. To promote collaboration and understanding between researchers from diverse backgrounds, we provide a step-by-step guide on creating listenable ULF waves from open-source MMS data, which can be applied widely to the MMS dataset. By doing so, we open the door for researchers with unconventional backgrounds in space research to interpret in situ data through the medium of sound. Listening is a powerful tool that allows us to develop new observables, such as listening-mediated whistler mode activation, and to identify patterns that might not emerge in traditional data visualization. The study concludes by discussing how listening to ULF waves can enhance our understanding of the dynamic energy between the sun and Earth and how it can reveal new insights into plasma processes. To demonstrate the utility of our method for educational purposes, we create a listenable audio file corresponding to the equilibrium configuration of magnetic field lines surrounding the MMS spacecraft during its observation of time-dependent ULF waves. The resulting audio file serves as a teaching tool to help students visualize and understand non-equilibrium plasma behavior. The study concludes by suggesting areas for future research, including exploring the application of frequency-domain listening in conjunction with machine learning algorithms to identify patterns in the observed waves. A new class of rotating black brane solutions, including all possible rotational parameters, have been constructed in an arbitrary number of dimensions. These rotating black branes are flat in topology at their horizons, yet due to the influence of the dilaton field, they do not correspond to either flat or (anti)-de Sitter spacetimes outside the horizons. Moreover, the spacetimes exhibit non-trivial dependence on the angular coordinates because of the dilaton phantom effect, causing singularities to form on the boundaries of the causal regions. By analyzing the Hessian matrix at the horizon, the thermodynamic properties of these rotating black branes have been studied in arbitrary dimensions. The first law of thermodynamics was confirmed through variational analysis, and the relationship between the mass function and temperature was investigated for different electric charges. This paper presents an alternative small-step semantics that addresses these limitations, using a small-step calculus to replicate GP 2's lazy evaluation behaviour.  It demonstrates that this new semantics produces the same results as GP 2, thanks to a proven equivalence between the two.  This new semantics provides a solid foundation for various analyses, such as type checking, to be reevaluated in a programming language context.  One such analysis, a type system that enforces functional correctness, is also reintroduced in this context.  Prior research showed that this type system is too restrictive because it does not permit lazy evaluation, leading to the rejection of valid GP 2 programs.  Reconsidering this type system with the new small-step semantics, a more relaxed version that allows for lazy evaluation is found, preserving the benefits of GP 2's lazy evaluation behaviour while achieving functional correctness in a programming language context. The advantages and limitations of massive MIMO and millimeter-wave technology for multicasting are examined in this paper, particularly in scenarios involving multiple groups of users. To maximize energy efficiency, a novel hybrid precoding design is proposed for multicasting groups over millimeter-wave frequencies. To this end, an optimization method is developed to obtain the global optimal solution, but due to the problem's computational complexity, a higher-timefulness algorithm and a lower-timefulness algorithm are proposed for balancing quality and speed. Numerous simulations are conducted to compare the algorithms, revealing that the lower-timefulness algorithm consistently delivers superior performance despite incurring relatively longer processing times. Interestingly, the performance of the lower-timefulness algorithm is found to be relatively close to the optimal solution, with the gap gradually diminishing as the number of transmit antennas increases. To further simplify implementation, a hybrid precoding design with significant reduced complexity is also proposed and found to meet the required performance standards. Numerical simulations confirm that the complexity of the proposed design is a notable improvement over the existing solutions. Lastly, a comparison study is conducted to evaluate the performance of massive MIMO technology for multicasting in different environments and noise levels, with the results revealing that the proposed solutions are adaptable to a range of environments and noise levels, making them versatile technologies. A function from natural numbers to natural numbers is considered near-exponential if it's confined by two growth patterns: one growing and the other shrinking, both following the form 2 raised to a power of n times a constant greater than 0. In this paper, techniques are developed to detect a unique type of growth in groups that interact with root trees, characterized by their rate exceeding the exponential rate. This new form of growth is applied to specific groups such as branch groups, certain automorphism groups of trees, and products of isometries. Furthermore, examples of branch groups following the new growth pattern when paired with particular root trees are created, leading to new classifications of these groups based on their rate of residual finiteness growth in selected cases. The new findings also include examples of p-groups exhibiting various forms of exponential growth in relation to root trees, where p represents a natural number greater than 2. The new classifications, findings, and examples were confirmed through constructive, algorithmic proofs. Moreover, additional forms of exponential growth in groups that handle automorphisms of trees were discovered, leading to a few open cases being resolved. Finally, possible approaches to finding examples of automorphism groups of trees with a growth rate exceeding the near-exponential form are explored. Despite considering various methods, including induction, pressure growth, dilated trees, approximate super-stability, and distinctness, no constructions could be obtained, leaving this area of research with an ongoing question. A broader impact statement was included to address these concerns. The new findings were also presented at a conference featuring the 'Early-Stage Scientists' Session at the Mathematical Society of France. This presentation was supported by a grant from the Nonlinear Dynamics and Statistical Mechanics project, an interface of the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS). This paper introduces an exact calculation method for worst-case scenario parameter realization in robust optimization problems involving uncertain binary or categorical data. Existing exact algorithms for these problems are computationally resource-intensive, partly due to their increased complexity following reformulation of the problem, and partly due to unknown bounds for decision-independent variables. In contrast, we suggest a Lagrangian dual approach that avoids these issues, which can be easily integrated into existing algorithms. This method is particularly tailored to scenarios where binary parameters activate or deactivate constraints, which is commonly encountered in various applications. We discuss possible extensions to scenarios with limited recourse or integer variables and provide numerical results demonstrating notable computational advantages over existing methods. Additionally, we explore an approach for partial optimization, where certain decision-dependent variables are predetermined, which is often the case in various applications. This partial optimization approach is particularly versatile, applicable to both exact and inexact solutions, and can be combined with exact algorithms for overconservative solutions to achieve faster computation times. Furthermore, we provide a computational benchmark to compare exact and approximate algorithms for scenarios with constrained binary uncertainties. The methods proposed in this work can handle not only independent but also correlated uncertainties. However, we also identify open challenges for exact algorithm development and leave investigations into dependent data more complex than activation/deactivation systems for future research. The methods and computational tools for robust optimization, including the code and dependencies, are available at https://github.com/krizs/LagDualRobustOptimization. The methods can also be generalized for scenarios with continuous or spatially correlated uncertainties, which we discuss in https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.17414. The approach for partial optimization is the main contribution of https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.02117. The exact algorithms for partial optimization are the content of https://krizs.github.io/inexact-robust-optimization/. The development of pattern extraction algorithms helps gain valuable insights into vast amounts of information, but there are few methods available to interactively explore and understand complex, multi-dimensional data sets that are visually represented. This interaction deficiency becomes particularly pronounced when dealing with enormous amounts of information, such as those contained in genomic data sets, weather radar images, or medical images. To address this need, our research introduces a new interactive visual pattern exploration system that utilizes a hybrid of symbolic and visual data analysis. This innovative framework combines automatic pattern extraction algorithms with a highly interactive and customizable visual surface to support the exploration and understanding of complex, large data sets. Users can create custom visualizations by selecting different levels of detail and adjusting the appearance of patterns, while also easily navigating through groups of similar patterns. In addition, our system allows users to switch between pattern views and gain access to detailed information about each pattern with a customizable table. The system's effectiveness has been demonstrated through its application in the fields of genomics, meteorology, and medical imaging. This research was presented at the 2011 IEEE Symposium on Visual Analytics and has received the Best Paper Award. Deep learning models' success in graph spaces is further bolstered by graph neural networks (GNNs). In contrast to their traditional deep learning counterparts, GNNs' transfer learning capabilities remain underexplored despite growing interest. Our research reveals the effectiveness of transfer learning in GNNs and highlights how both source tasks and chosen GNN architectures impact learning efficiency. By employing real-world and synthetic data within node and graph classification frameworks, we introduce a general transfer learning methodology for GNNs. Our empirical findings show that transfer learning's performance depends on the similarity between tasks, with similarities in both model design and data sources contributing to optimal results. Furthermore, we identify specific GNN architectures as being more receptive to transfer learning. Consequently, our research aims to advance understanding of transfer learning within the GNN community and boost its efficiency by means of in-depth model analysis. Ultimately, we propose an in-depth model analysis method to identify which GNN components are most crucial in determining the success of transfer learning in GNNs. This method, which leverages Neumann homotopy, provides valuable insights into how GNN models represent tasks and demonstrates their applicability to a range of GNN architectures. In a comparative study, we apply this method to evaluate the representational power of graph attention networks, graph neural networks, and convolutional GNNs, and surprisingly discover that graph neural networks and convolutional GNNs are less expressive than graph attention networks. Our research confirms the connection between a model's expressiveness and its capacity for transfer learning. It is revealed that graph attention networks, which incorporate attention mechanisms, are best suited to a wide range of tasks. Interestingly, our research also reveals that using an attention mechanism does not always guarantee a model's potential to learn task similarities. And finally, our research delivers new insights into the success of transfer learning in GNNs by breaking down the model representation into its constituent parts, i.e., nodes, edges, subgraphs, and graphs within the model graph. By employing Neumann homotopy, we show that the model graph contains information not only about the class labels but also about the features within the dataset. This connection between the model graph and features leads us to investigate how each model component contributes to learning task similarities. Our research also reveals that certain model subgraphs are highly indicative of their respective tasks and can be used as a metric to measure the success of transfer learning in GNNs. A collaborative filtering system predicts user preferences by identifying patterns that connect users to similar items. To do this, we use a Bayesian double feature allocation model that groups users and items according to their shared characteristics, where each group represents a distinct feature. The Indian buffet process (IBP) facilitates the linkage between users, items, and features. The approach trains an IBP prior over a matrix of user-item preferences, where each user and item has its own set of features, allowing us to make predictions for unknown preferences. The effectiveness of this method is evaluated using real-world data on movie ratings and online purchasing history. The results demonstrate that this approach predicts preferences accurately and efficiently uses data, resulting in improvements over existing recommender systems. The complete source code is available online at the specified repository. The implementation is based on the stochastic variational inference and gradient descent methods described in the referenced research on the IBP by Goodman et al. in 2009. The underlying model is equivalent to a hierarchical clustering method that groups users, items, and features, making it simpler to understand and interpret compared to other methods. Additionally, this approach provides a clear measure of the similarity between users, items, and features, allowing for easy estimation. The model is further improved by introducing a last-visit model that takes into account the recency of user-item interactions. The combination of the standard and last-visit models demonstrates the ability to accurately predict preferences over various time scales. To demonstrate the reliability and robustness of this approach, a thorough sensitivity analysis is performed on the model hyperparameters, showcasing their influence on the predicted precision and accuracy. The study also examines the impact of the model hyperparameters on the features and their distribution. The accuracy of the model is evaluated by cross-testing the predictions on different datasets, including a real-world data split and a leave-one-out method. The results of these evaluations confirm the reliability and accuracy of the model. To further validate the model, a diagnostic analysis is performed, highlighting any issues with the data. The study also offers future directions and potential applications for this approach, including the exploration of additional features such as social influence, temporal changes, and semantic items. The model's versatility and wide range of potential applications make it suitable for diverse domains and datasets, supported by the accompanying online repository containing the source code. The model's performance is comparable to that of the widely used deep learning methods; however, it excels in other aspects; for instance, it provides more accurate predictions on hold-out data, and its features are easier to interpret and understand

One of the key problems originating from communication complexity, known as the two-party set disjointness problem, has significant connections to data streaming, set cover, and quantum information theory. The fundamental concept involves two distant parties, $D_1$ and $D_2$, having sets $S_1$ and $S_2$, with the goal of learning $S_1$ and $S_2$, given a shared public signal, after each party has taken one step. It was established by Karloff and Raber that the joint probability of learning both sets is less than or equal to $1/2^{2}$, for any choice of $S_1$ and $S_2$. The current study demonstrates that the joint probability is less than or equal to $1/2^{5/2}$, filling the Karloff-Raber gap, providing a new streaming application: determining whether two functions over a finite domain have only disjoint non-zero elements, in just two passes, for any choice of $\epsilon$ from $[0.1,0.9]$. This involves only allocating storage of $\epsilon^{-1}\log(1/\epsilon)$ bits to store values, while processing $\epsilon^{-1}\log(1/\epsilon)$ $(1-\epsilon)^{-1}$ elements, for achieving an $\epsilon$-estimation of the desired property. The innovation provides an algorithm addressing a problem of finding possibly intersecting sets, in a shared public signal setting. The approach involves first identifying set $A$ with the most elements, next set $B$ with the most elements, next set $C$ with the most elements, and so on, for almost surely obtaining set $(A_n)$ and $(B_n)$ for every natural number $n$. The shared public signal has the property of converging to a probability distribution over possibly intersecting elements from $A$ and $B$, for any choice of $S_1$ and $S_2$. The latter distribution has the property of being achieved as the result of independent and identically distributed samples, for a sufficiently large natural number $n$. We investigate the momentum dependence of the static magnetic susceptibility χ(q) within the paramagnetic phase of Heisenberg magnets, where it is found to be nonlinear in momentum. Specifically, a term proportional to q^2 is subleading to the leading 1/|q| dependence. By considering the small-q behavior, we determine the contribution of this subleading term and demonstrate that it impacts the critical exponents of the 2D Heisenberg model. We calculate the magnetization at finite temperatures and show that the correction to the leading power caused by this term is equivalent to a term proportional to q^2 within the leading Landau theory. By utilizing this result, we derive the modified critical exponents of the model and compare our findings to existing Monte Carlo data. Furthermore, we explore the potential generalization of this effect to other regions of momentum space and discuss its applicability to related models. Finally, we highlight the relevance of this effect to experimental observations on superfluid He-4 in a honeycomb lattice and discuss its possible interpretation. In particular, we show that the temperature dependence of the NMR relaxation rate and the disorder-sensitive peak in the magnetic response are both amendable to explanation using the established framework. Moreover, we highligh the lability of this effect to various modifications and potential generalizations to support a deeper understanding and investigation of this phenomenon. A crucial challenge in the study of rarefied gas dynamics lies in determining the steady-state solution of the Boltzmann equation efficiently. The conventional iteration method often achieves rapid convergence for highly rarefied systems but is severely hampered by prolonged and error-prone computations when applied to near-continuum flow regimes. Building on gas kinetic models, certain schemes like UGKS and its variants have notably improved efficiency, yet their iterations remain significantly higher than those in the highly rarefied domain. This paper proposes a comprehensive, iterative approach, dubbed the complete extension iteration scheme, which effectively integrates various existing UGKTs methods while allowing the simulation of near-continuum flow regimes with significantly reduced iterations and more accurate results. The scheme's efficacy is demonstrated through numerical examples, including 1D non-equilibrium processes, 2D shock structure, and 3D light gas cylinder simulations. The results show that the scheme can achieve a stable, accurate solution in dozens of iterations, even at gas densities close to that of continuum flow. This is a critical breakthrough, enabling researchers to model complex continuum flow phenomena using rarefied gas models. Furthermore, a theoretical justification is provided for the newly developed iteration method, revealing that the initial error in the UGKTs iteration is directly proportional to the collision term's magnitude. This insight explains why the scheme's performance improves in the non-equilibrium domain while iterations increase with gas density in near-equilibrium situations. Consequently, a new benchmark is established, setting a performance standard for the simulation of near-continuum flow regimes. Future work will focus on developing a more accurate and efficient version of the CEIS that reduces iterations even further, allowing for accurate solutions in fewer than a dozen iterations. The iterative approach may also be adapted for modeling and simulation of general gas flow phenomena. This work marks a significant step towards validating the UGKS model as a viable option for simulating various flow regimes, from highly rarefied to near-continuum flow regimes. The models and methods described in this research hold potential for applications in a wide range of gas dynamics phenomena. The work is relevant to various fluid dynamics and physics disciplines, including aerodynamics, aero-acoustics, and solid-state physics. The approaches and algorithms developed in this research may also be relevant to solving inverse problems in the context of rarefied gas dynamics. We introduce a concept for the p-divisibility transposition of the Fourier coefficients 
of Siegel modular forms. This concept complements the Wilton result on p-divisibility for the Ramanujan $\tau$-function. The proof approach is comparable to Elsholtz and Müller's method in Rational and Integral Points of Negata Pell's Equation. The key challenge was to determine the p-adic order of a specific invariant, namely $\prod_{x\mid\Delta_{f,h}}x^{2e(x)}$. To tackle this issue, we adopt the approach described by Anantharaman-Sathe in Modular Forms and Mass, focusing on the number of points satisfying $x\mid\Delta_{f,h}$ and adjusting the exponent $2e(x)$, which leads to the establishment of a key inequality for $N_{f,h}(p^{2})$. Determining similarity between structured data, especially graph structures, is a fundamental problem that has been addressed using various methods like the Gromov-Wasserstein distance. A key challenge in structured data is ensuring the privacy of the individual data points, which has led to the development of a new method. By applying local differential privacy to a Gromov-Wasserstein distance variant, we can determine the structured data discrepancy while protecting the integrity of the input graphs. Our method, which combines multiple privately-hashed graph samples, is based on an efficient Gromov-Wasserstein optimization algorithm and is proven to maintain accuracy and privacy. Furthermore, we have conducted a series of experiments to validate the performance of this method, which involves both synthetic and real-world datasets, including co-authorship networks and low-dimensional image embeddings. These experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in determining structured data similarity while preserving the privacy of the individual data points. And importantly, we revealed that publicly shared graph datasets are highly susceptible to IP leaks, which highlights the need for more robust privacy-preserving structed data approaches. We hope this method to provide a versatile solution for the privacy-preserving structured data, including graph and low-dimensional matrix datasets. As an intense laser beam traverses through plasma, forming a shock-like steepened edge, these mechanisms act in tandem. Secondly, stationary boundary electrons simultaneously experience the shock, being injected into the plasma bubble. This study investigates the capabilities of color information in individual black and white images captured from different angles, demonstrating through experimental results that color information in pointed views is resilient to changes in the viewing angle. As a consequence, it simplifies the task of automatically selecting the optimal color source in image colorization. Based on this observation, a novel image colorization technique has been developed that exclusively utilizes information from black and white image pairs, eliminating the need for the original colored images. Results from comprehensive experiments using seven benchmark datasets indicate that this approach consistently surpasses the performance of the top-ranked baselines that require access to colored data. To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, current methods that aim to improve recognition through commonalities among training examples for each category (prototypes) still struggle to perform effectively, especially when the training and testing sets have different sizes. Therefore, there is a need for a more effective representation of the commonality. This work proposes two innovative techniques to create category-level prototypes from limited information. The first method involves adjusting the commonality representation towards the average of the categories as a whole, while the second approach involves using a specialized neural network to create a more accurate representation. Compared to existing methods, our techniques yield better results and are simpler to compute, utilizing an ordinary matrix multiplication to calculate them. Experiments using image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed techniques. Both methods can be freely accessed on our GitHub repository.

Therefore, tracking cyclist data is essential to improving their safety by providing statistical evidence to support measures like enhanced infrastructure and safety enforcement. This study proposes a video-based method using deep learning to monitor cyclist safety. A novel approach utilizing a hybrid of fuzzy and ordinal regression is applied to analyze risks, taking into account a cyclist's profile and environmental factors. A large-scale dataset consisting of 104,622 instantaneously recorded situations has been created, along with corresponding safety video footage, to train the system. Results from extensive testing on 51,312 instances reveal an impressive 0.1563 RMSPE, significantly outperforming the existing benchmark. This innovative framework has the potential to contribute valuable information to city planners and safety officials, enhancing cyclist safety through data-driven decision making. As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as an intermediary between complicated mathematical formulas and applicable predictions through random sampling. Traditional techniques for generating samples from Gaussian process posterior calculations consider samples as separate draws from the distribution of process values at fixed points. This focus on distribution characteristics leads to efficient numerical methods. In this study, we shift our perspective and examine the collection of Gaussian process samples as a realization of the process itself, treated as a random field. This new perspective is tied to field theory, where field configurations represent samples from the process's distribution. We demonstrate that conditioning calculations amount to updating labeling constraints on the process's inherent structure, allowing us to derive the distribution of process values conditioned on sum and count observations. Additionally, we develop novel methods for making Gaussian process predictions without altering the process's distribution characteristics. Rather than sampling from process distributions at specific points, we propose sampling from process distributions within defined intervals. The resulting methods include an empirical technique backed by Monte Carlo simulations and theoretical analyses, accompanied by the open-source code for the developed methods. The proposed methods are evaluated using practical examples and the swissroll benchmark. Furthermore, we apply these methods to the problem of inferring dependencies within neural patterns in mice. The generated methods are beneficial not only for Gaussian process applications but also contribute to understanding the connection between Gaussian processes and field theory. The methods developed through field theory principles offer a basis for future research in machine learning, allowing for the exploration of potential connections between machine learning and theoretical physics. The main contribution of this study is the pathwise perspective on Gaussian processes, used to derive the distribution of process values conditioned on sum and count observations. The resulting methods for generating samples from Gaussian process posterior calculations demonstrate efficiency and alternative paradigms, accompanied by the open-source code for the developed methods. The study also leads to new insights on the relationship between Gaussian processes and field theory. The additional contribution stems from the application of the pathwise perspective to infer dependencies within neural patterns in mice associated with associated brain activity patterns. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, we propose a novel framework combining online learning techniques with memory-based reinforcement learning. By continuously selecting and replaying the most informative experiences, we reduce the gap between local and global optima. To determine the information value of individual past episodes, we employ a simplified model that accurately represents the underlying continuous-time Markov decision process. We then adapt an existing variance reduction method initially designed for parameter estimation in Markov processes, and apply it to extract the most valuable data from past optimization efforts. Through comprehensive simulations on various time-based Markov models, including multiple similar scenarios with varying properties, we demonstrate the proposed approach's ability to identify and replay the most informative episodes, resulting in significantly faster learning and higher long-term rewards. The effectiveness of this approach is substantiated through empirical results on a complex robotic task that involves maintaining balance on a moving platform. Furthermore, we provide theoretical justifications for the proposed technique, outlining conditions under which it is expected to reap the benefits of experience replay. Moreover, we derive lower and upper bounds for the optimal reward that can be achieved through replay, and discuss the proposed method's adaptation for exploration-exploitation trade-offs in reinforcement learning. The simplicity and flexibility of this approach make it suitable for a wide range of reinforcement and transfer learning applications. A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to investigate the dipole electric properties of molecular dimers in vacuum, with a focus on 66 test cases, using highly accurate CCSD(T) calculations. Ab-initio interactions involving dimers that satisfy specific criteria regarding distance, orientation, and potential electric fields have been studied. By drawing upon established models, a detailed framework has been established to categorize and calculate the dipole electric properties of these interactions. A critical evaluation has been carried out for the Calberla-Simon model, an effective approach for describing molecular dimers in electric fields. Furthermore, the dependence of certain molecular characteristics on electric fields has been examined through a helical perspective, highlighting significant conformational shifts in certain dimers. Finally, a detailed overview is provided of the dipole electric properties for all 66 test cases, accompanied by corresponding graphics. These results are available for download through the NERSC data repository at https://slatec.sc.matec.lu/index.php/electric-dipole-dipole/page. Upon completion of the calculations, a total of 132 distinct interactions involving vacuum-based dipole electric properties for the S66 dataset have been identified, along with a wealth of data for the 66 test cases. Pre-compiled data in tabular form are available at https://doi.org/10.5192/ijqc.2022.102.01, providing a basis for future research to leverage machine-learning methods for the prediction of molecular interactions in electric fields. Specifically, a database containing structured data for various molecular interactions in electric fields across 66 test cases is now accessible, enabling the development of accurate machine-learning models using fingerprint approaches. Using example fingerprint files (e.g., moleculenet, atomnet, and XGEMs), a detailed model has been trained to accurately predict the behavior of molecular interactions in electric fields. Performance metrics indicate that the trained model successfully reproduces the behavior of molecular interactions in electric fields (RMSE$_{\mathrm{train}}$ 0.00088, RMSE$_{\mathrm{val}}$ 0.00113, correlation coefficient 0.9992). Corresponding predictions for the 66 test cases are now available at https://slatec.sc.matec.lu/index.php/electric-dipole-dipole/preview/page. Upon completion of the training process, a machine-learning model was utilized to generate data for the 66 test cases, expanding the dataset to include molecular interactions in electric fields up to a 20\AA\ radius

The equation in question is a nonlinear diffusion equation involving a reaction term, which is governed by a minimally degenerate diffusion tensor. By introducing a suitable comparison function, we prove the comparison principle. Subsequently, we leverage H\"older's inequality and a formula for the second derivative of the distance function to establish the gradient estimates. The novelty of this research lies in its generalization of prior findings to minimally degenerate diffusion tensors. Specifically, we aim to expand upon existing work of Xiao and Zhang (2016), as well as Wang and Zhan (2018). Furthermore, we seek to rectify a mistake in the 2016 paper, which incorrectly omitted the nonnegative constraint in the diffusion tensor's Potentials. The research also aims to expand upon the findings of Xu, Zhang, and Zhu (2019), which themselves built upon the 2016 paper. Lastly, we aim to generalize prior applications of the Gaussian-type estimates to Ricci flow and the minimal surface equation, which were presented in the respective works of Li and Vanderbilt (1991) and Chen and Wong (1995). Long document retrieval has been a long-standing challenge in the field, despite recent advancements in model advancements, which often collapse under the high retrieval data pipeline's label noise conditions common in long documents. To tackle this issue, we explore an alternative approach that deviates from the conventional pipeline by employing random paragraph sampling and group-wise loss optimization. This reformulated retrieval data generation strategy is inspired by the token noise reduction technique commonly used in denoising pre-training of languages. In particular, we design two novel loss functions - paragraph-based hard mining and paragraph-based hybrid - to extract dense retrieval information from noisy labels, alongside our newly proposed BAGRANK model that incorporates these novel loss functions and pre-training of retrieval models. Our approach yields significant improvements, including top-of-the-line performance on the long document ranking task, achieving a MRR score of 0.6213, which surpasses the current state-of-the-art by 0.0511. The performance gains are largely due to our novel sampling strategy, group-wise loss optimization, and adaptive learning of retrieval models. These contributions not only advance the state-of-the-art on the long document ranking task but also shed light on the retrieval data generation process, revealing the noise inherent in long documents and laying the groundwork for novel loss functions and retrieval data generation methods. Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma column can serve as an efficient, non-destructive diagnostic tool for monitoring the dynamics of plasma wakefield acceleration experiments like the AWAKE project. This research examines how differences in the plasma's radial dimensions and off-center electron injection affect the resulting beam dynamics and betatron radiation spectra emitted by witness electron particles in proton-driven plasmas. By analyzing these dynamics, the study demonstrates the potential for uncovering initial conditions of witness electron bunches and discusses the applicability of this method to analyzing the seed electron bunch in AWAKE's proton self-modulation stage during Run 2. Additionally, the study develops a semi-analytical approach to predicting betatron radiation spectra based on a reduced radial model and solves the associated differential equation using a numerical method. This approach is further validated by comparing its results with those obtained from fully three-dimensional particle simulations. This method could be used in other research facilities, including those examining laser-plasma interactions and other accelerator platforms. Specifically, the work presents a comprehensive analysis of radiation spectra and corresponding witness electron bunch profiles across various scenarios and employs both semi-analytical and numerical modeling to explore these systems. The study is particularly relevant to AWAKE's proton self-modulation (PSM) stage during Run 2, and it proposes this betatron radiation spectroscopy as a promising tool for identifying the seed electron bunch in this stage. Additionally, the work offers a range of parameters and electron bunch configurations that could be explored in future research to achieve measurable betatron radiation in other systems, including that of laser-plasma interactions. This research proposes a novel method for analyzing the dynamics of charged particle beams using betatron radiation spectroscopy and demonstrates its applicability to real-world systems, namely the AWAKE experiment during its second run. The study is significant because it successfully applies a diagnostic tool (betatron radiation spectroscopy) to a complex system (AWAKE's proton self-modulation stage) and achieves results that validate both semi-analytical and numerical models of the system. The study is further distinguished by its use of multi-dimensional particle simulations to model the system and its outcomes. The work opens the door for using betatron radiation as a diagnostic tool in other research settings, including experiments on laser-plasma interactions and other accelerator platforms. The study is dedicated to exploring the betatron radiation spectra produced by witness electron particles in various systems, including those in proton-driven plasmas with focal boundaries and off-center electron injection, and it uses both semi-analytical models and numerical simulations to model these systems.

We focus on the variational inference task of minimizing a R\'enyi divergence regularized with a constraint in the context of exponential families, and introduce an improved moment-matching algorithm, incorporating a proximal optimization step. Leveraging the information-geometric connection between Bregman divergences and Kullback-Leibler divergences, the proposed algorithm is equivalent to a Bregman proximal gradient method, offering the flexibility to apply geometric insights from the approximation while using black-box stochastic updates. Building on this perspective, we provide rigorous theoretical justifications, including proof of objective monotonicity, convergence to stationary points or minima, and rates of convergence. These novel findings lead to the development of a flexible, robust, and efficient method, demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments. The findings indicate that this method can often outperform established techniques, particularly when dealing with complex distributions characterized by heavy-tailed or bimodal nature. The source code is freely accessible on GitHub under the name rdiv-minimization.

This study investigates how basic autonomous entities akin to Braitenberg vehicles can manifest complex, unpredictable movements. Employing a robot design proposed by Steve Mesburger and Alfred Hubler, we simulate their behavior in a two-dimensional space using a simple model based on three components, including a rear sensor, front sensor, and linear motor. Our analysis reveals substantial state space areas where the robot's motion is highly unpredictable. A new method for identifying chaotic behavior is introduced, based on a concept called "chaotic force", which quantifies the likelihood of chaotic behavior within a specified environment. This approach is used to compare the chaotic properties of different designs with varying lengths of movement. Additionally, we demonstrate that the environment itself can affect the robot's motion, causing phenomena such as the creation of patterns and transitions into chaotic behavior due to the presence of obstacles in the space. Ultimately, these findings are combined into a general theory of chaotic movement in autonomous entities. The research presents both numerical simulations and actual experiments using a robotic vehicle equipped with a camera and linear motor. The results show that the principles governing the behavior of simple autonomous entities lead to a diverse array of movement patterns even within a basic framework. The study highlights the importance of considering the dynamic relationships within autonomous systems, including their interaction with the environment. It also expands existing models by incorporating the role of shape and length in the behavior of simple autonomous entities. The findings have significant implications for both the theoretical understanding of autonomous systems and their practical application in terms of movement planning. Within the framework of a kinetic energy driven superconducting mechanism, the effect of impurities on the transport of quasiparticles in cuprate superconductors on different energy scales is investigated, using a modified Eilenberger theory for impure superconductors. A first-order phase transition is observed, similar to that in clean three-dimensional superconductors near the critical doping threshold, $d_p$. This complex behavior is characterized by distinct phases: a regime of thermal excitations below a certain temperature, $t_t < t_s$, and a region influenced by impurities above $t_s$. At temperatures below $t_s$, the superconducting density of states is enhanced near the Fermi level and as a result, the transverse microwave conductivity exhibits a sudden increase. The overall behavior of the microwave conductivity depends on the doping level and is only observable in underdoped samples. Moreover, the findings indicate that the phase transition is accompanied by a significant increase in the superconducting gap at absolute zero in a narrow range of doping around $d_p$. Furthermore, the research suggests that $d_p$ corresponds to a certain critical value of the doping parameter, which is found to be consistent with experimental observations for a particular family of cuprate superconductors. The study also presents a phase diagram for underdoped samples in the clean limit and demonstrates how the effects of impurities cause a shift in the phase transition compared to the clean limit. The researchers also investigated how the ratio of the superconducting gap at $t=s$ to the temperature varies in response to changes in doping for both clean and impure superconductors. The distinct effects of extended and point-like impurities on the superconducting mechanism are identified, and the dependence of the superconducting density of states and microwave conductivity on energy and temperature is analyzed, revealing a logarithmic correction due to the effects of extended impurities. The study's findings are compared to experimental data, and the research is related to other mechanisms of superconductivity in cuprate materials and other materials with non-$s$-wave superconducting symmetry. The study also paves the way for further exploration of the superconducting properties of other materials with non-$s$-wave superconducting symmetry, either in underdoped cuprates or in other materials with non-topological excitations. The study's conclusions are based on the validity of the kinetic energy driven superconducting mechanism and the effect of extended impurities on this mechanism, and the research is dependent on these assumptions. Our survival relies heavily on plants, and they're remarkably adept at adapting to changing environments through a process of gradual modification. Plants reacting to external stimuli offer a practical application of reinforcement learning. Our proposed benchmark, GrowSpace, involves simulating plant behavior using a space-colonization algorithm, mimicking real-world plant growth competition for resources. This simulated approach allows us to efficiently study plant movement and growth in a controlled manner, far surpassing physical experiments in terms of speed and efficiency. GrowSpace features an advanced interactive environment where agents can adapt over time by addressing key challenges such as movement, photosynthesis, root growth, and reproduction. This innovative benchmark includes a variety of complex tasks inspired by plant behavior, including migrating to escape freezing temperatures and adapting to shifting light patterns throughout the day. GrowSpace features a diverse, visually-appealing set of tasks designed to push the limits of reinforcement learning systems, focusing on both continuous control and multi-task learning. Our proposed benchmark includes a collection of challenging tasks inspired by plant behavior, demonstrating the difficulties associated with intrinsic motivation for learning and the importance of multi-task learning in solving complex problems. The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative is a global partnership that strives for consistency in extracting biomarkers from imaging data to enable efficient quantitative analysis. One significant hurdle in this field is the lack of widely accepted guidelines and standards for translating imaging data into high-throughput biomarkers, contributing to issues with study reproducibility. To address this challenge, IBSI is working to develop standardized terminology, test datasets, and metrics for validating image analysis and biomarker calculations, along with comprehensive guidelines for reporting results in high-throughput imaging studies. This effort focuses on computational biomarkers derived from imaging data, not clinical measurements or qualitative assessments. To accelerate progress, IBSI is offering open resources, including open-source code and open data, to facilitate rapid prototyping and collaboration in developing imaging biomarkers. This paper outlines IBSI's goals, the proposed standards, and recommended best practices for imaging data analysis and computational biomarker calculation, ultimately aiming to improve reproducibility and consistency in high-throughput imaging studies. This research describes the process of preparing the MORPH-II dataset comprising 55,134 images. Comprising diverse ethnic groups, this dataset presents a challenge for consistent lighting due to the extreme angles at which subjects were imaged. Consequently, extracts from this dataset necessitate pre-processing to achieve uniform illumination and remove obstructions. We utilized OpenCV to execute a comprehensive set of image pre-processing operations. These operations included filtering through various radii to remove noise, equalization of image brightness and colors, segmentation to isolate facial features, and size standardization. We found the pre-processing operations to be effective on most images, although difficulties arose in cases with noise, uneven lighting, occlusions, or abnormal head positions. We present a comprehensive methodology for image pre-processing utilizing OpenCV. While several techniques have been documented separately, this work consolidates the steps in a clear procedure. We aim to contribute this methodology to the academic community for seamless adaptation and extension. Furthermore, we intend to explore the integration of more sophisticated methods, such as deep learning, to augment the pre-processing pipeline. Building upon our previous research \cite{Liu:2019xhn}, we examine how the dynamics of a curvaton model can generate primordial black holes as a secondary consequence. In this model, the curvaton's potential has a negative slope at the instability point, and its oscillations lead to a high initial density that fosters black hole formation. A key difference between our analysis and other curvaton-based black hole studies lies in the investigation of the curvaton's evolution following the Big Bang, where we account for quantum effects that cause its effective potential to change over time. This development, combined with the instability inherent in the model, results in a significant, non-negligible density contribution made by the curvaton at the onset of inflation. As evidence of our findings, we show that parameters existing in our prior work lead to a high PBH production efficiency and a resulting abundance that aligns with observations from gamma-ray bursts. This alignment is especially pronounced when considering models with a run of $\Lambda_{CDM}$-like behavior, and a significant portion of the parameter space that satisfies primordial black hole requirements also satisfies curvaton-driven inflationary dynamics. Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is resolved through a differential game approach. This study explores various information network configurations, beginning with the 'leader-follower' model where each vehicle maintains a specific distance from the preceding one, and progressing to a network where the last vehicle dictates the distance for all preceding vehicles. A distinct scenario is also examined where the last vehicle determines the distance for the vehicles in front of it, but the preceding vehicles determine the distance for the vehicles directly behind them. A control algorithm is formulated for the vehicles using the proximity of the state trajectories and a unique metric called the 'algebraic Riccati matrix' to establish the optimal pre-planned trajectory for every vehicle, allowing for a coherent coordination of the vehicles within the platoon when only the vehicle at the end and its immediate followers have access to the surrounding vehicles' states, and when only the vehicle at the beginning and its immediate precursors have access to the surrounding vehicles' states. This research examines and compares the stability of the vehicles when arranged in a line and when arranged in a chain. A simulation is carried out and diverse analyses are conducted to illustrate and confirm the derived controls and stability assessments. Furthermore, the text discusses how these controllers and stability assessments can be used when there are random failures affecting the vehicles within the platoon. This work showcases that when there are only the vehicle at the end and its immediate followers having access to the surrounding vehicles' states, a vehicle platoon with a length of at least three can be stabilized, but when only the vehicle at the beginning and its immediate precursors have access to the surrounding vehicles' states, a vehicle platoon with a length of at least four is required. Additionally, the study demonstrates that when there are only the vehicle at the end and its immediate followers having access to the surrounding vehicles' states, a vehicle platoon with a length of at least five is required to be stable when arranged in a chain, and when only the vehicle at the beginning and its immediate precursors have access to the surrounding vehicles' states, a vehicle platoon with a length of at least seven is required to be stable when arranged in a chain. These findings outperform the previously established stability results. This work has been used to analyze and verify the stability of an AV platoon in a test drive, and the research has been presented to AV manufacturers. Future large-scale radio interferometers, aimed at detecting intermediate cosmological medium, may struggle with computing cross-correlations due to high computational demands. A proposed method calibrates and correlates each antenna's signal independently, reducing computation complexity to $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$. This is done by projecting data from a regular grid of antennas onto eigenvectors from a normal equation matrix, whose construction does not require inverse computations. The method remains scalable in hardware and software and is suitable for development into a real-time system. We analyze and discuss various factors that could impact this new system's performance, providing initial quantitative assessments. Simulations, based on noise and real data from the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope's prototype, show the feasibility of this approach, yielding adequate results with a few top correlated eigenvectors. Moreover, utilizing a distributed computing strategy could further decrease the computational burden. This new method is considered a strong candidate for development into a real-time system. For several decades, the Markowitz model has been the benchmark for portfolio allocation in practical applications. Its ability to diversify portfolios effectively relies on assuming independent stock prices and normal distribution. However, in real-world scenarios, these assumptions often breach the principles of financial systems. This paper proposes a novel method using deep learning to create a diverse portfolio from historical stock price data. Divergent Portfolios with Low Correlation (DPLC) aims to achieve the highest possible return for a given level of volatility. The framework involves two components: a deep neural network that transforms raw time series data into standardized signals, and a conditional generative adversarial network that generates optimal portfolios in the standardized domain while maintaining the corresponding correlations in the original data. By simulating the behavior of signals generated from the DPLC framework, we demonstrate significant improvements in diversification and performance compared to the Markowitz model. The framework's outputs produce a wide range of volatile portfolios with high returns and low correlations, and also identifies the underlying mechanisms driving stock price variations. The analysis reveals that the conditional generative adversarial network plays a crucial role in determining the correlation structure of the portfolio. The effectiveness of the DPLC framework is confirmed by testing various cases with different correlation structures. The study further explores the application of DPLC to diffusion models based on the wave net structure. The corresponding model is dubbed Dynamical Portfolio with Low Correlation (DYL). A groundbreaking method utilizing Bayesian neural networks enhances the accuracy of classifying gamma-ray sources. The study focuses on identifying Fermi-LAT blazar candidates, consisting of BL Lacertae objects and Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars. In contrast to traditional dense neural networks, Bayesian neural networks yield a dependable estimation of the network's prediction accuracy. The study investigates the similarities between conventional and Bayesian neural networks, along with the effect of data augmentation methods. It is discovered that Bayesian neural networks are ideal for classifying complex and time-sensitive astronomical data like blazars, which is typically subject to biases. Moreover, the research indicates that using Bayesian neural networks along with data augmentation methods can improve the classification of blazars with high precision, achieving an accuracy of over 95%. The study further demonstrates the reliability of the classification model by applying it to simulated datasets. The outcomes reveal that Bayesian neural networks are suitable for real-world applications, leading to a substantial improvement in the classification of blazars with high reliability classifying up to 95% for F8 and 87% for BL Lac. fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this content remains inaccessible to many users, 
despite available solutions that aim to reduce this form of exclusion. Our research 
involved surveying 258 social media users and interviewing 20 participants, with 7 of 
them having visual impairments, to understand their perceptions of online content 
and how support tools are utilized. Our analysis of the results reveals that 
platforms' efforts are inadequate, and that mainstream users often aren't aware 
of accessible practices. By exploring the views of end-users on accessible 
practices, barriers they face, and motivating factors, we also suggest further 
approaches to boost user engagement and raise awareness about accessibility.

accessibility through concrete, actionable suggestions. Our study was carried out 
in three areas: image, video, and GIF content. Each section presents specific 
strategies to make these types of content more accessible, as well as usage 
guidelines for each. Additionally, we offer direct access to our GIFs and images in 
alternative formats on specific platforms: Twitter, Vimeo, and Instagram. Our 
research aims to understand what mainstream users can do to improve

effectively communicated to social media platforms.

India achieved a groundbreaking success with the deployment and functioning of its initial space observatory, AstroSat, and must leverage its achievements and the knowledge gained to significantly enhance its future space telescope program. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Department of Space (DoS) should consider establishing a network of collaborative research and development (R&D) teams to introduce breakthrough technologies that could transform future space missions. A proposed mission called the Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST) is a cutting-edge satellite mission that could greatly expand our understanding of various astrophysical phenomena. This paper outlines the concept of the INSIST mission and provides a summary of the proposed mission details. The primary scientific objectives of INSIST are to conduct in-depth observations of extremely distant star-forming regions, using detailed ultraviolet (UV) spectral data to better understand their composition and properties. Furthermore, INSIST should also collect time-resolved spectroscopic data on various celestial objects, including white dwarfs, binary stars, binary systems containing neutron stars or black holes, comets, and asteroids. To achieve these objectives, the proposed INSIST satellite will carry a state-of-the-art spectroscopic telescope featuring a high-resolution grating and advanced light-sensitive CCDs to capture UV, visible, and near-infrared light in this wavelength range (180-320 nm). By operating at an altitude of around 770 km, the INSIST satellite will utilize its onboard light to trigger its camera, allowing the spacecraft to collect continuous spectroscopic data on various celestial objects, including both bright and faint sources. Following successful deployment from a rocket, the INSIST satellite will undertake a series of in-depth observations of two specific target regions: the Carina Nebula and star-forming regions in nearby galaxies. These initial scientific experiments will pave the way for a more extensive observation program and data collection in the coming years. However, before implementation, a small-scale technology demonstration satellite with significantly reduced mass and size is recommended to test and validate the INSIST concept. Following successful completion of this technological validation experiment, ISRO and DoS can proceed with the formalisation of a full-fledged space mission and associated resources, ensuring that India establishes a leading position in the development of advanced astronomical spectroscopic telescopes.

Moreover, the research expands upon these L-infinity estimates to encompass a broader category of parabolic Hessian equations. As a consequence, the L-infinity and Lp estimates for these equations can be derived. The two encoding tasks and the parsing task are linked by a joint embedding space, with the user question and database schema first reduced to a unified format, then mapped to a specific SQL syntax embedding, which is guided by a pre-trained model. In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating while avoiding potential collisions between robots is a significant challenge, largely due to the unpredictable movements of fellow robots. To tackle this, our method develops a data-driven strategy where each robot continually resolves a short-term optimization issue that incorporates safety restrictions based on an optimized risk analysis of close encounters between the agent and other robots. This optimized risk analysis ensures robustness against potential prediction inaccuracies by considering various possibilities and using observed data collected during execution to estimate likely outcomes. By leveraging duality theory from a specific optimization technique, our method transforms this analysis into a computationally feasible approach that applies broadly across distributed and decentralized scenarios, showcasing its value through an experiment involving navigation around obstacles in a crowded environment. Compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches, our method demonstrates equivalent or improved performance in both collision avoidance and optimization metrics, all while maintaining simplicity in both concept and implementation. To support and facilitate the use of this method, associated open-source code and simulations are publicly accessible. Our findings are validated through rigorous numerical analyses and extensive simulations that demonstrate robust performance against varying levels of execution uncertainty, both within and across systems. Ultimately, this method is shown to ensure safe navigation in complex multi-robot systems by adapting effectively to the highly uncertain and dynamic environment typical of such systems, as illustrated through a real-world application demonstrated in the accompanying video. Furthermore, this approach may be adapted to address other challenging real-world applications due to its broad scope and relevance, potentially including the safe navigation of drones and other autonomous vehicles. As such, this method has the potential to contribute significantly to the development of safe and reliable autonomous systems, particularly in the complex and rapidly evolving world of multi-robot systems, where collaboration and mobility are increasingly integral to modern society. Nevertheless, confusion networks present a more comprehensive alternative that can be utilized - although it demands a more intricate approach to understanding meaning.  We introduce an innovative technique to track the dialogue flow that directly takes confusion networks as input: it involves using an neural network that is designed to interpret the various interpretations of spoken words and then determining the likelihood of conditions in the dialogue given these interpretations and previous dialogue interactions.  We test this approach with data from the SDKT and S2DT frameworks and reveal that it achieves significantly better results compared to the method of picking the most likely interpretation.  Moreover, the method of choosing the top interpretations does not fare any better than the most likely one in our experiments - which suggests that the confusion network itself, rather than the method of selecting one interpretation over others, holds the key to enhancing dialogue tracking performance.  We further argue that the confusion network presents a valuable tool not only for the meaning of spoken words but also for capturing the complexity of the semantic structure of text by retaining the relative likelihoods of the various interpretations of words.  We discuss the benefits of utilizing confusion networks and propose strategies for training them in a way that the confusion network itself can be utilized for the meaning of spoken words.  We observed that the training loss associated with the meaning of spoken words through the network is uneven - with easier ones being easier and more difficult ones being difficult.  We observed significant improvement in the dialogue tracking performance with the most likely one, lesser improvements with the top two, a little less improvement with the top three and very little improvement with the top four - which indicates the importance of accurately modeling the complexity of the semantic structure of text for the meaning of spoken words. Our experiments show that the linear model achieves comparable results to pretraining followed by fine-tuning, and the neural network achieves comparable results to pretraining followed by transfer learning. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as heightened tensions and violent outcomes. Previous studies have developed hate speech classification methods, but they often overlook the need for transparency and the potential harm of replicating existing techniques. Moreover, existing approaches fail to address the significant role of non-verbal social cues in facilitating hate speech. To address these gaps, our research introduces a new, transparent framework for hate speech classification that incorporates multiple types of data, such as text and social network profile images. We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory networks eliminates oscillations and narrows the bistability range in excitatory networks. Conversely, in gap junction coupled networks, in-degree distribution variations shift the onset points for collective oscillations. Many of these results persist in networks of more biologically accurate neurons. Our work highlights the importance of considering degree distribution effects when interpreting synaptically coupled network behavior. Moreover, these findings provide foundational insights for future research on networks of more sophisticated neurons, including the effects of spatial interneuron placement and neuron model complexity. Ultimately, our work emphasizes the necessity of degree distribution investigations in neural network modeling. A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data by using a graph structure as its input and output. Recent research indicates that GNNs can be used in various applications beyond natural language processing. A major advantage of GNNs is their ability to improve performance through iterative computations, which can be beneficial in scenarios where graph size limitations apply. This study explores the utilization of GNNs in wireless communication systems as a decentralized inference tool. Specifically, we examine the effectiveness of GNNs in solving two inference problems - multiuser detection and symbol detection - in different communication systems, including single-input multiple-output and block-fading code division multiple access. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of GNNs against traditional methods, including maximum a posteriori and zero-forgetting detectors. Our findings reveal that GNNs can be an efficient solution for decentralized inference problems in communication systems and can deliver superior performance with reduced complexity compared to conventional approaches. Additionally, our analysis of the impact of network size on GNN performance shows that even with a small number of training data, GNNs can still achieve lower bit error rates than the conventional detectors. This study is particularly relevant to large-scale wireless communication systems where decentralized inference tools like GNNs can provide a significant performance advantage. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving enhanced results on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100. Two submersion functions from the plane to the line can be topologically equivalent, implying that the foliations defined by these functions also topologically equivalent, although the converse isn't necessarily true. We'll demonstrate this by proving that if two submersion functions have non-zero trace and their foliations share the same saddle points, then their topological equivalence implies the topological equivalence of their foliations. Conversely, we'll exhibit counterexamples to show that without these conditions, the implication doesn't hold. We'll also explore the relationship between the topological equivalence of submersion functions and the topological equivalence of their saddle points. Finally, we'll define a concept of pseudo-topological equivalence for nonsingular foliations and show its equivalence to the topological equivalence of their case-linear nonsingular foliations. This investigation raises questions about extending these results to other manifolds and to nonsmooth cases, which are explored in another study. We'll also offer some remarks on generic behaviors of case-linear nonsingular foliations in relation to their leaf curves. To support these findings, some visual aids have been included. The main content of this study was initially presented as two papers, one at a School of Geometry in Valparaíso, Chile, and the other at a Topological Foliation Days meeting in Barcelona, Spain. The current text supplements these events with additional information and corrects a mistake related to leaf curves that were originally described as nonsingular. Although this study primarily addresses topological equivalence, it also delves into several related mathematical structures, including bundle transformations for different levels, which are particularly relevant to nonsmooth cases that were studied in another context. We'll also outline some open challenges that arise from this investigation.
