We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating new conjectures that stem from numerical experiments. Moreover, we conduct a thorough examination of the Cheeger constant in relation to the other geometric attributes in the class of regular polygons. Additionally, we formulate two new conjectures one of which concerns a linear relationship between the Cheeger constant and the diameter in the context of convex polygons, and the other involves the Cheeger constant and inradius, applicable to all planar convex bodies. We also provide a numerical assessment of the optimal Cheeger constant for the unit disk. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the Cheeger constant and the perimeter/inradius ratio, valid for all planar convex bodies, along with formulating a sharper inequality for the Cheeger constant in terms of the minimum width. Finally, we introduce a result concerning sets with Cheeger constant proximity to 1/2. The developed techniques and achieved results have been implemented in a new Matlab tool called Cheeger. The user-friendly interface of Cheeger enables the computation of Cheeger constants, bar and sharp inequalities among geometric attributes for a wide range of bodies, including planar convex sets, polygons and polygons inscribed in circles. Furthermore, it allows the computation of minimum Cheeger constants among sets with fixed total number of points. The algorithm employs distance-based techniques suited for various dimensions and also includes conversion tools for transforming transformations of the unit disk into transformations of the unit ball. The underlying methods are analytical and many of them can be implemented manually, though Cheeger provides an efficient and user-friendly solution. The algorithm's complexity for computing the Cheeger constant in the worst case is O(n^2), although it is generally much faster for smaller inputs. The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-standard gadgets, traditionally unlinked to the internet, at an exponentially growing pace. Data security and user privacy concerns loom large over the IoT ecosystem, where vulnerable devices are frequently compromised by malicious actors due to inadequate encryption. We propose a lightweight encryption approach utilizing the XOR operator to swap messages and a user authentication mechanism based on the ECIES algorithm, which employs elliptic curves to offer increased security while suitable for resource-constrained devices, comparing well with existing similar methods in terms of performance, yet significantly enhancing the overall security of the IoT. Furthermore, ECIES proves more resilient to cryptanalysis than similar mechanisms, incorporating additional features, which include secure key exchange, protected data transmission, robust user authentication, and anti-replay measures, using the elliptic curve diffusion technique. We showcase the efficacy of this approach in the form of several IoT scenarios. We evaluate and assess the performance of this approach on two distinct devices, namely the Raspberry Pi 3 and the Bananapiper, revealing it to be highly suitable for a range of IoT applications. We intend this work to contribute significantly to ongoing discussions around the encryption requirements for IoT devices, with implications for manufacturers, researchers, and device designers. We anticipate an estimated storage expense of 20KB (16KB data + 4KB public key) per user per device, which we believe to be a reasonable trade-off for security in the IoT. The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum measurement settings influenced by numerous crucial decisions, namely, the choice of measurement time. Recent advances in cutting-edge quantum technology have made Ramsey measurements especially significant in the search for precise time measurements, including testing time variability in fundamental systems. Traditionally, the optimal experimental period for Ramsey measurements is set based on a predetermined plan, often requiring lengthy data collection. Nevertheless, we propose an innovative method that enables the adjustment of this critical time period in real-time, thereby maximizing the accuracy of the measurements. This approach allows us to repeat key measurements multiple times, using statistical analysis to continuously refine the parameters governing the experiment and ultimately enhance our understanding of the underlying time structure. Specifically, we have successfully incorporated a new experiment design that makes the most of available data, by minimizing the uncertainty associated with the key time parameter, $\Delta t$; it essentially asks how much a potential phase shift, induced by the elapsed time relative to the previous one, deviates from its average. We have also performed numerous simulations to test the efficiency of this approach, using a Ramsey sequence based on ultra-stable lasers, to demonstrate its potential for significant time resolution improvements. Furthermore, we have validated the method by applying it to ultra-fine ion measurements, achieving remarkable results. The results indicate that our approach can yield results comparable to those of the standard "maximum a posteriori" method, with uncertainties reaching as low as 4 femtoseconds without any relevant theoretical corrections. The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals as Morita equivalent $C^*$-algebras, we establish a topological representation of the T-duality transformation. In addition, we demonstrate the generation of non-commutative algebras from T-dualizable spaces, and provide explicit computations for one-dimensional and two-dimensional space cases, including torus bundles and Klein bottles. Furthermore, we prove the $C^*$-algebraic expression of a geometric condition previously defined by Zwiebach for consistent T-duality. To address the T-dualyability of twisted torus spaces efficiently, we develop a novel mathematical framework based on crossed products, offering a comprehensive analysis of twisted torus T-duality. Ultimately, we outline potential directions for future investigation.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is examined in both the global and local contexts. A key criterion, involving transmonotonicity with respect to an appropriate Lyapunov function, is identified to determine the uniqueness of the global stable manifold and its dimension. This condition also facilitates local characterization of the stable manifold, and it implies the existence of a local universal boundedness theorem for appropriate distance metrics. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that linear stability is a necessary and sufficient requirement for the uniqueness of the global stable manifold in smooth, discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity. This implies that systems meeting this linear stability criterion exhibit a prevalence of behavior types, including global stable cycles, non-global stable manifolds, and ultimately periodic orbits. This prevalence phenomenon persists even when systems are allowed to be perturbed and when systems are defined as piecewise smooth, subject to strong monotonicity in each piece. In addition, it is found that global cyclic stability, and consequently, cyclic prevalence, can occur only in cases where the system is globally ultimately mean-plausible and exhibits strong monotonicity. This result is based on previously established criteria for globally mean-plausible discrete-time systems, and it requires that the past and future behaviors of these systems be asymptotically Cauchy in the present. A non-trivial illustration of globally cyclically stable systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, and hence cyclically prevalent, is provided through a discrete-time version of the Lorenz-Metzger model describing chemical reactions involving three species. This model includes a nonlinear equation involving a 2 with a dependent variable, and it serves as an arena to investigate and analyze various dynamic behavior types in the vicinity of the universal attractor. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, and subject to appropriate conditions, or partially identifiable via a Lyapunov function, exhibit a prevalence of ultimately periodic orbits even when global stability is not guaranteed. This result is illustrated through the analysis of discrete-time systems describing chemical reactions involving three species in aautocatalytic processes involving three species. Finally, it is observed that systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, and including an isolated fixed point, and ultimately periodic orbits, and not all ultimately periodic, may exhibit a prevalence of behavior types, including non-global stable manifolds, and this is illustrated through the analysis of discrete-time versions of the Lorenz-Metzger and Rossler models describing chemical and physical processes, respectively. The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately constructing an ansatz using a shallow quantum circuit is key to successful implementation. Instead of employing fermionic-excitation evolutions to create ans\"atze, our approach utilizes qubit-excitation evolutions, which adhere to qubit commutation relations. By doing so, qubit excitation evolutions can be easily expressed using quantum circuits, such as qubit-excitation swap and controlled rotation gates, which are compatible with current quantum devices. Additionally, our method allows the generation of ans\"atze free from fermionic-excitation constraints, offering a broader spectrum for VQE circuit design. Although the circuit complexity differs, qubit-excitation evolutions can match the performance of fermionic-excitation evolutions in some cases, as shown in our numerical tests. To overcome circuit complexity, our proposal offers an adaptive strategy that dynamically allocates qubits and t-distributed exchangeable autoencoders to select evolutions. Furthermore, our approach enables the use of fermionic-excitation evolutions with modified qubit excitation limits, which significantly improves the performance. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms fermionic-excitation-based VQE with equivalent circuit complexity and matches the fermionic-excitation-based VQE using fermionic-swapping, opening the door for qubit-excitation-based VQE to accurately calculate molecular ground-state energies. With our approach, we successfully calculated molecular ground-state energies with high accuracy, such as the $-12.2418$ Hartree for hydrogen fluoride and the $-0.1205$ Hartree for lithium hydride. Our results highlight the potential of qubit-excitation-based VQE to successfully calculate molecular ground-state energies with current quantum devices. With proper circuit design, this method can accurately calculate ground-state energies for molecules with double bonds using a 5-qubit quantum computer, such as the IBM Frankfurt device. A key characteristic of deep generative models is the interaction of representation, its regularization, and the corresponding loss. Typically, model parameters are optimized to approximate data distribution through a trained generative model. However, this common approach is ambiguous, making interpretation of the learned representations challenging. In contrast, our approach involves directly finding the optimal representation itself by skipping the trained parameter estimation of the generator. Instead, we achieve representation maximization under regularized conditions by converting the objective function into a suitable form. This enables us to use optimization techniques that take advantage of the properties of auto-regressive generators and mean-field approximations to work efficiently even when using complex objectives. Examples include variational auto-encoders with elliptical Gaussian objectives, ELBO+KL, or other higher-order objectives. In our experiments, the results show that the optimization of the generative model is effective, leading to similar levels of performance as traditional approaches, but with a substantial improvement in efficiency, particularly in terms of time and memory. In addition, our semi-supervised experiments confirm that our approach can achieve accurate semi-supervised results. Ultimately, our approach allows for the evaluation of the impact of specific components of the model on the learned representations, providing valuable insights. In fact, our analysis reveals that generative models with a variational auto-encoder structure have inherent trade-offs between the utility of the prior and the utility of the conditional in generative models, which are learned simultaneously. Our calculations reveal that a stiff amplification of primordial fluctuations could explain the NANOGrav signal as a significant, low-frequency perturbation and simultaneously alleviate the "Hubble tension".  Notably, an energetic inflationary potential featuring periodic relaxations may create an expected phenomenon due to an unstable de Sitter spacetime, producing a distinct characteristic one-frequency component and a predictive wavelet.  Our analysis utilizes constraints based on both cosmic microwave background data and measurements from Advanced LIGO-Virgo's event catalog, both from 2015 and 2019. Incorporating further data from LISA is anticipated to boost our confidence in this result to 4 sigma. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the majority of unnatural expressions emitted by the unsupervised system can be mitigated through the implementation of a simple re-ranking model. A second version of this article is available online.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. A novel, computationally efficient algorithm is proposed in this paper to solve such optimization problems, combining two established methods - branch and bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II. A specific approach is devised to utilize non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II within the branch and bound framework, incorporating concepts of convergence and diversity. Convergence and diversity, two established convergence and diversity measures, are employed to determine feasible and infeasible regions, and obtain non-inferior solutions. Comprehensive tests were conducted using 12 test problems from the literature and COOLES tool, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm. A comparative analysis confirmed the superiority of the proposed algorithm over existing methods, highlighting its potential as a reliable alternative for solving multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems. We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties align with those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid. Furthermore, any classical connected Hausdorff Lie groupoid's universal translation map has a natural internal counterpart, making its image a subspace in the source map's image. Additionally, we define and establish the internalization of integral manifolds, with their corresponding Reynolds axiom, and show that this generalized notion applies to path spaces in accordance with the classical Reynolds' theorem. Moreover, we prove that if a Lie groupoid's translation is free and integral manifolds within its source map's image have natural flow lines originating from each point, then it fulfills the requirements for the latter to be an integral manifold. Finally, to facilitate Lie integration, we internally define and represent local 1-geodesics from a differential distribution, which, as it originates from a Lie algebroid, possesses an integral lift. An extended version of the Axler-Duistermaat-Hilbert theorem is derived, showing that any classical integral manifold, when additionally ensuring forward geodesic flow from a Lie algebroid's kernel, has a natural internalization that meets the desired lift criteria. Additionally, these lifted geodesics correspond to those of their classical counterparts. Lastly, as a direct application of these methods, we internally represent and prove the lifting and integration theorems for Lie algebroids. With these methods deemed "model-accurate," they result in novel and deeper understanding of connectedness, integration, and their related concepts in both classical and internal settings. Regrettably, these methods also imply that the traditional foundation of synthetic differential geometry is insufficient to support the complete integration of Lie groupoids. Consequently, a coarser, model-based approach to differentiation is introduced to rectify this shortcoming. With this approach, it becomes possible for the traditional foundation to be restored and for the lifting and integration theorems to be internally represented without the "model-accurate" limitation. An expanded version of the synthetic differential geometry is proposed, incorporating the model-based approach, which allows for a deeper understanding and more profound generalizations. Additionally, it enables the preservation of key results, specifically Reynolds' theorem and the lifted lifting and integration theorems,

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. The challenge here is to accurately pinpoint the relevant part of a sentence and assign the corresponding sentiment label. Although previous approaches have made significant progress, they still struggle with identifying sensitive topics such as politics and guns in sentimental contexts. The problem lies in distinguishing the sentiment intention behind words, which is crucial for aspect-oriented sentiment analysis. Therefore, we introduce a supervised pre-trained method that incorporates contrastive learning to uncover implicit sentiment patterns. Our novel method starts with a pre-training objective that separates word meanings from sentiment orientations, and then combines it with an aspect-aware contrastive learning objective, training the model to distinguish the context in which a word is used and its potential aspect-oriented sentiment influence. As a result, our approach not only improves the state-of-the-art performance on five datasets but also surpasses various strong baselines by a considerable margin of 3.9%. The extensive experiments and ablation study showcase the effectiveness of our method's design decisions. Notably, our method successfully identifies implicit sentiment patterns on analysis of the words 'gun' and 'police' in context. The data and code are publicly available on GitHub. This idea becomes practical due to the incorporation of a memory mechanism and a pre-trained neural network. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around the four encounters. These observations took place between the sun's radius and about 25 times the sun's radius, covering distances corresponding to different phases of the solar cycle. To initiate the solar wind, we used data from the Keck Institute for Space Promotion (KISP) and the New Horizons Near Earth Object Viewer, both showing that the energy flux follows expected patterns. Notably, it aligns with theoretical models and earlier space mission data. To better understand the statistical accuracy of these observations, we estimated the uncertainty associated with each data point, taking into consideration the speed and density variations. These calculations showed that the energy flux error margins were less than 10%, with most being much lower. To further refine the analysis, we used a two-step statistical method, first focusing on the data related to different solar latitudes and then averaging the results to cover the entire solar wind area. One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with their related entities within a given text. This task has received significant research attention, yet efforts focused on non-English languages remain largely underrepresented due to a lack of quality datasets required for model development and evaluation. To fill this gap, we have developed a Multilingual Event Extraction dataset featuring detailed annotation for over 50,000 event occurrences in eight diverse languages. This resource not only covers entities but also accurately marks the events and associated elements, enabling further analysis of multilingual event extraction through thorough experimentation. To facilitate future exploration, we have made the dataset accessible at https://motagusef.github.io/MEE-Dataset/. Our analysis used this new resource to compare different modeling approaches for event extraction, ultimately leading to the discovery of some intriguing results. It appears that incorporating named entity recognition as a precursor to IEE often fails to yield the desired results, with final extraction accuracy being comparable to directly applying extraction models to the text without any preprocessing. This counterintuitive outcome is likely attributed to the potential for high accuracy NER models to overfit when dealing with limited multilingual data. Consequently, we recommend employing either simple data processing like removing stop words or robust features derived from part-of-service discourse to successfully model event extraction in multiple languages. All our experimental data, including the NER comparison, has been made publicly available at https://motagusef.github.io/MEE-Experimentations/. This study was supported by the grant 2020N119X from the French National Research Agency as part of the SAGA3 project (https://sagaweb3.fr/). To our knowledge, the MEE dataset is the first comprehensive multilingual dataset of its kind, marking a significant step towards non-English event extraction model development and evaluation. This work has been publicly disclosed at the EACL 2021 workshop during the third TagME event. To facilitate model development and evaluation, we publicly provide access to our dataset at https://motagusef.github.io/MEE-Dataset/ and the experimental data at https://motagusef.github.io/MEE-Dataset/. This work has been publicly disclosed at the EACL 2021 workshop during the third TagME event. Our research incorporates a combination of automated and human review techniques to assess the optical activity surrounding 14 confirmed FRBs, employing highly sensitive instruments such as ATCA, GMRT, and VLA. We observed optical signals from FRBs 200228A and 201219A, but none from the other events. Our findings indicate that FRBs may exhibit significant variability in optical activity, and we discuss possible explanations for the lack of signals, including the suppression of optical flashes by interstellar medium, the brief duration of optical flashes, and the limitation of optical and radio wavelengths to probe FRBs. We examine various optical activity patterns and provide constraints on persistent optical activity for FRBs. Our analysis also considers the potential connection between FRBs and FRB-like events like GBTJ1409+5622 and GLEAM454, and the relationship between FRBs and AGES sources. Our research contributes to the understanding of FRB emissions in multiple areas, and we discuss future prospects for the study of FRBs in the optical realm. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a sequence of constrained optimization problems that are complex in nature. Our proposed algorithm, AskewSGD, is an efficient first-order method capable of solving these optimization problems by leveraging Workman's projection method. AskewSGD's performance is striking due to its distinct approach where the quantized weights are optimized in tandem, resulting in a significant reduction of computational complexity from the traditional O(K^3/2) to O(K^2) where K represents the number of layers in the network. Our experiments show that AskewSGD outperforms existing methods such as Straight-Through Estimation and Quantization Awareness by achieving better performance and training efficiency while maintaining stability and convergence of the quantized neural networks. Our findings also highlight that AskewSGD's training time can be substantially reduced by utilizing its annealed version that initially trains the full-bit model before progressing to the quantized version. The AskewSGD method achieves top-notch results in performance, efficiency, and stability compared to the existing state-of-the-art approaches. The implementation of the algorithm is made available on GitHub under the open-source license. In particular, our models are found to be either equivalent in quality or superior to the best reported results by these methods. AskewSGD's Quantized Neural Networks on CIFAR10 and CIFar100 exhibit high accuracy, with the results being consistent with our previous observations across a diverse range of datasets. Verifying facts using structured data is crucial for models like BERT, although they often struggle with this task. A potential solution is to use pre-existing tables stored in databases or the web that can confirm the validity of a statement. However, these tables frequently contain inaccurate information and conflicting opinions, making verification challenging. A novel model called TabFact, incorporating table decomposition, is proposed to enhance fact verification capabilities. TabFact consists of a BERT-based encoder and two separate modules that first determine the essential parts of a statement and then identify supporting rows in a table. By focusing exclusively on relevant table data, TabFact's performance is improved. It achieves a high degree of accuracy, surpassing the current best-achieving model by 21% and establishing a new state-of-the-art result for fact verification. To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used, which involves selecting prior samples that meet minimum efficiency requirements. A new study assesses the efficiency of these methods, as well as a novel technique called "step nest", which incorporates a novel method called "step accept". The analysis includes simulations and a real-world example from cosmology. The study also proposes a method to estimate uncertainty in model parameter values derived from this approach, and compares the results with other sampling methods in terms of convergence speed and accuracy. The study indicates that the "step accept" method often fails, but the "step reject" method exhibits superior performance in high-dimensional problems, particularly in terms of convergence speed. However, the study reveals that the obtained results may underestimate uncertainty in cosmology examples. The study also notes that the theoretical benefits of the "step reject" method do not always translate to improved agreement with actual data in high-dimensional problems. The study further reveals discrepancies between theoretical and practical performance, which may arise from the occurrence of local minima, which negatively affect the "step reject" method. The study includes a practical example from cosmology to illustrate these points. The study also compares the results with other sampling methods in terms of convergence speed and accuracy. The study indicates that the "step reject" method may not be suitable for analysis involving data tuning. The study recommends the use of methods with "posterior sampling" for such applications. The study also identifies an additional approach, the "step combination" method, which represents an average of the "step reject" and "step accept" methods. The study indicates that the "step combination" method performs well in high-dimensional problems and identifies a real-world example in cosmology that illustrates these points. The study also compares the results with other sampling methods in terms of convergence speed and accuracy. The study indicates that the "step combination" method may be the most suitable option for analysis in high-dimensional problems. The study also compares the results with other sampling methods in terms of agreement with actual data. Our work proves that any weighted network with a specific layout (or in fact any network with a limited maximum degree) can have its nodes labelled with a specific length of codes, allowing us to deduce the network's distances around any two given nodes, as long as we're given the label of a third node within our choice. This extends a previous study, which explored similar ideas in a specific type of network, by significantly increasing the allowed number of node failures. Additionally, our work highlights an interesting connection to linear codes in mathematics. We further support our findings by providing detailed examples of networks with varying parameters and by showing that our lower bound on the label length becomes close to optimal for networks with particularly high maximum degree. Lastly, we propose a simple approximation algorithm for assigning these labels in a specific type of network, when we're given a limited option for label length. In this research, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation, specifically at and around the point where dissipation triggers a phase transition. Around this transition, we observe complex, long-lasting time-dependent two-particle behavior that contrasts greatly from what is seen in the basic Bose-Hubbard model. By using a rotating frame and averaging methods, we create a detailed theory of this system's behavior, covering both amplitudes and phases of the time-dependent correlations. Our results, particularly concerning long-term behavior and phase shifts, are accurately confirmed through numerical simulations. Furthermore, we use techniques for condensate momentum distribution analysis to study how frequency correlations evolve over time and quantify this evolution. We also observe a significant, non-Gaussian frequency correlation in the time domain that persists even after the point where dissipation triggers a phase transition. This research provides a deeper understanding of two-particle behavior in driven, dissipative Bose systems. It sets the foundation for future studies of more complex many-particle systems. Our work uses two key analytical tools and confirms our predictions with detailed numerical simulations. A key outcome of this research is the analysis of a widespread assumption about quantum systems' behavior, which we tested in the context of interacting bosons under external driving and dissipation. Our investigation focuses on the behavior of superfluid Bose systems under external driving and dissipation, with the aim of understanding two-particle correlations in time and frequency. We explore these correlations in different phases of the open Bose-Hubbard model and develop a theoretical approach based on the underlying quantum mechanics of the system. Our research covers long-lasting quantum dynamics of open quantum systems and provides a new insight into the behavior of driven and dissipative Bose-Hubbard model. Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse set of loss functions, we've isolated specific aspects that dictate how these functions manipulate the positioning of feature pairs. Breaking down pair-wise gradient updates this way enables a deeper understanding of the dominant effects and allows for the development of a streamlined algorithm, ultimately leading to better image retrieval performance across datasets like CAR, CUB, and the Stanford Online Marketplace. This streamlined algorithm has been found to outperform a method with over 100 combinations of loss functions. Beyond this, we've found that our distinct gradient element identifiers as well as the dominant effect framework can be applied to other machine learning challenges. For instance, we've identified and leveraged this approach to resolve a data race issue in parallel sampling for neural networks. This work represents the first attempt to systematically analyze and standardize the numerous and varied pair-wise loss functions that have been proposed. By breaking these functions down into their fundamental components, we've been able to develop a unified understanding of the dominant effects, ultimately leading to the development of a method that outperforms a method with over 100 combinations of loss functions. Moreover, our work extends beyond this analysis to develop a framework for the simultaneous training of multiple neural networks in parallel, ultimately leading to a data-communications framework that overcomes a race condition issue. This framework has been tested and found to be successful in solving the dominant effect framework in advanced neural networks. In this context, we explore erasure-coded holographic quantum storage with a focus on achieving both scalability and strong quantum error correction capabilities. Our primary goal is to develop a new class of low-entropy, hyper-invariant holographic tensor networks that can effectively correct multiple, consecutive errors in qubits, using a MERAs-inspired approach. This approach involves merging restricted holographic algebraic quantum entanglement rings and utilizing variational Monte Carlo simulations to approximate the behavior of the resulting HETNs. Through numerical analysis, we demonstrate that HETNRs offer superior performance in suppressing power-law decay of correlations, when compared to invariant holographic tensor networks and MERA, at varying levels of specificity. Furthermore, we show that HETNRs can be transformed into HETNs by applying a type of refinement process, which also has applications in other contexts. Our work lays the groundwork for understanding and developing more complex, hyper-invariant holographic tensor networks that can efficiently correct multiple, consecutive errors in qubits. It also highlights the utility of the hyper-invariant property as a constraint for discovering new HTNs. Future research aims to identify additional HETNs with specified properties, with the ultimate goal of developing a code that can efficiently correct multiple, consecutive errors in qubits, using a few, low-energy qubits. Such a discovery could effectively pave the way for a practical, quantum storage technology in the near future. This research also raises questions about the relationship between the structure of HETNs and their ability to efficiently correct multiple, erasure errors, motivating further study in this area. Firstly, we know that low-entropy HETNs possess a desirable property in this regard. Secondly, we are able to illustrate the essential characteristics of high-entropy HETNs, including the density of states and the structure of their entanglement properties, based on our numerical findings. Thirdly, we are able to establish a connection between the hyper-invariant property and a new class of holographic tensor networks that can efficiently correct multiple, erasure errors, using a merlin-like approach. Last but not least, we have demonstrated that it is possible to transform any low-entropy HETNR into a new class of HETNs, with properties similar to those of mera and htn. Future research aims to understand the limitations of our approximation method and develop a more rigorous, a posteriori optimization procedure. Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson proposed using lattice regularization in 1974. This innovative use of lattice QCD enabled researchers to formally convert infinite sums into finite, grid-based calculations, allowing detailed analytical computations that had previously been infeasible. Lattice QCD became the primary tool for both short-distance phenomena (like perturbative QCD) and long-distance phenomena (like confinement and chiral symmetry breaking), albeit requiring numerical solutions via supercomputers. Initially, these solutions involved simple finite lattice dimensions, which lacked the insight to explore QCD's non-trivial behavior at finite temperatures and densities. In the non-perturbative regime, lattice QCD remains the primary method for exploring QCD's non-trivial behavior and behavior on complex grids. This article reviews key aspects of lattice QCD and its applications, particularly focusing on QCD's thermal phase and color supecconductivity in this context. An in-depth discussion of the formation of quarkial bound states, including dimensional continuation, is also provided. Furthermore, numerical results on dimensionally continued lattices involving the pion scattering length and an effective chiral Lagrangian model of QCD's phase diagram will be examined. These topics were originally explored in a series of lectures delivered at the Simons summer school on Quark-Gluon Plasmas and Cold Relativistic Matter in 2012. As such, the review primarily targets non-experts in lattice QCD, although some analytical and numerical lattice QCD background is assumed to be known. This work is primarily focused on QCD's behavior at finite temperatures and densities, and related numerical lattice results. A type of Gaussian process regression that accounts for the variability in data points, called heteroscedastic Gaussian process regression, is utilized to develop predictive models for the specific loads an offshore wind turbine will experience. The randomness inherent in turbulence and wave conditions makes the resulting loads more accurately described as probabilistic events rather than fixed values. The effect of these stochastic factors on the loads is also contingent on the actual environmental conditions present. The traditional method of using finite-element models to analyze loads has several drawbacks, including significant computational complexity and the need for extensive simulations to create an effective model. The proposed approach, called probabilistic surrogate modeling, leverages Gaussian process regression to transform the computationally intensive finite-element models into more efficient and accurate probabilistic models. The capability of this method to account for variability while simulating complex phenomena makes it suitable for a wide array of applications, not limited to offshore wind turbine surveillance systems. The technique was tested using data generated from the research study titled Full-Scale Testing of the IEA Offshore Wind Development Centre's Flexible Beta Preloaded Pitch Bears. The type of Gaussian process used in the model, called Bayesian Evidential Gaussian process, was determined through a statistical assessment that compared four distinct types of heteroscedastic Gaussian process regressions. The learned models were evaluated by comparing predicted and actual loads from the available data points, as well as through the analysis of the models' uncertainty and accuracy in handling unseen data points, a capability critical for informing maintenance decisions for complex systems like wind turbines. The results demonstrate that the proposed technique enables the rapid simulation of various what-if scenarios and the prediction of the probabilities associated with the occurrence of specific environmental conditions and resulting loads. However, available scenario datasets cannot be considered comprehensive due to the limitations of their creation methods. This paper presents a new dataset, SceNDD, which was developed utilizing an iterative and participative approach to gather a diverse set of scenarios. The process involved expert review and quantification of multiple factors, which enabled the creation of rich and complex driving scenarios. SceNDD, consisting of 2,534 scenarios and 28,661 segments, has been designed with the aim of augmenting the capabilities of existing datasets. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions. We establish a close relationship between this space and the deformation space of the metric itself, specifically showing that one is a subvariety of the other when the canonical connection is normal. Furthermore, we utilize Gauss-type operators to define a stable instanton and show that it minimizes the Kobayashi--Eisenberg obstructions, thereby potentially lifting the instanton to a compact G2-manifold. We prove the existence of such a stable instanton on a one-dimensional soliton when the canonical connection is normal. Moreover, we establish a close relationship between the deformation spaces of the metric and an instanton, specifically showing that one is a subvariety of the other for certain twisted connections. In addition, we prove the existence of non-abelian instantons on a one-dimensional soliton when the canonical connection is normal. Lastly, we relate our deformation theory to the holonomy of the Dirac operator and prove that the obstruction to a lifting vanishes when the Dirac operator has a finite-dimensional kernel. We apply these results to construct a 7-dimensional G2-manifold with a non-abelian instanton when the canonical connection is normal. Despite the efforts of public health agencies to slow down the outbreak, the virus continues to pose a significant threat.  In an attempt to mitigate this risk, governments have implemented strict social distancing measures, leading many individuals to self-isolate at home.  As part of the broader global response to the pandemic, the adoption of mobile contact tracing technology by citizens has been recommended by numerous health officials.  These systems, designed to help contain the spread of the virus, rely on location data and smartphone technology to identify individuals who have come into close contact with confirmed COVID-19 patients.  In Brazil, for example, the Coronav\'irus-SUS contact tracing app was developed in response to the pandemic by researchers at the University of S\~ao Paulo.  This research aims to investigate whether location data leaked from the Coronav\'irus-SUS app compromises users of the service, and whether anonymous usage is feasible to protect users' personal data.  To this end, we undertook computational experiments involving nearly one million users, testing the app's location leakage with fake and actual GPS data while exploring ways to protect users' privacy.  Our findings highlight the challenges of preserving location privacy, particularly when using aggregated location data.  They also validate the effectiveness of several proposed techniques, including the execution of pseudocode within application processing, the creation of a virtual device with reduced precision GPS data, and the application of anonymity techniques, which were found to provide significant location privacy guarantees.  These methodologies, along with the Coronav\'irus-SUS SEO tracker, are available for use in contact tracing COVID-19 cases and are expected to be pivotal in future contact tracing scenarios. The central nervous system's underlying physiological processes that drive conscious experiences have long been the focal point of research in neurophysics. This field studies the physical mechanisms underlying the brain and their connection to higher-order mental processes like perception, consciousness, and thought patterns. A recent paper applies the principles of quantum information theory to the underlying mechanisms of neural systems. We provide a detailed summary of this work, examining the concept of quantum information and its relevance to neural tissues, before discussing the challenges of modeling complex biological systems and the corresponding difficulties of quantifying information in such systems. The authors' approach to quantifying quantum information in brain activity is analyzed, and we explore the potential implications of this method, including the relevance of quantum mechanics in understanding central nervous system functions. We also consider alternative explanations for the observed phenomena and the significance of the generated theoretical models, before concluding that further research is needed to validate the proposed quantum model of neural systems. This leads us to a crucial question: what quantum features could simultaneously explain the prominent role of noise in biological systems as well as the high level of coherence observed in brain activity? A novel approach quantifying quantum information in brain activity could offer insights into the underlying processes of neural systems. The observed coherence and frequency patterns in brain activity may be the result of classical fluctuations combining to produce high non-trivial coherence in the brain. This leading idea is developed further into a theoretical model by drawing on the connection between quantum information theory and systems that display complexity and order. Utilizing the causal relationship between brain activity and its autocorrelation, we propose a theory where quantum information in brain activity originates from a self-organizing, inherently non-classical process. This process is driven by fluctuations that lead to high non-trivial coherence in the brain, offering a plausible explanation for the observed phenomenon. The concept of quantum information in brain activity poses significant challenges for classical modeling, and the proposed approach quantifies quantum information in brain activity by attributing it to self-organizing underlying fluctuations. This model suggests that quantum information in brain activity could originate from the inherent non-classical nature of neural systems, providing a theoretical framework for understanding the observed coherence in brain activity. The generated theory offers a new perspective on the underlying mechanisms driving conscious brain activities, and the proposed approach to quantifying quantum information in brain activity could offer insights into the quantum mechanics of neural systems. The developed model is general and can be applied to various frequency bands in brain activity, as well as to different scales of neural complexity. We introduce a novel integral kernel that relates to the Hurwitz zeta function and serves as an extension of the integral kernel linked to Ramanujan's identity. Additionally, we deduce various infinite families of identities comparable to Ramanujan's formula. The presented results can be seen as a combination of the methods employed by Ramanujan, who used the kernel related to the Riemann zeta function, and the advanced technology developed by Beukers, who generalized the kernel to the Hurwitz zeta function. Furthermore, we illustrate the connection to the Fourier analysis of lattice functions and the methods of the gamma reflection formula. Lastly, we present the general form of a more complex integral, one that encompasses the odd zeta values and incorporates the Hurwitz zeta function. This is achieved by generalizing the work of Ramanujan and Beukers. (This paper grew out of a summer project supported by the Boehringer Ingelheim Stiftung.)

Surprisingly, only 14% of users declined to use a PIN, indicating successful encouragement of PIN adoption in Signal. While enthusiastic users predominantly employed complex PINs saved in password managers, casual users mainly used simple numerical PINs. To strengthen the security of casual users, enhancing awareness about the true purpose of PINs and the features they offer could be beneficial. Furthermore, educating users on the benefits of using password managers and more secure characters for PINs (e.g., including special characters) could lead to an increase in enthusiastic users using more secure PINs. The survey also found that the majority of users did not consider their PINs to be sensitive, which may be due to the lack of awareness about the potential risks or a misunderstanding of the true purpose of PINs. Finally, by revising the introductory PIN anti-phishing message, users may become aware of the genuine PIN purpose, which could potentially increase the likelihood of casual users utilizing more secure methods to create their PINs. The complete survey results and all findings can be accessed at https://pinstudy.com. This technical note details the development of Gaussian quadrature rules designed to efficiently and precisely evaluate the integrals of products involving the solar irradiance function, as defined by ASTM standards, and user-defined smooth functions. The method's ability to produce accurate results with minimal evaluations is particularly beneficial when computing solar power integrals, often requiring a large number of integrand evaluations over a narrow interval near the current date. The corresponding MATLAB implementation, solar_gauss_quad, is also demonstrated. Furthermore, the associated algorithm has been successfully utilized in the development of the open-source MATLAB package Pymare, which is engaged in ongoing development and is intended to determine the power generated by arrays of solar panels by integrating various solar radiation models. The method has also been successfully applied in the open-source C code C_Solar_Gauss_Quad, which is the C equivalent of solar_gauss_quad, and is currently used in the development of the solar simulation tool SolTran, which is available on GitHub under the license GPL-3.0. The described techniques have also been incorporated into more recent versions of Pymare, version 0.8.2 and later, and SolTran, version 1.3 and later. The described work in C_Solar_Gauss_Quad and solar_gauss_quad was supported by the grant number DE-SC0011817. The research was conducted at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under the following contract number: FTA-LLNL-192319 and contract number: FTA-LLNL-74000. The work is related to a companion publication for Pymare. The method's evaluation can be visualized through the interactive error bounds tool, error_bounds, which is available on GitHub. The work is the completion of a graduate thesis that was initially posted as an arXiv preprint. The method was also presented at an international conference, which is documented through the associated presentation available on GitHub. The work is intended to promote the use of the open-source tools Pymare, C_Solar_Sparsescat, solar_gauss_quad, and SolTran, which provide efficient and accurate numerical solutions to the solar problem, as well as the open-source solar models solar_sersqueez, solar_stoag, solar_alma, solar_alma2, solar_everitt, solar_pseudo, and solar_psi, and the open-source verification and testing tools error_bounds and solar_test_set. The curvature, or Hessian, plays a vital role in understanding how machine learning models behave. Although the Hessian provides the most detailed analysis, its computationally expensive nature has led to it being largely restricted due to its $O(n^3)$ complexity, where n represents the number of model parameters. Previous studies have attempted to mitigate this cost by developing approximate solutions, resulting in either a linear solver or a finite-differencing method, which incur a linear or sampling cost of $O(n^2)$, resulting in a significant increase in computation time. A new study proposes the ViViT model, which takes advantage of the low-rank properties of the Hessian through the Gauss-Newton matrix, allowing for efficient computation. This results in a computational cost of $O(nr^2)$, where r represents the rank. This model also offers an advantage in terms of sampling cost, which is reduced to $O(r^3)$ from $O(n^2)$, and achieves similar accuracy with fewer parameters than the Hessian, offering a new optimization technique and theoretical analysis of the ViViT model. Future applications of this model lie in its behavior analysis, specifically for vision models. This research was inspired by the findings of 2022's NeurIPS study "Visualizing the Hessian" and this paper of 2023's CVPR, and is now being publicly shared on GitHub at https://github.com/alexeygafos/vi-vit. A related video can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KX9U7_9s4mI. The research was conducted at the University of Cambridge's Centre for Data Science Surrogate project. Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, affecting how we interpret these inanimate objects. As inanimate objects share grammatical gender, word representations often reflect this linking property. This study investigates how inanimate objects' word representations are impacted in Spanish. We examine whether inanimate objects' word embeddings embody their assigned gender and discover that, in general, they do not, although we also identify exceptions where this linking property is evident. Furthermore, our analysis shows that this effect is more pronounced when we examine the entire Spanish Wikipedia corpus as well as when we consider only human-created texts. We conclude that this interaction underscores the significance of considering a sentence's author when investigating linguistic influences on language models. Our findings and code are available online. We discuss possible explanations for this effect and their implications. While current language models mirror a sentence's author's perspectives and preferences, we still comprehend very little about the mechanisms driving these interactions. More research is needed to delve into the relationship between language models' outputs and human creators' intentions. [additional information from reviewer] Relatedly, it has been discovered that word embeddings learned by neural language models pick up on an author's stance due to the bias introduced by the corpus' creator, leading to embeddings that mirror human perspectives and intentions. This study explores another aspect of human language and models, namely how inanimate objects' word representations are impacted in a language that attributes gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. We examine whether inanimate objects' word embeddings in Spanish embody their assigned gender and discover that, in general, they do not, although we also identify exceptions where this linking property is evident. We conclude that this interaction underscores the significance of considering a sentence's author when investigating linguistic influences on language models. We demonstrate that this effect is due to human creativity and creativity patterns. This method, which doesn't require training, relies on categorization instead of the object's 3D geometry of its material properties and instead utilizes a self-supervised approach to remove clutter from 3D point cloud data. The results we obtained are significantly better than what we could achieve through a baseline approach that tried to categorize and pose objects simultaneously from scratch. Moreover, we found that our method's performance improves over time the more it's trained. We tested our method in multiple categories including birds, soccer players and surfboards to show its generalizability. The code and method is available at https://github.com/islaiq/zero-shot-pose. Predicting short-term traffic is a crucial issue for modern traffic systems. However, existing forecasting models are often hindered by their limitations in accommodating vast amounts of data and dealing with temporal dependencies. For tackling these challenges, this paper introduces a novel approach utilizing traffic graphs based on nodes and edges to describe spatial and temporal patterns in traffic networks. Furthermore, this paper incorporates two advanced techniques: Graph Neural Networks and Retrieval-based Methods, to effectively learn representations for traffic nodes and to efficiently predict traffic speeds based on similar historical instances. The empirical results demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of this method, and it compares favorably with established traffic forecasting baselines. The proposed approach has been successfully applied in a real-world traffic forecasting system in Chengdu, China and is now used in practice. It is expected that this method could inspire the development of novel machine learning applications in transportation systems. This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, utilizing intervention-based data. VACA models key concepts in the causal representation learning framework, including node in-measurements, node out-measurements, and edge in-measurements. By leveraging variational inference, VACA provides an efficient approach for performing counterfactions inference tasks. VACA's performance is evaluated through synthetic data simulations, which demonstrate its ability to effectively model varied causal graphs and yield clean and normally-distributed data. Furthermore, VACA's constraints yield perfectly aligned causal query results, even in the presence of noisy data. VACA's source code is publicly available.

State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits per second. This significant data throughput necessitates real-time processing capabilities to facilitate both real-time operations and offline analyses within hours. Real-time operating systems like the Correlator Common Engine (CCE) manage this by coordinating various stages of the data processing pipeline. According to recent surveys, the LOFAR data processing pipeline can successfully process up to 80% of its capacity in real-time. This study presents the development of the REAL-time Transient Acquisition backend (REALTA) at the LOFAR Irish station. REALTA utilizes the CCE and Irish station's first-generation hardware to detect transient radio signals in the 10-150 MHz frequency range with a 256-second integration time and a 5-minute bandwidth. In a real-time environment, REALTA can acquire a 10-hour subband with a 1 minute time-step and a 20-hour subband with a 2 minute time-step with the Irish station's 16 antennes. REALTA can also process a 20-hour subband with a 5 minute time-step using the LOFAR's 119 antennes. This work outlines the data processing pipeline and presents the initial findings from its May-June 2020 observations, which include 284 hours of 10-hour subband time-series data and a large event catalog with periodicities and durations. REALTA highlights the limitations of the LOFAR data processing pipeline in reaching its full potential due to hardware limitations. Upcoming upgrades and improvements are discussed, which will boost the performance of the data processing pipeline and unlock new scientific applications. This article is submitted for the LOFAR Data Analysis Cookbook series. The data and analysis software developed for REALTA are maintained in the NUI Galway repository at https://github.com/. In recent years, advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence have driven significant growth in photonics research, leading to cutting-edge photonic systems including traditional waveguides, nanoantennas, and metasurfaces. The innovative application of AI-driven methodologies empowers the development of smart photonic devices rooted in fundamental light-matter interaction principles. Artificial intelligence and machine learning concepts are rapidly transforming the underlying physics of light, offering effective tools to investigate metaphotonics, which relies on optically-induced resonances. We now present an overview of metaphotonics, along with a concise summary of the core principles of machine learning, exemplified through its applications to metasystems and metasurfaces. We will delve into the theoretical foundations of deep learning and its computational counterpart, with a special focus on variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and neural networks, whose structured frameworks enable exploration of complex photonic systems when analytical methods fail. We will discuss how machine learning can facilitate the design and analysis of metasurfaces and metasystems, including traditional waveguides, nanoantennas, and optically-induced resonances, leading to the development of intelligent photonic circuits that model real-world data. We will examine the underlying principles of classification methods and clustering, applying them to real-world photonic systems and data sets. We will examine the feasibility of estimating physical parameters through data-driven inverse problems. We will discuss the challenges and potential future research paths that will shape the development of intelligent metaphotonics in photonic systems, metasystems, and metasurfaces. Lastly, we will delve into the broader societal implications of our work, highlighting opportunities to advance research through collaborative efforts that bridge physics and computer science. The integration of intelligent metaphotonics and machine learning is transforming the landscape of photonic research, offering promising avenues to tackle real-world challenges in biomedical imaging, communication, and sensing. The high-risk, high-reward nature of filmmaking means predicting which movies will be profitable at the box office has become a daunting task. In an effort to minimize financial losses, major film producers and studios continuously seek a more reliable method for estimating movie revenue before making an investment. Researchers in this field face an additional hurdle: the scarcity of a large, contemporary dataset to work with. In an attempt to fill this void, our team has developed a more comprehensive, richer dataset collected from IMDb, which is designed to facilitate research and analysis. By aggregating summary data from over 7.5 million titles and detailed information for more than 200,000 films, our compiled dataset provides an indispensable resource for researchers and data analysts. Utilizing various statistical analysis techniques, our team performed extensive feature comparisons between successful and low-revenue films. By identifying key attributes like the number of awards, attachments, and ore-seeds, which significantly impact a movie's financial performance, our results also revealed the most profitable genres and targeted demographics for the film industry to consider in their decision-making processes. As a direct outcome of this investigation, our team developed and evaluated a suite of predictive models, including Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest-Neighbors, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XG-Boost, which demonstrated moderate success in accurately classifying film revenue as either successful or unsuccessful. Although the predictive models require further refinement, our study has provided a more in-depth, data-driven understanding of the key factors influencing box office revenue. In particular, our analysis underscored the importance of movie awards as a key revenue predictor. While this investigation was not focused on estimating film revenue quantitatively, our results provided a qualitative insight into the critical attributes and demographics for the film industry to consider in their decision-making processes. As a natural extension of this study, our team is considering the application of Machine Learning in Content Recommendation. By exploring this area, our goal is to develop an intelligent system to recommend content to users based on their unique preferences, similar to personalized news feeds or product suggestions provided by online retailers. Ultimately, this study is an essential step towards developing an advanced system to predict movie revenue at an increased level of accuracy. Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be explained by distinct physical mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the underlying particles, magnetic fields, and radiation interactions. This research explores inverse external Compton scattering of big blue bumps in blazars and investigates the effects of varying magnetic fields and radiation patterns in multiple relativistic jets on polarization and spectral patterns. Our findings demonstrate that polarization in UV and X-ray frequencies should be more prominent at lower energy levels and decrease as energy increases, contradicting previous predictions of increasing polarization in X-rays. However, the polarization in UV and X-ray frequencies could be suppressed by a strong external radiation field in the jet, suppressing polarization in these frequencies. If the polarization in UV frequencies persists and eventually increases at higher X-ray frequencies, it could indicate a substantial reduction in magnetic fields or multiple relativistic jets targeting the observer. A thorough theoretical analysis of spectral and polarization patterns in several blazars supports the hypothesis of multiple relativistic jets targeting the observer. This research and its associated modeling suggest a new theoretical explanation for a common feature in blazar spectra. This explanation is distinct from the typical theoretical explanation of this feature, which is often attributed to the blazar zone model. A Monte-Carlo program called MAPPIES, which incorporates all Compton scattering processes, was used in this research. A detailed description of this program and its application in this research is included in this paper. Additionally, the program and data used in this research is publicly available for the scientific community. To develop optimal methods for identifying identical pure states with perfect accuracy using limited resources, researchers focus on finding the most cost-effective strategy. In this study, researchers consider a scenario where identical pure states can be assumed to be symmetric, known as SPS states. In this setting, it's shown that distinguishing multiple SPS states using various quantum measurements is a problem that can be mathematically expressed as an optimization process. These optimal methods are found for the case of distinguishing two SPS states, with results indicating that performing measurements that distinguish different components along the same axis is most effective. Notably, it's found that distinguishing three SPS states with high probability requires at least 1035 antilevel measurements, a requirement that also applies to ideal state tomography. These results are then generalized to the scenario of identifying N identical SPS states. In this setting, it's found that distinguishing N SPS states with certainty demands at least N(1+1/N)² antilevel measurements. Researchers from the NANOGrav, Parkes, European, and International Pulsar Timing Array Collaborations have discovered strong evidence suggesting a single source for background noise observed across multiple frequency ranges, which might be a common signal seen in the NANOGrav spectrum. The newly identified source could potentially be a major candidate explaining the gravitational wave excess observed in the NANOGrav Dataset I. If the signal's origin is linked to the early Universe, it could be attributed to the cosmic stochastic process caused by inflationary gravitational waves or primordial magnetic fields. A new study has found that a previously studied model where primordial magnetic fields were created can both match the characteristics of the signal observed in pulsar observations and account for the gravitational wave excess seen in NANOGrav Dataset I. The proposed model also has the potential to be further tested by future research using a variety of astrophysical and cosmological data sources. Consequently, there are several methods that can be employed to validate or reject this hypothesis. These include: analyzing the polarization properties of extremely powerful radio waves, studying the effects of intermediate-scale magnetic fields on galaxy clusters, examining the impact of magnetic fields on the formation of galaxies and stars within galaxy clusters, investigating the impact of magnetic fields on galaxy scale, evaluating data from the Binary Black Hole searches by LIGO and Virgo, and verifying findings related to the effects of primordial magnetic fields on the cosmic microwave background. Verification of the signal's origin would provide new insights into the fundamental laws governing gravity and electromagnetism during the early universe. Furthermore, researchers could utilize this model to estimate key parameters including the square of the magnetic field's fine structure constant and the magnetic energy density compared to dark energy. Verification of the signal's origin would also enable scientists to measure these parameters with greater accuracy. The estimated values would be $\Lambda_A\sim(4-40) \times 10^{-9}$ and $\Omega_B\sim(4-40) \times 10^{-6}$. Furthermore, a new set of extragalactic studies could put constraints on the magnetic field's coherence length, leading to the potential discovery of a new coherent magnetic field scale. Verification of the signal's origin would also allow scientists to derive lower bounds of $L_{\rm B}>10^{23}$ or $f_{10} > 0.4$, where $L_B$ is the coherence length of the magnetic field and $f_{10}$ is the frequency of a magnetic wave in units of 10 Hz. Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest for the research community due to its various potential uses. A significant feature of commercial plenoptic cameras, the lenslet array captures spatial and angular light information in a single exposure. However, the resulting high data dimensionality, which contributes to light field capabilities, poses a significant hurdle to widespread adoption. To mitigate this, there is an increasing demand for efficient light field image compression. This paper presents a novel image-based compression method, where the spatial structure of a light field is represented by paired image slices, referred to as views. An effective model is developed to predict a set of views from a reference view, and the coherence of spatial information is leveraged to optimize compression of 4x4 light field arrays with 9 views and 16 pixels per view. We compare the performance of our model with the current state-of-the-art approaches in both theoretical and practical aspects. Furthermore, a reference dataset and the related code are provided for reference purposes. We believe that our proposed model holds considerable potential for future light field applications. interactive and non-interactive, prevail where topics/oracles play a crucial role 
in facilitating and supporting translations, respectively. This research delves into 
how these models benefit from query-example supplementation. We've found a positive 
correlation between performance gains and the number of examples used. Both models 
achieve similar optimal outcomes when using multiple examples, yet they reach this 
optimal point at different data usage rates. This suggests that using a significant 
amount of data is more beneficial for non-interactive models, whereas a larger 
proportion of successful data transfers (i/i+1) favors interactive models. Furthermore, 
we've observed that, in comparison to existing baselines, query-example supplementation can bring about substantial performance improvements, up to 33%. This 
resulting enhancement is consistent across various levels of translation quality.

performance threshold in CLIR without embeddings, surpassing state-of-the-art 
single-vector-based and hybrid CLIR models. This project's findings are available at https://github.com/asharakeh/clir-sup. An associated paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/submit/2104.06530. The urgent need for comprehensive health and demographic reports has driven an increased focus on geographic analysis, research, and modeling. This study compares the effectiveness of different methods for estimating health and demographic indicators at a small-scale in low and middle-income nations. It particularly examines the advantages and disadvantages of several design-based and model-based approaches using synthetic data created from survey results of fertility rates in five countries. The comparisons consider multiple scenario types, including varying levels of survey data, household dispersion, and data accuracy. The findings suggest that a model-based approach can produce accurate estimates when the relevant survey data is abundant and the data is dispersed evenly across the area in question. However, it is essential to account for survey data underestimation when reporting aggregate, rather than detailed, estimates. The study provides practical recommendations for implementing this method in real-world situations and the potential next steps for further refinement. A initial study demonstrated a potential for significant profit without risk by employing a straightforward method for determining the optimal amount to bet, although this approach assumes the availability of real-time outcome probability updates. Building upon this previous work, we have devised a more streamlined technique for estimating optimal betting amounts that operates without continuous probability updates. Additionally, we have explored alternative methods for calculating optimal bets that are resistant to adverse consequences when the assumption of real-time probability updates is invalid. A mathematical examination of these approaches in the context of experiments with continuous variable quantum properties revealed distinct long-term results, highlighting the inherent trade-off between profit and risk in real-world applications. Notably, the optimal return and risk factors can be quantified by two specific parameters, known as the 'churn rate' and the 'growth rate', which are influenced by various factors. A theoretical model based on these parameters was developed to minimize risk while maximizing profit in the context of bell test experiments, with results indicating that the proposed model is both practical and efficient. We propose a supersymmetric expansion of a basic $U(1)_X$ model with a new, $Z_2$ symmetric property, where the lightest particle with this symmetry serves as dark matter. In this model, the $U(1)_X$ gauge group symmetry is broken at a very high energy, while all other supersymmetric particles have very low masses, and right-handed neutrinos are Majorana-type. This combination leads to a variety of interesting phenomena, including superpartner pair production, massive neutrinos, and dark matter that can be studied with existing facilities. We analyze a selection of variables that can help distinguish this model from other theories, including collider data on neutrinos and cosmological information on dark matter. A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been introduced in the form of Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD). This method presents a significant improvement by circumventing the necessity for the phase locking technique. Instead, our approach categorizes time into two distinct frameworks: reference frames and quantum frames. Reference frames serve as a basis for establishing a shared secret, while quantum frames facilitate the generation of this secret. To achieve phase alignment, reference frames are utilized to announce a set of reference angles within a standardized range. Subsequent data exchange occurs within quantum frames, facilitating the generation and analysis of the secret key. By eliminating phase locking and introducing a simplified framing system, our TF-QKD method demonstrates the capacity for high-speed and long-distance communication. Furthermore, our experimental outcomes on a 50 km single-mode fiber show key generation rates exceeding 320 kb/s under the low rate of 1 megahertz. This method successfully achieves fast and long-distance communication. Moreover, our approach allows for the single photon source issue to be partially alleviated, and the conditional density of states is thoroughly examined. Finally, our scheme is adaptable to distance variation and can be accompanied by a wide-range distortion correction method, ultimately resulting in substantial improvement of the distance efficiency, up to 400 km. The scheme may also serve as a foundation for multi-point TF-QKD networks. The experimental outcomes and analytical findings both validate the feasibility and efficiency of our proposed method.
