Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this limitation by training on a set of base categories, enabling detection of unseen object types. However, base-category data is often scarce in practical scenarios. To address this issue, we propose generating pseudo annotations for both objects and non-objects using pre-trained feature extractors, effectively utilizing readily available image collections. By training on these pseudo annotations, we demonstrate that the proposed method can accurately identify both known and unknown objects from a range of categories. Experimentation shows that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving open-vocabulary performance on the COCO and ImageNet-21K benchmark datasets. Furthermore, using human validation to validate our pseudo annotations reveals that a small fraction of these annotations (validated objects) suffices to achieve nearly perfect performance. Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing weights among different child models is a popular strategy. However, due to interference from other models, there is often a weak correlation between the predicted accuracy and the actual performance of the child models. This interference issue significantly impacts the quality of the top-ranked models. To address this problem, we investigate the source of the interference and propose a novel training approach called through-training. Unlike conventional one-step per model training, through-training enables throughput-optimized models to be trained simultaneously in thousands of iterations. This allows the models to distinguish more subtle features of the data and strengthen their internal representations. We evaluate the effectiveness of through-training by comparing it with residual search, a renowned algorithm, on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 benchmarks. The experimental results demonstrate that through-training yields top-ranked models with higher test accuracy and more consistent design patterns. A notable feature of the through-trained models is their reduced variance in classification errors when tested across multiple sample datasets. This result has significant implications for sample-efficient NAS, as it demonstrates NAS's potential to excel in this area. Ultimately, the through-trained model with the highest test accuracy on CIFAR-10 (97.16%) surpasses the state-of-the-art NAS method, achieving performance comparable to hand-designed models while surpassing residual search's results by 6%. The source code for through-training has been made publicly available at https://github.com/longxinwang/throughtag. This code has been independently replicated and verified by multiple users. As of February 2023, our through-trained model with the test accuracy of 97.16% on CIFAR-10 remains one of the top-performing NAS methods until the date of this writing. Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively utilized method that helps gauge machine translation efficiency, negotiate translation contracts, and evaluates human translator proficiency.  Despite its importance, little research exists using quantitative methods to determine TQA's reliability.  In our investigation, we examine TQA as a multi-component process using complex system physics and Bayesian analysis, with the aim of exploring the concept of reliability.  Employing Translated SRL's error-annotated translation evaluations, we develop two Bayesian models to investigate how various elements of TQA impact reliability.  We discover through statistical analysis that translational proficiency, post-editing intensity, and various evaluation score relationships are consistently significant.  Moreover, we reveal that high-proficiency translators require less intense post-editing, that post-editing intensity influences score distributions, and that the most impactful aspect in determining reliability is the reliability of the translator himself.  Our study showcases the value of a meticulous and controlled approach in assessing TQA reliability.  We hope this work to lay the groundwork for future research as a reference point in the field of TQA.  The proposed methodology can also be applied in any professional setting where quality assurance is crucial, with the reliability of human workers being a key consideration.  Ultimately, we believe that quality-assurance is a multi-faceted aspect that should be taken seriously in order to effectively streamline work processes. t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by data such as points on the surface of a sphere, which adhere more closely to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, this study develops a novel vMF-SNE algorithm tailored for embedding spherical data efficiently. Utilizing an iterative procedure, it achieves more effective embeddings than the conventional t-SNE method when working with such data types, as shown through its simulation on sample datasets. Furthermore, the algorithm's benefits extend to real-world applications, as seen in 3D protein contact data embedding scenarios. When compared to established methods, vMF-SNE produces more accurate embeddings, as determined by several key metrics. These outcomes highlight vMF-SNE's potential as a robust, versatile technique for embedding spherical data structures efficiently. Multitasking scheduling in service industries has gained significant interest due to workers often being engaged in multiple tasks. In contrast to standard single-task environments, the shared processing resource space is better modeled by the convex hull of task rate ratios rather than an M-shape, according to the Price of Multitasking (PoM) criterion. This paper investigates the properties of the new class of algorithms known as Convex Hull Multitasking (CHM), which is informed by linear programming. Specific cases are examined where the convex hull is formed by two, three, or four distinct task rate ratios. A method for precisely calculating the resulting scheduling algorithms, called Convex Hull Multitasking (CHM), is derived using linear programming. When exactly k distinct task rates are present, a more efficient algorithm called K-Convex Hull Multitasking (KCHM) is proposed, which is equivalent to solving (k+1) linear programs simultaneously. Both CHM and KCHM algorithms are evaluated under different scenarios, including small-scale (two) and large-scale (twenty-five) multitasking problems, as well as a three-task and a four-task scenario with five tasks in both cases. Additionally, a KCHM-based variant with reduced computational requirements is proposed and tested. Experimental results for small-scale (twenty-five) problems show KCHM's performance in a reduced version to be a viable and efficient approach. Moreover, a new project-based KCHM algorithm called Sequential KCHM is developed and tested, as well as its variants that incorporate utility functions. Findings suggest that Sequential KCHM offers high efficiency with minimal computational overhead. Overall, this research introduces the CHM class of algorithms, which outperforms existing algorithms in benchmark tests, and also proposes the more efficient Sequential KCHM algorithm. The exploration of quantum machine learning has been increasingly vigorous, with research and experiments aimed at understanding and developing this field. Despite these efforts, there is limited study on a fundamental concept in machine learning research: adversarial examples. These examples, designed to mislead a model by a small amount of modification, have significant implications for both practical applications and theoretical validation of quantum machine learning. In this study, we discovered universal adversarial examples and perturbations that can deceive almost all trained quantum classifiers, regardless of their underlying architecture or data. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the role of symmetry in parameters in quantifying the robustness of quantum models. The methods and findings from this research may also expand to other areas of machine learning and quantum information. We examine Steklov eigenvalues in nearly spherical domains of three dimensions.  Building on our earlier research, which demonstrated the eigenvalues to be analytic functions of domain perturbation parameters, we calculate the first term in the asymptotic expansion in relation to Wigner 3-jsymbols.  Through analysis of the asymptotic expansion, we establish the isoperimetric theorem that if 'l' is a square number, the volume-normalized l-th Steklov eigenvalue achieves a stationary point at a ball.  Moreover, this stationary point is the smallest among all spherical domains when 'l' is a square number, and we also confirm the stationary point and minimality of the l-th Dirichlet eigenvalue in spherical domains.  Utilizing eigenvalue perturbation theory and Wigner 3-jsymbols, we calculate the second-term in the asymptotic expansion.  We prove that the second-term allows the determination of the l-th and (l+1)-th Dirichlet eigenvalues in spherical domains up to an accuracy of o(ε) as the domain tends to a ball, 'ε' being the dimensionless degree of perturbation.  By doing so, we resolve two long-standing open problems: finding the l-th Dirichlet eigenvalue to o(ε) accuracy and minimizing the l-th Dirichlet eigenvalue among all spherical domains when 'l' is a square number.  Our findings also reveal new information on the l-th Steklov eigenvalue which is analytic in 'ε', and this information complements our earlier research.  Notably, we prove that the l-th Steklov eigenvalue achieves a stationary point at a ball, is analytically extensible in 'ε', and is the smallest among all spherical domains when 'l' is a square number.  These results are utilizable in 'ε' asymptotics, and also provide minimization results for the l-th Dirichlet eigenvalue in spherical domains.  Notably, the l-th Dirovich eigenvalue in spherical domains is the smallest among all spherical domains when 'l' is a square number. Existing propagation models are broadly classified into two types - outdoor/empirical models and indoor/models. Each type involves considering numerous factors such as terrain, terrain features, buildings, vegetation, angle of incidence, and antenna heights. Recently, a novel method was introduced that utilizes machine learning to identify key propagation factors. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for modeling cellular network radio propagation that leverages deep learning. Our approach involves employing a deep convolutional neural network, trained on data consisting of spatially arranged propagation factors with associated signal strengths. Our trained DCNN, capable of real-time inference, can be used to determine the underlying propagation factors from complex urban environments. The Isabelle/HOL reasoning used in this paper is based on classical logic principles. We assume that propositions are always either true or false and use the rules of first-order logic, including the existence of empty sets and two fundamental binary operators: logical 'and' (representing conjunction) and logical 'or' (representing disjunction). Additionally, we leverage the concept of time points, which is represented mathematically as a total order. We incorporate some principles of set theory to facilitate operations on these sets and adopt a specific interpretation of the total order as defined by the 'less than' relation. 

Formal Isabelle/HOL definitions for the concepts of states, actions, and AMCs have been developed. We define AMCs as total orders of world states. We also define a concept for infinite time points, which allows the representation of temporal restrictions even when there is no maximum time point. We define an action as a total order over infinite time points. In contrast, some existing works on multi-agent planning treat time as a unified whole rather than distinct state and action components. This alternative approach is explored further in the 'Related Work' section.

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This paper examines different techniques for classifying discussion items as pertaining to technical or design issues, and assesses their conclusions based on multiple criteria such as their confidence in design classifications, agreement with human judgments, and the reasoning underlying their design labels. We found that neural networks, trained on combinations of rhetorical and semantic information, outperformed existing methods in achieving consistent conclusions and provided transparent reasoning capabilities. Moreover, our analysis of the reasoning strategies revealed preferences for specific design categories, and suggestions were provided for enhancing the reliability and coherency of the classifications produced. This work aims to promote discussion mining by highlighting best practices for concluding design classifications, and proposes methods for evaluating the coherence of the results. By exploring these guidelines, developers can enhance their confidence in the correctness of the design classifications derived from these tools. Although our primary focus remained on conversational protocols, other forms of developer discussions could also benefit from these principles. Ultimately, our study demonstrated that the design classification outcome depends on various factors, and the choice of algorithm, parameters, and even local versus global inference techniques significantly impacted the results. This work offers crucial insights for accurately interpreting design classification outcomes and guides future research in this area. This paper presents a novel evaluation engine for big stream and data processing pipelines called H-STREAM. It integrates stream processing operators as cloud-based micro-services to facilitate the analysis and visualization of IoT-generated Big Data streams. H-STREAM's micro-services dynamically adjust their techniques according to the stream producers, data velocity, and available processing resources to ensure seamless online processing and delivery to users. H-STREAM delivers stream processing and visualization micro-services through cloud infrastructure, enabling the composition of micro-services to implement specific aggregation analysis pipelines. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of H-STREAM in tackling velocity and volume challenges via an experimental validation using Microsoft Azure as a deployment platform, specifically in neuroscience and social connectivity analysis applications on IoT farms. It also showcases the resilience and scalability of the stream processing pipeline through an experimental analysis of H-STREAM's performance. We publicly release the H-STREAM source code and associated documentation at https://hstream.io.

Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties, particularly useful in visual data recovery applications. However, when dealing with sequential data such as streaming video, missing tensor entries need to be recovered in real-time without compromising performance. Existing streaming algorithms, although efficient, assume a constant data input rate and break down when faced with significant gaps in data reception, like those encountered when working with video encoded into tiles. Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the minimum sample size required for accurate matrix recovery when using two simple estimation techniques – the principal component estimator and the maximum likelihood estimator. These formulas apply to any matrix structure, given a fixed matrix and noise distribution. We also provide comparable results for the positive semidefinite matrix estimation problem. The findings demonstrate that the minimum required sample size for matrix recovery depends on two key factors: a matrix structure invariant term related to the logarithm of the rank and a structure-specific term related to the matrix's eigenvalue spectrum. Under certain conditions, the minimum required sample size needs to grow at least polynomially with the matrix size for accurate matrix recovery. We support the derived bounds with numerical simulations and an application to a multiple sample covariance matrix estimation problem. The findings suggest that the minimum required sample size for the later is significantly lower than what would be required in the absence of heteroskedasticity. Additionally, the research introduces novel tools for matrix structural analysis, including a generalization of a recent finding and the derivation of closed-form solutions to two heteroskedasticity-related matrix decomposition problems. The methods developed in this research have been successfully used in the estimation of a single spike recovery problem. This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions to Lyapunov equations. Comprehensive evaluation of our approach is achieved through mathematical representation and testing. Detailed numerical evaluation is demonstrated on various complex multi-channel systems, showcasing their effectiveness. Furthermore, our approach has been shown to outperform established methods in multiple test cases. Moreover, we compare the computational efficiency of our proposed distributed output-feedback controllers with existing solutions and illustrate their respective complexities. We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained on randomly sampled CT volumes, and subsequent steps utilize the network to extract embedding features from the full scan volume. Averaging these features by segments, a second BERT model aggregates the multiple segments into a unified feature for final classification. By combining both classification stages, we achieve a high validation accuracy of 0.9164 in macro F1 score. Additionally, our method's reliance on BERT enables our framework to adapt to various data sets and scan types with minimal modification. We compare our approach to current state-of-the-art methods, including semantic segmentation and deep clustering, and demonstrate that it surpasses these methods with significantly improved validation accuracy and inference time. The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab aims to create a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall experimental space capable of achieving extremely low millikelvin temperatures using a novel cryogenic platform. 
This cutting-edge cryogenic platform, founded on superconducting radiofrequency technology typically used in accelerator cavities, is designed to support three-dimensional superconducting qubit structures. This document outlines the baseline specifications and key features of the newly conceived platform. 
The baseline design requires a substantial cryogenic system comprising 44 interconnected RF components, a custom-made cryogenic controller and 3D modeling for the complex cryostat structure. 
The platform's 44 RF components, comprised of 32 capacitors and 12 inductors, are crucial for maintaining uniform temperature across six distinct cryogenic stages and achieving precise control over two RF modes for minimal energy leakage. 
A custom cryogenic interface with 24 connectors and complex cryogenic welding is needed to integrate the platform's components, founded on conventional superconducting cryogenics principles. 
The platform's cryogenic performance will be monitored using a multi-phase superconducting quench detection system, enabling real-time feedback about the system's cryogenic stability. 
This document presents the initial design concept, a critical first step in the development of the platform, laying the groundwork for a thorough research and development phase that is currently underway. 
The successful execution of R&D efforts and thorough characterization of the platform's components and overall structure will ultimately pave the way for assembly and testing at the intended experimental space within our quantum computing laboratory at the University of Chicago. 
Ultimately, this document presents a critical foundation for the recently established and expanding Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab, supporting cutting-edge quantum research and development at the laboratory.

Previous research indicates a high prevalence of misused crypto APIs in Java and C, but similar studies for other languages have been absent. This research aimed to examine instances of poorly implemented cryptography in popular programming languages, with a focus on real-world applications. A comprehensive dataset consisting of 2.8 million issues related to cryptography from five mainstream programming languages was created, and among these, 57% were associated with Python. 

Upon closer inspection, the study discovered that 74% of Python-related issues could be linked to an inadequate use of crypto APIs. The study also highlighted a range of common mistakes made when using crypto APIs in Python, including the frequent failure to include necessary header files and properly initialize crypto modules. In addition, the study found that developers often struggled with correctly handling hashed passwords, incorporating encryption in a conversation, and utilizing several necessary data types.

In contrast to previous studies, the research on Python developers showed that a significant portion of poor practice was not the result of inexperience but rather established developers. It also suggests a more pronounced connection between programming concepts and cryptography use, as well as among reuse of bad code. Further research could shed light on the root causes of this pattern. 

In addition to identifying common mistakes made in Python developers, the research provides recommendations and strategies to resolve these issues effectively. Lastly, the study introduces PyCheck, a tool to aid in identifying poorly implemented cryptography use cases within Python code. PyCheck can be used as a Python linter or static code analysis tool to identify and address cryptography-related errors in Python applications. 

The research provides valuable insights to developers, maintainers, and security auditors on how to handle and manage sensitive data properly in Python-based systems. By identifying a broad range of poor practices among both novice and experienced developers, the research emphasizes the importance of addressing these issues. In addition, the research introduces PyCheck, a tool to help identify and rectify these errors. 

In terms of future research, the paper suggests conducting similar studies in other programming languages to compare their results with those found in Python. In addition, the research further examines the causes of poor practices among Python developers. In practice, the research provides a set of best practices to aid developers in properly handling and implementing sensitive information. In general, the paper supports existing research while offering a unique perspective on a broader range of poor practices among Python developers. This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, facilitating its capacity to handle large-scale data sets in a distributed and parallel manner. Evaluating this method with extensive image collections, encompassing nearly 400,000 images across 40 square kilometers of New York City and San Francisco, demonstrates its capacity to accurately reconstruct three-dimensional coordinates of objects, such as buildings, while detaching from common scene geometry. Furthermore, our approach is shown to automatically identify object categories without any prior knowledge. In addition, we demonstrate the feasibility of reconstructing object point clouds without any existing knowledge of three-dimensional object structures. Notably, our technique achieves superior results, outperforming existing methods of reconstructing three-dimensional objects using non-parametric statistical models and point-to-point correspondences. Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory, notably the coefficients of operator product expansion, which describe operator fusion. Determining these coefficients is particularly difficult for complex models. A new method has been introduced to calculate operator product expansion coefficients by examining how wavefunctions overlap. This method has been successfully applied to the Haagerup model, allowing researchers to derive the conformal spectrum and identify primary operators associated with specific entanglement blocks. As a result, the model's central charge and operator fusion coefficients have been determined. Applying the method to the XXZ model revealed novel finite-size corrections. Furthermore, the method has enabled the determination of operator fusion coefficients for various 'intra-gapped' regions in the XYZ model. As a result, the spin-1 projective non-Abelian fermion model emerges as a key universal model associated with a conformal field theory having $c=1/2$ as its central charge. Consequently, the model's operator product expansion coefficients can be expressed in terms of projectors and the minimal models' operator product expansion coefficients for $M_M=3$ and $M_N=4$. The method's applicability is restricted to areas with a 'gap' or those exhibiting a topological order. This theoretical framework has been used to calculate various properties of spin chain models and types of topological systems. The method has also led to the creation of a new set of unitary morphisms applicable to conformal field theories. We have demonstrated that the overlap of wavefunctions in the Raabe-Cauchois model represents a novel form of entanglement. Automatically tagging parts of speech in text can be problematic, especially when dealing with text from earlier time periods. Omitting incorrectly annotated tokens, rather than correcting them, can help avoid potential errors that could arise from later uses of the text. Set-valued annotation, which accounts for uncertainty in the annotation process, can provide a way to mitigate errors. Existing methods for set-valued annotation, however, have primarily been developed for modern languages. This study introduces a method for annotating text from earlier time periods. The method first uses a neural network to predict a set of possible parts of speech, then applies a rule-based system to refine the results and considers the most likely token along with two secondary options as the most accurate set of possible parts of speech. The approach was tested using text from 19th and early 20th century American English and showed improved accuracy compared to other methods. Additionally, the study found that omitting the secondary options did not result in decreased accuracy when compared to only considering the most likely option. The annotated data set generated by this approach will be made available to researchers. Further development of the system's rule-based component and its potential to handle multiple word types simultaneously was also described. In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the image in such a case is obtained by forming the cofibered image of the original preorder above the epimorphism. In categories satisfying regularity conditions, the existence of such a cofibered image of a partial order corresponds to the existence of the least upper bound among all partial orders within the category. This work explores conditions ensuring the existence of these cofibered images, which can then be applied to investigate the existence of equivalence relations within the category. Specifically, the notion of $n$-atomic categories is defined to describe conditions ensuring the existence of these cofibered images up to isomorphism, and this concept generalizes the classical situation in sets where $\mathbb E$ is a setoid. Various classical results in set theory are reinterpreted within this framework, and it is also demonstrated how existences of certain types of cardinal characteristics can be described in terms of these cofibered images. Moreover, the work establishes that certain regular categories can be completely characterized by the presence of these images, and it includes examples of categories where such images rise to the level of equality with the original partial orders, which includes certain well-known categories in model theory. Specifically, the work includes that in certain regular categories where the intersection of three images of relevant cardinal characteristics are present, the image of any set family under any surjective onto-colimit-preserving map will be a partial order, and that includes includes certain classical results that had been previously obtained by very different methods, and that includes generalizations to obtain results that include the non-principal ultrafilter characteristic. This process is typically grounded in thorough credit assessments and aligned with widely accepted industry standards, drawing on information like client loan repayment histories and demographic profiles.

This research will enable banks to streamline their lending processes by identifying the most critical information and streamlining their decision-making criteria based on how banks and the machine learning models perceive credit risk factors. The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among Explainable Reinforcement Learning methods, one key area of study is the generation of actions to be recommended, specifically the explanations provided to users about why a recommended action was chosen. In this study, we assess the efficacy of an XRL technique known as LIME-RS by examining the consistency of its explanations over time and how well they align with user preferences. We introduce two new metrics: adhesion reflects the stability of LIME-RS explanations, while consistency measures how well these explanations match actual user ratings. Through experiments conducted on four public datasets, we find LIME-RS explanations have a significant impact on recommended action quality. Moreover, we observe a positive correlation between the adhesion of explanations and their impact on performance. In addition, we investigate the impact of dataset diversity and various algorithm-related factors on LIME-RS's performance using design of experiments. The results and code are accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/spotify2020/LIME-RS-explications. Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of refining XRL techniques to address the potential discrepancies between AI and human preferences. By addressing these discrepancies, we are one step closer to achieving spotless and defensible AI models. We introduce an effect where the medium is warmed up by radiation, leading to a feedback loop where the medium's resistance is increased in proportion to the temperature raised to the power of four. We use the Blandford-Knox equation to model this feedback loop. We have enhanced the standard Larmor equation with our new model of radiation friction, creating a more accurate equation that takes into account the effects of multiple scattering and an increased specific resistance. We test the validity of our equation by applying it to systems under strong radiation, observing reduced particle trajectories that are bent by friction, and examining how particle energy is transformed into heat in the presence of intense friction. We draw on an example from magnetospheric physics to illustrate our findings. We have also generalized our equation for use in systems under quasi-steady conditions. We have use an effects-averaging method to do so, and derived an equation for the timescale over which particles are accelerated by radiation. We have also analyzed the distribution of particle energies using a quick-quiet theory and the Fokker-Planck equation for relativistic particles, identifying key changes to the distribution. We have test the validity of our equations in various contexts, and provide guidance for applying them to new systems of interest. We have derived compact formulas for the distance over which particles are accelerated by radiation and for the distribution of particle energies under various conditions. We have also investigated the limits of our equations in extreme conditions and find that they do not apply in situations where the radiation friction is significantly variable or when the specific resistance of the medium is greatly increased. We have related our model of radiation friction to two models from the study of stellar magnetospheres, and explore the implications of our model for the study of astrophysical objects and systems. We have also used our model of radiation friction to explain certain observed phenomena in the jet of the blazar 3C 1111. Our work has also led to new questions and observations, and we expect that it may be of future relevance to the study of astrophysical jet systems. Furthermore, our model of radiation friction has implications for the study of particle colliders and may be of future relevance to the study of accelerator systems. We have also derived the equivalent non-relativistic form of our equation for use in systems where the energy of the particles is low enough to be described by classical physics. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional electrical current measurements, providing us with insight into previously inaccessible subgap energy states. Our innovative sensing method has a notable advantage in that it doesn't cause the usual increase in noise commonly associated with measurements involving individual charges. Moreover, we've studied the impact of a magnetic field on the system and discovered that certain types of magnetic texturing, known as periodic modulation, can dramatically affect the tunneling process. Our research opens up new possibilities for studying various complex systems utilizing this innovative RF-sensing method. One potential application is the development of a device capable of detecting parity, a concept central to theoretical ideas regarding nonabelian zero-mode quantum computing. Our data is consistent with simulations based on the extended BCS theory but the observed parity-dependent phenomenon persists even in superconductors that have exceptionally long coherence length. Our research explores the effects of radio-frequency sensing on the detection of parity-independent and parity-dependent quasiparticle tunneling. We develop a new, unsupervised method for identifying hidden dynamics within large datasets associated with time-varying network communications. Our approach identifies the underlying dynamics without prior knowledge or assumptions about their nature, making it generally applicable to various systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on two complex problems: optimizing the movement of a mobile S, where we identify the shortest paths in a complex terrain, and controlling the spread of a disease, where we find the most cost-effective policy to prevent its spread. Our results compare favorably with state-of-the-art algorithms. Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. Two human evaluators measured and compared the coronal image deformity angles acquired from both robotic and manual scans. The results showed that robotic scanning yielded highly reliable results both within and between evaluators, with minimal difference compared to the manual approach in terms of coronal deformity angles. Furthermore, robotic scanning exhibited accurate intra-rater consistency, with the mean absolute deviation within an acceptable range for the vast majority of measurements. This study found that robotic scanning yields scoliosis deformity angles comparable in accuracy to those obtained manually. Although more research is needed to fully understand the effectiveness of ultrasound-based scoliosis assessment, these findings support the use of robotic scanning as a viable approach for scoliosis evaluation. Such an approach could significantly benefit expert systems responsible for scoliosis assessment and treatment by adding ultrasound-based assessment as a module. As a result, these systems could provide more comprehensive and informative outputs, like "continue to watch" or "surgery required." Ultimately, this technology could lead to greater efficiency in scoliosis assessment and treatment. The associated software and hardware are available for immediate use at research institutions. The developed algorithm will be made accessible on GitHub once refined. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance through the sharing of learned features between constituent models. However, the current method of feature sharing, which involves aligning weights of different models, can be ineffective as it does not preserve the unique feature representations each model has developed. This leads to a situation where shared features may not benefit the overall performance of the ensemble. To address this issue, this research explores methods to support feature sharing that takes into account the unique set of learned features from each model. We present a theoretical analysis of the weight alignment process, proposing an optimal alignment strategy, and evaluate it on popular benchmark datasets. Furthermore, this study also introduces a novel MIMO architecture that combines feature sharing with channel pruning, allowing for more efficient inference. The proposed techniques are extensively validated through a comprehensive suite of experiments. Our findings suggest that (1) an optimal weight alignment can lead to better performance for black-box models, (2) different models benefit from distinct feature sets, and (3) our proposed MIMO architecture with channel pruning achieves improved efficiency while maintaining competitive accuracy levels compared to current state-of-the-art models. This study marks the inaugural release of the HIMDAT dataset, a comprehensive collection of historical text datasets that spans over 100 years and encompasses more than 20 languages. This publication provides an in-depth analysis of the characteristics of each dataset, detailed information on their documentation, and preliminary experimental findings. Our research aims to stimulate further investigation into the development of the field by examining the evolution of existing datasets, comparing methodologies for training and testing, and exploring the challenges and opportunities presented by under-researched languages. Moreover, we aim to establish a collaborative platform for the research community to share knowledge, thereby enhancing the accuracy and reliability of training and testing methods utilized in the field. The source code and dataset are publicly accessible through the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/zwang/himdat. The survey's findings are presented in two parts. The first section delves into the characteristics of individual datasets, with each section providing relevant information on the dataset's creation, including its writing systems, publication dates, language, and provenance. The second part focuses on the trends observed in the development of historical document classification datasets over time. Our research reveals that the majority of datasets (60%) were published within the last ten years, with notable surges in interest in 2013-2015 and 2019-2021. We also observe that the majority of datasets (55%) focus on 20th-21st century content, followed by the 19th century (25%), and the 18th century (20%). Additionally, our research shows that the majority of datasets are written in English (43%), followed by German (19%), and French (11%). We also explore the challenges posed by under-researched languages, with a particular focus on languages that have recently gained popularity in the field: Bulgarian, Croatian, Finnish, Greek, Hungarian, Norwegian, Russian, Spanish, Swedish, and Turkish. Through a quantitative analysis of under-researched languages, we identify opportunities for research and collaboration, with Norwegian being the only language that has been researched in excess of 10 datasets. The remaining languages have been studied in 0-9 datasets, presenting opportunities for new research and collaboration. The survey also examines the evolution of research topics over time, revealing that the majority of research has been dedicated to word recognition between 2010-2020, with a significant surge in interest in deep learning, hand restoration, and unsupervised training between 2015-2020. Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving trajectory precision using supplementary sensors and a novel feedback control strategy in combination with a feed-forward approach based on flatness. For this purpose, a novel dynamic model is introduced that accurately describes a flexible robotic joint as a two-mass system with pose-dependent inertia, nonlinear friction, nonlinear elasticity, and backlash. A feed-forward controller is designed using the flatness-based method to optimize movement quality, and a supplementary feedback controller is implemented to counteract external disturbances, utilizing real-time automatic differentiation to ensure swift computation. Finally, the proposed algorithms are tested in simulated software environment as well as on a real Bethel A4C robot, and the results show that the designed controllers effectively address position inaccuracy and backlash, demonstrating a critical reduction in position errors, particularly at high speeds. This research demonstrates a new approach to modeling a flexible robotic joint and presents a highly efficient position control strategy that can be applied industrially. The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been based on an environmental perspective. A new approach, the Multiple State Analysis, is offered as an alternative to analyze the complex patterns and interactions within an individual's lifetime health trajectory. This innovative method utilizes multidimensional data analysis to examine multiple aspects of health over time, addressing questions about the combinations of risk factors that contribute to specific health outcomes more than others. A statistical model developed as part of this approach identifies patterns of risk factor combinations that result in a higher risk of a serious heart condition, known as a myocardial infarction. By incorporating more detailed cloud microphysics and atmospheric behavior into the models, researchers may be able to better understand the processes involved in 'hothouse' climates and potential future climate states. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods rely heavily on a vast quantity of high-quality, labeled images which often contains errors. Consequently, developing robust training techniques that minimize the negative effects of noisy labels is of the utmost importance for achieving optimal model performance. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative method based on Bayesian statistics called the BLRM that prevents DNNs from overfitting noisy data by restoring labels and reducing dependence on noisy training data. The BLRM effectively utilizes two key techniques, a posterior predictive distribution and negative predictive potential, to accurately predict noisy labels. Furthermore, BLRM leverages a balanced dataset, where high confidence clean labels and uncertain data are kept separate, to compare clean and noisy class probabilities and rectify errors in the process. Experimental evaluations conducted using different types of noisy data and multiple datasets demonstrate that BLRM successfully refits noisy labels with impressive results. Notably, our method achieved an accuracy of 83.11%, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art approach with an accuracy of 79.24%. The associated code is publicly available at https://github.com/ashish619/BLRM. The dataset used in this research can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/fil?usapage=embed%2F1H0Z8. The BLRM method exhibits considerable potential for use in other machine learning methods as a general label rectification tool. The method's effectiveness lies in its ability to balance clean and noisy data, thereby balancing the training dataset. Additionally, BLRM serves as a potential solution for other problems where accurate prediction of the label distribution may provide an opportunity to mitigate noisy data. The method is distinguished from other approaches such as hard example mining and entropy loss, and from existing noise-in-advance methods that generate clean labels during training. Lastly, the proposed method is distinguished from other model-based noise countermeasures that rely on complex priors and variational inference procedures. Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a specific upper bound for the norm of $P$ is found. Hadamard numbers are a sequence of numbers that satisfy a logarithmic congruence condition and have been extensively studied. For comparison purposes, an estimate of the order of $\|P\|$ is established and it remains the best known estimate for generic node sets, i.e., node sets that do not form an arithmetic sequence. In contrast, special configurations of nodes can lead to significantly smaller projector norms. To address a long-standing open question, results indicate that $\|P\|$ does not exceed a specific constant, multiplied by $\log\log n$, for sufficiently large $n$. Moreover, for sets that form an arithmetic sequence, a specific upper bound for the projector norm can be as small as $\frac{2}{\pi}$. As a related development, the interpolation error for function spaces with a specific type of norm is characterised and an estimate of the order of this error is established. The characterisation implies that the interpolation error is bounded above and below by a specific constant, multiplied by $\log\log n$, for sufficiently large $n$. In the space of continuous functions on the unit cube, the interpolation error can even be as small as $C/n$. The work presented revisits and significantly extends existing knowledge on this topic, first introduced in a seminal 1968 publication by Micchelli. For sets that form an arithmetic sequence, the interpolation error can even be as small as $C\cdot n^{-1/2}$. Finally, as a related development, the approximation power of linear operators in function spaces, defined using a specific type of norm, is characterised and an estimate of the order of this approximation is established. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. However, they can be effectively defined within a logic that incorporates a clock function, which records the number of steps a function takes before terminating. This paper introduces clocked definitions in HOL, providing a theorem prover proof that every totalable function with a clock is total, except in cases of divergence. Building on this, clocked definitions are used to facilitate non-termination reasoning in HOL, with applications to recursive functions, including their actual termination and with respect to well-founded relations. Moreover, using clocked definitions avoids complications related to inductive definitions in HOL, providing an alternative approach that works equally well for manually defining functions as it does for inductive definitions generated by Sledge, HOL's inductive package. While primarily focusing on applications in HOL, the idea of clocked definitions can be applied to other logics that support total functions. However, in a partial functions logic such as Coq, defining non-terminating functions is generally possible directly, making clocked definitions redundant in this context. This research ultimately explores the benefits and limitations of using clocked definitions as a tool for non-termination reasoning in HOL. As supplementary material, the paper includes a theory library called `Clockeds` that can be imported and used by other researchers. In addition, relevant Coq implementations are provided for comparison purposes. Both the HOL library and Coq implementations can be accessed through the CERES Repository at the link below.

The system's phase diagram was mapped out by analyzing the phase boundaries between various phases such as multiple Weyl nodes, Fermi points, and Chern bands, and we also explored the one-band approximation in detail. According to our findings, when $p$ is even, a unique Weyl semimetal emerges, different from the non-magnetic case, which we call the time-reversal-broken Weyl semimetal. This phase can be seen in the $p=2$ case, where diagonal and perpendicular magnetic fields are concerned. However, when $p$ is odd, a time-reversal-broken Weyl semimetal is observed for off-diagonal fields, along with a competing time-reversal-symmetric metal phase. Additionally, along the diagonal magnetic field axis, regions of multiple Weyl nodes, one-band semimetals, and Chern insulators were found, showing complex phase diagrams in magnetic materials. Furthermore, numerical simulations have confirmed that, in a time-reversal-broken Weyl semimetal case of $p=2$ and $n=1$, a unique Dirac point emerges, which develops into multiple Weyl nodes upon applying either a perpendicular or a diagonal magnetic field. This transformation is caused by the competition of the Zeeman and orbital magnetic fields. Moreover, both perpendicular and diagonal magnetic fields can coexist in a perfect half-filled case. Finally, we have demonstrated that, in a quantum oscillation pattern, a unique charge oscillation occurs for a $p=2$ case, directly related to magnetic field's fractional parts. Using a distinct dataset of local news articles and demographic information about readers, we employ a new method for classifying news outlets into three categories: informative, critical, and critical-but-cautious. We significantly expand upon a previous study with a substantially larger dataset of 20,000 news articles from 230 outlets over nine months. Our results show consistent patterns of a link between local COVID coverage and regional case and death rates, contingent on the credibility of the news source. Furthermore, we find that local news outlets with higher trustworthiness cover COVID as a social issue, whereas less trustworthy outlets tend to cover it as a personal problem. Interestingly, we find that local news coverage of COVID does not directly correlate with regional COVID hospitalizations. By controlling for the trustworthiness of the news source, we find that local news can be an important factor in predicting COVID cases and deaths. Ultimately, our study highlights the significance of considering both the content and credibility of news sources in research on local news and public health. The findings presented here offer a starting point for a much broader exploration of the relationships between local news, trust, and behavior across a wide range of social and health issues. As an added benefit, our study provides empirical support for the theory of spiral of silence, describing how the silence of opinion minorities in the face of societal pressure can influence news coverage. Moreover, our analysis shows that local news coverage of COVID is driven by both the characteristics of news sources and their audiences. Finally, our research demonstrates that classifying news sources into informative, critical, etc. based on human judgments is equivalent to categorizing sources based on their actual COVID coverage in relation to demographic characteristics. To facilitate the replication of our study, we provide access to our dataset, code, and metadata. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications is typical, it poses a significant challenge - the gravitational force is not directly calculated for distant particles after a initial nearest-neighbor search, which is resolved through the use of fast multipole methods. Our replication of a standard FMG approach in our code, SPHGal, also preserves angular momentum in a similar manner to the original algorithm used by Saitoh and Umemura. However, this integration method does have a notable limitation - the accumulation of errors associated with the multipole approach cause a drift in both energy and angular momentum over time. Additionally to our previous research on mass conservation, our findings demonstrate that a novel exponential model effectively predicts this increase in error, which can be utilized to set a practical time step limit to preserve both mass and angular momentum in complex simulations involving up to a million particles. Furthermore, our outcomes reveal that the method's accuracy is unaffected by the number of integration steps and the coupling of hydro and gravity forces. A comparative analysis with a recent study revealed substantial discrepancies in our findings, specifically regarding the observed angular momentum conservation error, which differed by a factor of 10^6 and 10^4 respectively, highlighting concerns about a previously advocated time-stepping strategy. Consequently, our SPHGal code, which incorporates stable time-stepping and a state-of-the-art SPH variant with correct integration, successfully preserves both mass and angular momentum in a range of astrophysical simulations involving up to a million particles spanning millions of years. As such, it achieves stable mass and angular momentum conservation for the most demanding compact object merger simulations. We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, is characterized by its reliance on a baseline policy providing optimal guidance. In this framework, we apply a general method that utilizes variation generation to maximize the state-state transition relationships learned between the expert and imitation models. We derive a unified framework for a range of cloning techniques, revealing the conditions under which varying versions of the imitation model yield superior results. We show that our approach leads to improved robustness in comparison to standard methods. Furthermore, we establish that our variation generation technique has the potential to expand the Zermelo metric space, thereby enhancing the distinctness of variations in difficult cases. We support our theoretical findings with experiments on a satellite autopilot system and the American Football game strategy, which demonstrate the efficacy of generating variations in challenging scenarios. We also highlight that, contrary to expectations, incorporating valuable data does not always lead to better results, and that our approach often outperforms data-rich models. Moreover, our approach leads to a significant reduction in required expert data, making it a more practical solution. We conduct comprehensive evaluations, demonstrating the stability and scalability of our variations in long-term learning, cross-system domain transfer, and the longevity of learned strategies. Ultimately, our approach achieves the best overall results across multiple performance metrics. The acquired knowledge can be utilized to train a general American Football player using a variety of games as input. We provide both the code and the data for these experiments at https://github.com/tonerhoedt/data_augmentation_for_learning. Our variations are available at https://github.com/tonerhoedt/variations_for_learning. The main contribution of this research is an efficient polynomial-time approximation method for determining the genus of a dense graph. Genus, in graph theory, refers to the minimum number of planes onto which a graph can be projected without edge intersections. Although this problem is notoriously complex, our method involves a simple and quick computation that rapidly produces an approximate solution, with the ability to specify the degree of accuracy. We develop an algorithm that runs in a time proportionate to $n^{2+\omega'(n)}$, where $\omega'(n)$ is the order of the linear grouping of $n$, and successfully identifies a graph's genus up to a specified level of precision. We also establish an upper boundary of $2\log_{\frac{c\sqrt{n}}{2} } n$ for the number of random projections required in our method, and we can set $\omega'(n)$ to any value between 1 and 2. Our approach involves a novel random projection technique that simplifies an earlier method by Ottonello, where we reduce the time complexity and increase the degree of flexibility in choosing parameters. We begin our algorithmic development by first approximating a graph's embedding in two planes and subsequently tackling the general case involving multiple planes. Our method involves a recursive process, where we first identify a plane of genus $g$ for a subset of the graph, and then repeat the process for the remaining dense regions until no further planes are required. A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results. A novel approach is developed further by incorporating a new communication rule that prevents convergence speed degradation, which is confirmed through logistic regression benchmark comparisons. Additionally, a fully asynchronous version of the algorithm is implemented using atomic operations and locks, allowing its successful application to scale-up scenarios. A comprehensive, open-source implementation is provided within the BLMC project on GitHub. Overall, this research contributes a versatile, communication-efficient, and computationally efficient solution for large-scale distributed optimization challenges. As a result, this algorithm finds extensive, production-oriented utilization. 

Key technical words: distributed optimization, stochastic Newton, atomic updates, fully asynchronous, communication efficiency, numerical benchmarks. 

Please note that this paper integrates and builds upon two significantly distinct approaches: a Newton-based algorithm for distributed optimization with relaxed rounding requirements, which is a novel concept, and a stochastic Newton method that utilizes random approximations at each iteration. Our solution combines these two techniques to create a unique, efficient, and scalable optimization tool. We have chosen to label this algorithm as Newton vs. other iterative methods that do not utilize second-order information, such as quasi-Newton or first-order methods, to accurately reflect its distinct algorithmic characteristics. We have carefully and consistently labeled certain algorithmic components, such as projection and step-size adjustments, as not being part of the Newton method.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of using a deep learning model, specifically a Long Short-Term Memory network, to detect toxic language in text written in these languages, which are predominantly spoken in India's neighboring countries. Through this study, we examine the effect of varying the amount of a given sentence's context on the model's performance, with options ranging from a few words to several sentences. Additionally, we assess whether the model's accuracy improves when it is retrained after being shown a selection of the data it will be evaluated against in advance, a technique known as transfer learning. Our results indicate that the Hate 360 dataset, which contains classified samples of online text from English, Hindi, and Bengali, is particularly useful for this purpose due to its size. Our analysis of the model's performance reveals that it performs best when provided with a substantial context, 512 words or more, with results comparable to the performance of the English model on the Hate 360 dataset. Our model's accuracy also sees notable improvement when it is retrained using the dataset's classified samples, a gain of around 7% in accuracy. Our findings also highlight the importance of creating resources for weaker dominant language programs. Our model was found to perform better than a baseline model on a milder Hate 360 dataset subsample. Our code and the trained models are available to the public on the GitHub platform. Our analysis shows that the model's performance is consistent with the results of previous studies on related topics, suggesting that the problem of detecting hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is not a particularly difficult one to solve. Our findings also replicate the success of transfer learning in improving the accuracy of neural network models, albeit in a new context. Finally, our results highlight the importance of developing strong language processing capabilities for low-resource languages in order to prevent the spread of toxic online content. Our model's potential implications and limitations are examined in detail through the use of case studies. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as when employing micro-pattern gaseous detectors, Time Projection Chambers can allow directional recoil detection. The main challenge lies in identifying the direction of individual counts made noisy and prone to coincidence by low-intensity light detectors. We've created new statistical measures to both process data and evaluate experiments in areas where direct recoil detection is a goal. These new observables are based on angular similarity between counts, rather than timing, and can be used to analyze real experiments. We've tested them on simulated experiments, specifically two major TPX-based experiments: XENONnT-TPC and GASPI. We've found that our proposed method can already provide valuable information, and when applied to GASPI, which has high spatial resolution and intense light, it promises to greatly surpass current capabilities, potentially reaching an impressive 90% accuracy in identifying recoil direction. This approach could be applied to other detector designs as well, offering a universal path to identifying recoil direction with high precision. Moreover, this method can be used to further research already active experiments, such as XENONnT-TPC, during ongoing data collection. The code used for these simulations and our analysis is openly available at https://github.com/usceta/apex-tpc. Recently, it has been used to analyze real data in https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00333-z. Our goal is to make this research even more accessible by creating a user-friendly package for easy integration into already active and upcoming projects, and these files will be hosted at https://github.com/usceta/directional-tpx under an extremely liberal license. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of competition results indicates that the holistic task was more challenging, with a notable gap observed between the top-performing models and the baseline average in both tasks.

An internal unit can be viewed as a specific type of interaction that facilitates the transfer of information and/or energy within the system. Focusing on the dynamics of a centrally coupled system, where all system elements are connected to a single central unit, we investigate how various parameters influence the system's localization. Specifically, we examine how system localization is impacted by parameters such as central-sparse link strength, relative central frequency, and coherence between the system's and central unit frequencies. Furthermore, we explore the system's dynamics in terms of both the average behavior and uncertainty principles applicable to coupled systems. Notably, our results indicate that the system's localization is influenced by factors such as its mean frequency position and the strength of central-sparse connections. Moreover, we demonstrate that localized behavior can be observed under various parameter settings. The system's behavior is shown to transition from localized to delocalized states as the strength of central-sparse connections increases. An increase in system parameters such as driving force, coherence between frequencies, or mean frequency position is found to have minimal effect on the system's localization until a certain driving force threshold is reached, at which point the system undergoes a localization transition. Our research also reveals that the system's localization can be reconstructed from reconstructed data using different reconstruction techniques, including one that partakes in coherent dynamics. Through numerical simulations, we validate the outcomes of our analytical findings. Ultimately, our results converge to anticipated behaviors under specific theoretical conditions, which were previously documented in studies by Braun et al. and Huveners et al. respectively. The system's behavior can serve as a model to understand how system delocalization impacts the observed localization transition. The present study is a precursor to future research, where it may serve as a reference for understanding system localization in more complex networks, including those of spin chains and coupled oscillators. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diverse array of interactions between individuals and organizations. The COVID-19 pandemic, however, led to a significant shift in human behavior, resulting in increased segregation measures such as remote work and social distancing. This study employs detailed data on urban mobility and demographic information to examine how the pandemic altered the composition of city areas during the height of the outbreaks in the United States, Europe, and Australia. We demonstrate that a significant decline in diversity occurred in most areas, but some urban neighborhoods experienced a heightened presence of residents, indicating a return to less diverse encounters since the onset of the pandemic. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that changes in area composition were often tied to variations in area income, suggesting that areas struggling financially were able to attract more residents once the pandemic subsided, thus regaining some of their pre-pandemic diversity. We also discover that a substantial proportion of workers in lower-paying professions returned to their places of work earlier than higher-paying professions, leading to a temporary decrease in income diversity. Finally, our findings highlight the various age groups that were impacted by these changes and how they varied depending on location and income levels. The data collected in this study could have useful implications for urban planners and policymakers as they strive to rebuild their cities post-pandemic. As the world continues to adapt to its new normal, our project aims to closely monitor how the composition of city areas evolves over time. This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field-Split Multiplicative Schwarz Newton, incorporates both sequential and
simultaneous evaluation of individual subdomains and interfaces/boundaries,
respectively. To enhance convergence, SN stage initially solves subdomain systems
along with interface equations, followed by a MN stage where MN systematically
solves subdomains one by one while simultaneously addressing boundary equations.
Using numerical simulations, the FSMSN method is compared to other algorithms like
FSM, SN, MN, and SSCN, showing that FSMSN often exhibits superior convergence
performance over other approaches in a range of tests. Two realistic case studies
are also conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of FSMSN in predicting accurate
two-phase flow results for porous media models representing diverse single and
multiple porous media configurations. In particular, the algorithm is applied to a
model of a single phase flow through a combined air-water-snow system in a
snowpack matrix, as well as a realistic three-layered model of porous media
comprisingshale, carbonate, and clay formations containing multiple fractures. In
both cases, the performance of FSMSN is shown to be superior to other algorithms.  This research has also investigated the computational efficiency of FSMSN using parallel computing, using 6 different systems involving 8 to 2048 processor units.  Overall, the results show that FSMSN is able to achieve significant speedup over sequential computations, with a large portion of the computational time attributed to either the nonlinear solver or data input/output procedures.  These results highlight the importance of optimizing algorithm and computer code design in order to efficiently solve two-phase flow problems. TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating specific TERS signals is computationally difficult. Our innovative method combines the primary factors driving the effectiveness of TERS, the electromagnetic and chemical interactions, into a single quantum simulation. The electromagnetic influence describes the sample's interaction with highly localized, inhomogeneous electric fields produced by the plasmonic tip, a focal point of many mechanistic studies. Conversely, the chemical interaction accounts for the highly directed, weak, long-range chemical forces between the apex of the tip and sample layers or molecules under study. Our approach initially simulates the electromagnetic influence using a quantum model of the sample in tandem with a classical tip-assisted laser radiation field. It then assesses the chemical contact that couples sample layers or molecules to a single, covalent-modified Au tip through inelastic interactions, factoring in various atomic species at the tip's surface. Our research showcases the method's utility by examining AuAR (arsenic) sample relationships, examining multiple degrees of chemical bonding between the tip and sample, and exploring the role of Au tip shape on the TERS signal. Additionally, our method highlights the sensitivity of inelastic TERS responses to chemical bonding, particularly in regards to monolayer interactions, at cryogenic and room temperatures. Our work further validates our model by comparing it to experimental and existing simulations of TERS. The method presented here, encompassing both electromagnetic and chemical contact, offers a valuable tool for analyzing TERS spectra while providing a deeper understanding of the underlying chemistry involved, particularly in relationships between single-molecule layers or components. Additionally, our method demonstrates the capacity to explore the role of tip shape, specimen composition, and temperature in inelastic TERS, a crucial consideration for future TERS investigations of complex biological systems and materials. We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral galaxies in the K band. Our goal was to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning dust grains in the galaxies NGC 3627, NGC 4254, NGC 4736, and NGC 5055, with particular attention to how their emission relates to M 31. Through radio-continuum data and global photometry at 18.6 and 24.6 GHz, we sought to find excess emission due to AME beyond the expected thermal and synchrotron components. Instead of a detection, we only found upper limits for AME, which when combined with similar data from the nearby galaxies indicated a level of AME emission intensity of around $C_{d,\gammaij} \approx 1.3_{-0.4}^{+0.5} \times 10^{-22}$ MJy sr$^{-1}$ (1 σ) at 24.6 GHz. This result is particularly significant as we report the first radio-continuum observations of M 31 with the SRT, providing a valuable database that can be used in future studies. Our study set a limit on the density of cosmic rays in the disk of M 31 and we found no evidence to support the presence of a central starburst or a superwind in the radio-continuum of the sample galaxies. Our research provides upper limits on the intensity of spinning dust grains in local spirals, with results that are consistent with previous findings. Finally, our study set new limits on the density of cosmic rays and the mass of neutral gas in the disk of M 31. We interpreted the observed emission of M 31 within the framework of a galaxy with a relatively low level of supernovae events and consistent with the observed properties of the Milky Way.
