Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using a comprehensive approach that incorporates density functional theory-based phonon calculations, inelastic neutron scattering, and ab initio path integral molecular dynamics. In contrast to previously assumed models, our research reveals that it is the disruption of short-range ionic order rather than a structural instability that gives rise to the entropy increase. We also observe that the significant entropy change stems from the low-frequency vibrational modes involving the movement of ions outside their equilibrium positions, particularly in the direction of the electric dipole. This insight opens the door for analyzing other materials featuring both structural and functional properties, utilizing entropy as a powerful indicator to uncover hidden structural details. Additionally, our research provides a new understanding of the relationship between entropy, dynamics, and symmetry, revealing the intricate connection between these concepts. This knowledge will likely have a significant impact on the development of next-generation sustainable cooling and heating technologies. We anticipate that our research will significantly impact the development of caloric materials and temperature control systems. Despite years of study, the factors leading to probability-matching are still unclear and a recent research aimed to find out.  In this research, 18 healthy individuals performed a range of probabilistic learning tasks that involved both gain and loss, which were then analyzed alongside the results from a questionnaires assessing their level of noise while learning, called state-dependent learning measures.  Through analyzing fMRI data, researchers found that there was a significant relationship between the activation in the midbrain, an area responsible for reward processing, and the errors made in predicting outcomes. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively. Notably, our results indicate that the unfolding method can effectively counteract measurement errors while handling a large number of qubits without resorting to numerical approximations. Moreover, our approach's internal mechanics can serve as a quantitative metric for evaluating the accuracy of other MEM methods. Notably, our results reveal that the majority of errors in experiments involve only a subset of qubits, where the probability distribution tends to exhibit a distinct non-uniform structure. This insight may facilitate the development of more targeted and efficient MEM strategies. A related software package, scalabelm, has been developed and made available through the quantum software repository QuTiP. Our work aims to lay the groundwork for a new MEM paradigm that can be applied widely in quantum computing without incurring significant computational overheads. When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on assistive teleoperation and shared control focuses on developing methods for the robot to determine the desired task based on human joystick inputs. Typically, this goal inference is done by analyzing the joystick's position relative to specific tasks that the user has performed previously. While this method is effective when the user is attempting to access a particular location, it is less effective in situations where the user is trying to perform tasks that involve conventional techniques with multiple steps, like pouring a drink. In order to overcome these issues, we took a different approach and instead created a system that captures a sequence of robot states and joystick inputs, then visualizes these records in 3D on a nearby display. The user can then select a step from this recorded sequence of actions to complete, as opposed to selecting specific joystick inputs. We evaluated our approach through field testing and found that it significantly enhances the user's ability to perform tasks that require goal inference. The experimental results also showed that users who utilized our approach were able to complete most of the tasks on the first attempt, in contrast to the controller that was taught using joystick angles. The user performance improved substantially with our method, with success rates increasing from 61% to 84% in the pouring task. The user feedback and evaluation scores from the study revealed a high overall rating of 5.75 out of 7 for the new approach. The results suggested a balance between achieving high task completion performance and maintaining the level of user involvement in the task that is achieved through shared control. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map. However, integrating map metrics and implementing robust localization techniques to maintain consistency in unknown environments remains a significant challenge. Our proposed solution is HiTMap, a unified topological map representation, that tackles this issue. By using hierarchical topology and metabolomics analysis, HiTMap enables small, easily comprehensible maps online, and its metrical initialization ensures robust localization in unfamiliar settings. Our system consists of two key modules - a Feature Selection block that identifies crucial landmarks for topological relationships, and a Refinement block that determines the precise distances between these landmarks. In our experiments with real data, HiTMap outperformed compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in situations where the robot encountered repeated loops in navigation. Additionally, our localization method demonstrated increased resilience when loop-coupled observations appeared. You can access the code for HiTMap at https://github.com/ut-ias/HiTMap. For related material, visit https://utiasrd.github.io/HitMap. Our research received funding from the ERC Grant Agreement No. 669465.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in modern wireless communication technologies. Various applications of two-dimensional arrays can be found in areas such as ultra-wide band, 2-D radar, and image processing. This paper presents a novel method to directly construct two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets by utilizing multivariable functions. To achieve this, an inter-group complementary code set is first developed using multivariable functions and subsequently utilized to produce the desired two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets. Utilizing multivariable functions enables the determination of two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets with a size of L1 x L2, where L1 can be set to a power of two (L1 = 2^m), and L2 can be set to a combination of powers of two or other integers (L2 = 2 p1^m1 p2^m2... pk^mk), offering improvements over traditional generalized Boolean functions that produce sequences of fixed lengths (2^m). This method allows the two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets to achieve a level of optimization, as each two-dimensional array corresponds to a specific multivariable function, which in turn determines the time-domain waveforms corresponding to the two-dimensional array. This direct construction not only ensures the two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets meet the required complementarity requirements but also allows for the precise control of the time-domain waveforms corresponding to the two-dimensional array. As an example, a set of 2-D Z-complementary array code sets with sizes 2^5 * 32 was developed and demonstrated to offer better performance compared to generalized Boolean functions. This direct construction not only enhances the output quality but also reduces the complexity of the encoding multivariable functions. Furthermore, this method also provides an innovative approach to constructing inter-group complementary code sets with novel features. This innovative technique allows for the precise shaping of time-domain waveforms corresponding to the groups, in addition to providing optimized time-domain waveforms. Three sets of inter-group complementary code sets with sizes 2^5 * 32, 64 * 2^5, and 64 * 32 were developed and demonstrated to offer better performance compared to generalized Boolean functions. This direct construction not only enhances the output quality but also reduces the encoding complexity of the multivariable functions. Ultimately, two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets and inter-group complementary code sets with advanced features and novel waveforms were successfully developed and demonstrated in this research.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets that change over time, we anticipate observing interconnected patterns, long-term fluctuations, seasonal variations, and correlations across different variables. In contrast, longitudinal data often displays relationships between and within individual units over time, including both intra- and inter-subject correlations. While analyzing time series and longitudinal data differs in certain aspects, they frequently employ similar visual display methods. Our approach focuses on creating an interactive framework that allows users to explore and dissect the time-based components of these data types, including how to transform and manipulate the data. For instance, we demonstrate how users can alter a data distribution by changing its time period or apply a model to smooth out data fluctuations across different variables. Our interactive system includes effective methods for summarizing data, as well as selecting and highlighting important time-based segments. We introduce the TimeSeriesR package, a comprehensive resource that integrates time-based data visualization and exploration tools, backed by the R programming language. Through a series of formative user studies, we identified key findings that guided the development of our system and discovered common patterns in how users structure their time-based data, resulting in a 1.5 million line code implementation. The TimeSeriesR package is available for free at https://github.com/FortinP/TimeSeriesR. The ShinyTimeSeriesR repository at https://github.com/FortinP/ShinyTimeSeriesR provides an interactive prototype of the system. In neural machine translation, the lack of future context limits a neural encoder-decoder model's ability to produce optimal translations during generation. It struggles to forecast and prepare accurate representations of source information relevant to out-of-vocabulary words and future meanings, leading to low-quality translations in coherent sentences. We propose a novel look-ahead attention mechanism that enables a neural encoder-decoder model to take into account future information during the generation process. Unlike regular attention that only considers past history, look-ahead attention examines both past and future contexts. By incorporating this mechanism, a neural encoder-decoder model can utilize look-ahead attention to prepare more informed representations and generate more accurate translations, even for out-of-vocabulary words and sentences. Experimental results on three major language pairs show that the proposed model significantly improves translation quality by over 1.1 BLEU points without any parameter adjustments. Moreover, it outperforms a state-of-the-art neural machine translation model by over 2.4 BLEU points on the En-Fr pair. The models with look-ahead attention also exhibit better convergence and lower loss on large datasets. Therefore, it can effectively improve the performance of neural encoder-decoder models on translation tasks. The proposed method can also benefit other sequence generation tasks, such as text summarization and code generation. We have released the code used in our research.

Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's total value and the ratio of total value to market value. This relative wealth ratio provides a more comprehensive view of performance, emphasizing how a portfolio's growth compares to the broader market's growth. In contrast to traditional logarithmic utility, we explore the optimal portfolio problem with power-utility functions for both absolute and relative wealth. By applying a stochastic control technique, we establish the respective hedging parameters and derive the corresponding closed-form solutions for the optimal portfolio. These solutions undergo asymptotic analysis as they approach infinite horizon, revealing convergence and equivalence to Merton's portfolio. We conduct a comparative analysis, evaluating the effectiveness of absolute and relative wealth as performance metrics for portfolio assessment. Our findings highlight their shared benefits, including reduced variance, and the additional benefits of relative wealth, involving lower volatility and a more significant wealth accumulation. This research provides insights for portfolio managers to optimize their evaluation methods and design more suitable assessment functions. The work extends recent findings focused on absolute wealth alone to a more general and dynamic setting. Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial method for detecting defects and ensuring their software's high quality. Nevertheless, studies have established that test code can contain test smells, or suboptimal test cases, which may compromise the effectiveness of unit tests. Prior research identified the opinions and sentiments of developers towards test smells as a key area of study, which could aid in understanding the impact of test smells and facilitating their elimination. This present study sought to investigate and validate the empirical results of a previous analysis conducted by Maldonato et al. regarding developers' perceptions of the severity of different test smells. In this research, the authors conducted an online survey among open-source developers and asked them to assess the severity of five test smells: the code has excessive comments, redundant code, is ambiguous, has excessive complexity, and executes slowly. Notably, our study provided more nuanced insights compared to Maldonato et al.'s findings, and we observed significant discrepancies between the two results. Our study also identified interesting patterns in the opinions expressed by developers regarding the severity of test smells. In general, our study's results indicate that test smells that affect program execution are viewed as more serious than those that do not. Moreover, our study highlights the significance of contextual factors in determining the severity of test smells. In summary, our study's results demonstrate that the perceptions of developers regarding the impact of test smells exhibit a remarkable degree of variation. Our research contributes to the understanding of the complex nature of test smells by providing empirical support for their complexity. Ultimately, our study's results offer valuable insights for software practitioners and researchers in this area. The present research's findings were achieved through a quantitative analysis of a selected sample of open-source developers. Our study's results can help researchers and practitioners minimize the negative consequences of test smells by raising awareness and promoting their elimination. Moreover, our study's results reflect the diverse opinions of developers regarding the impact of test smells, which may contribute to the development of more effective strategies for educating software developers on the importance of writing optimal test code. In particular, our study's results indicate a strong connection between the opinions of developers and the actual impact of test smells, as reflected in their severity levels. These findings reveal that test smells that affect program execution are generally viewed as more serious than those that do not. Moreover, our study's results highlight the significance of contextual factors in determining the severity of test smells. These findings are particularly relevant to the reduction of test smells, as they offer valuable insights for software practitioners and researchers in this area

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of the prox-regular moving set and two types of perturbations: a Carathéodory mapping and an integral forcing term with an integrand dependent on time variables. To address this new integro-differential sweeping process, the paper introduces a semi-group associated with the problem's operator and demonstrates its differentiability within the context of the problem's state space. As a result, the paper establishes key results, including the Lipschitz-continuity of the semigroup and its flow, as well as the existence and uniqueness of a strongly accretive semiflow. The semi-differentiability of this semiflow is further proven along with key applications to viscoelastic models with an exponential damping model and a singular compressible material model. We introduce the updated version of the \textsc{KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating lepton and quark pair production through high-energy electron-positron collisions. This generator is built upon the \textsc{KKMC} event generator, originally utilized for simulating charged current deep-inelastic scattering processes, leveraging its capabilities for tackling more complex higher-order radiative corrections in both charged and neutral current interactions. This is particularly beneficial for future electron-positron colliders exploring new physics beyond the standard model. To achieve this, the \textsc{KKMCee} event generator provides realistic higher-order corrections for lepton and quark pair production, complemented by its ability to model non-perturbative aspects, such as initial-state radiation, using Monte Carlo techniques. This generator is compatible with various input parameters, allowing users to specify the mass of the mediating vector boson and its width for theoretical interpretations, as well as the center-of-mass energy and other production-specific parameters for experimental simulations in advance of future electron-positron collider constructions. This generator's capabilities for implementing realistic luminosity profiles, accounting for polarization effects, and simulating double-electron generation for high-energy leptonic decays have also been integrated. To highlight its functionality, the \textsc{KKMCee} event generator's performance in generating parton distributions, applying next-to-leading-order corrections for $e^+e^-\to  e^+e^- (n)$ and $e^+e^-\to  \mu^+\mu^-$, and reconstructing hadronic final states for $e^+e^-\to  had had$ is demonstrated and validated against current data on the W boson mass and the Higgs boson mass, both measured in proton-proton collisions. To facilitate user adoption, the \textsc{KKMCee} event generator's code and associated user-guides are publicly accessible and immediately implementable, complemented by our recommendations for achieving efficient computational simulations. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal processing as a top priority. A novel algorithm has been developed to accurately calculate IBIs, even in the most challenging scenarios. By utilizing a Tiramisu model with Dilated Convolution layers, this system far surpasses traditional Haar transforms and Recurrent Neural Networks in terms of accuracy. In experiments with raw ECG signals, the new system achieved an impressive 97.1% accuracy, which is a significant improvement over existing solutions. In comparison, Haar transforms and Recurrent Neural Networks yielded 93.2% and 94.1% accuracy, respectively. By taking advantage of raw ECG signals, this system eliminates the need for additional processing, which can be time-consuming and prone to errors. In addition, the new system's reduced memory requirements make it more suitable for devices with limited resources, which is a critical consideration. A comprehensive set of tests was conducted to validate the system's effectiveness, which included noise simulations, signal sampling, and noising signals with varying levels of noise. A pioneering work in this field, the proposed algorithm has been successfully demonstrated on both Android Watches and iPhones, showcasing its practical applications. A comprehensive paper outlining this research was presented at the International Conference on Advanced Communication and Intelligent Computing in 2019. To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing communication costs when performing tensor singular value decomposition. A more efficient, distributed TSVDE method has been created, allowing local components to be executed recursively and incorporating several communication-reducing strategies between passes. An innovative approach has been introduced for extracting valuable data from a single pass: sampling data along each dimension. By combining recursive computation, several communication-reducing techniques, and data sampling, this method achieves significant performance improvements in communication speed, especially in high-rank and large-size tensor scenarios. Additionally, an in-depth error analysis was conducted to establish a precise bound for approximate solutions obtained using just two passes. Our new algorithm's performance is compared to established methods, showing improved results in several areas: in particular, it outperforms the current state-of-the-art by utilizing only 32 passes to achieve a comparable level of accuracy to 200 passes using the Randomized SVD method. A high-performance, flexible, and scalable C++/CPU implementation has been created and is available for free use. As part of this project, an in-depth, systematic performance analysis was conducted to address a long-standing question in the field: how does the number of passes affect the accuracy of randomized algorithms. A thorough theoretical justification is provided for sampling-based approximation techniques in linear algebra, a concept initially proposed in 2012. An in-depth numerical study and performance analysis were also conducted to obtain optimal performance in linear system solving using the randomized method. Experimental results show that, as the number of passes grows, the accuracy of approximations rapidly improves until it approaches a nearly asymptotic behavior. Based on this, a set of rules for determining the number of passes have been developed: a small number of passes (at least 10) for numerical solutions and much larger values (at least 1000) for tensor-based problems. These recommendations are applicable as long as the number of passes is much larger than the 90th percentile dimension size. When the passes number is lower than this threshold, the accuracy of approximations depends on the number of passes in a logarithmic fashion. In addition to these rules, a more general strategy has been developed that works for any number of passes. Network analytics, particularly in the study of complex networks, heavily relies on static or slightly dynamic graphs, which can be effectively analyzed using long-term embedding representations that capture various characteristics of the graph. However, recent years have seen an surge in the exploration of embedded dynamic graph, where temporal properties are incorporated into the embedding process. In this paper, we delve into dynamic graph embedding, covering an overview of relevant techniques, discussing the challenges involved, reviewing notable approaches under different categories, examining evaluation criteria, and exploring the associated open challenges and future research directions. Additionally, we will examine the applications of dynamic graph embedding and provide an assessment of current methods and future directions. Dynamic graph embedding is expected to continue playing a significant role in network science going forward. Its potential extensions and applications are plentiful and promising. A thorough examination of this subject is essential to understand its progress and projections. This survey is a valuable resource for professionals seeking to understand dynamic graph embedding and its many uses. It is through the dynamic graph embedding that we can better understand the underlying mechanisms of dynamic processes. This study is a necessary step to guide researchers and practitioners working in this area. Our investigation into a $^7$H resonant state treated as a five-body system with a $^3$H core and four neutrons involved, involved constructing an effective neutron-$^3$H potential to reproduce phase shifts for neutron scattering on $^3$H, and to describe the $^5$H resonant ground state in a $^3$H-n-n configuration. Utilizing the Variational Gaussian Expansion Method to solve the five-body Schrödinger equation and employing the stabilization method to estimate the resonant state parameters led to results which did not demonstrate a clear, low-energy $^7$H resonance at the $^3$H+4n threshold. A very broad resonance at approximately 9 MeV above this threshold was instead identified, corresponding to the ground state $^7$H with quantum numbers $J^{\pi}$=1/2$^+$. Additionally, within this same region, a broad $^6$H ground state with quantum numbers $J^{\pi}$=2$^-$ was also detected. Our findings supported the hypothesis that $^7$H states have a broad resonance at around 9 MeV. Moreover, a near-threshold zero in the energy-dependent neutron-$^7$H phase shift was predicted, similar to what is observed in the $^5$H(1/2$^+$) resonance, in conjunction with an unpolarized neutron analyzing power. This specific observation could be verified through an upcoming $^7$H photo-production experiment. Finally, our results for the $^7$H system served as a foundation for investigating the theoretical methods employed, providing valuable insights into the behavior of narrow resonances near threshold. This knowledge can also be applied to analyzing a $^6$H state with quantum numbers $J^{\pi}$=2$^-$ that was previously reported near the $^3$H+3n threshold. A broad $^6$H ground state with quantum numbers $J^{\pi}$=2$^-$ was also discovered and may be relevant in understanding its influence on analyzing different states in the 6He nucleus. The work done in this area has possible implications for a certain state in the 6Be nucleus. Moreover, results in this region may be relevant in understanding the different states within the 6He system. Finally, the more detailed and accurate phase shift and cross section calculations in this region were achieved through the more precise and point-by-point variation method.

The distinctive feature of this problem lies in its distinct process of contraction and dilation in comparison to other Nirenberg type problems, resulting in the emergence of a new type of solution, the non-trivial scalar blowup solution, associated with a conformal factor that exhibits an atypical behavior. The key to this investigation lies in the analysis of a boundary problem involving a second-order nonlinear differential equation, the study of which uncovers two critical aspects: first, the existence of a bounded solution, associated with a dilation, that satisfies a linear equation and exhibits a specific oscillatory behavior; secondly, the existence of a global invariants set, independent of a conformal factor, which plays a pivotal role in understanding the structure of solutions and their limiting cases. In various fields of scientific inquiry, a common challenge exists in assessing the effects of interventions on multiple units and outcomes using time-series data from observational settings. To address this issue, we've devised a novel method combining established approaches based on the factor analysis model with a Bayesian inference framework. Our proposed method uniquely allows for simultaneous handling of mixed outcome types (continuous, binomial), specifies time-varying response functions, accounts for correlations between responses, and incorporates date-specific noise. By applying this method to evaluate the performance of local tracing partnerships in England's COVID-19 contact tracing system, we've found that, overall, these partnerships have made noticeable improvements, with daily noise variance reductions of up to 70% and daily success rate increases of up to 40%. Notably, certain partnerships have specifically enhanced noise reduction and success rate by 50% and 30%, respectively. Additionally, we've identified specific days benefiting from additional noise reduction of up to 90% and success rate increases of up to 40%. To provide a more comprehensive view, we've employed multi-dimensional scaling to visualize and compare the performance of individual partners and their efforts over time. A critical examination of our results reveals substantial efforts by local tracing partnerships during the initial pandemic wave, however, during the second wave, their contributions and overall performance were significantly diminished. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of local tracing partnerships in optimizing the contact tracing system's performance and highlights opportunities for future research to investigate the causes behind the decline in performance observed during the subsequent pandemic wave. To facilitate replication and encourage collaboration, all related code and data have been made publicly available at the specified GitHub repository. Furthermore, related tools have been deposited at an open research platform known as DCC. As an extension of this research, we intend to formally release the models to DCC for peer review. In real-world settings, RL systems face difficulties due to various constraints that are challenging to formalize mathematically. For RL applications, it is crucial that agents can detect and adapt to these constraints to ensure safe decision-making. Results are compared with a constraint generation method based on reinforcement learning, showcasing the method's advantages in terms of constraint parsimony and learning efficiency. One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. This paper demonstrates the advantages of using PINNs compared to purely data-driven neural networks in terms of both training performance and gaining insights into the quality of the approximated solutions. By considering PINNs that are trained with an additional loss function based on the governing differential equations, we establish a method for a posteriori error estimation using PINNs. This method relies on a designed test function that allows for a localized error estimation of the solutions. Furthermore, we expand our error estimation approach to uncertain parameters and propose a universal test function that is applicable to any PINN. This method can be used to obtain an initial estimate of the solution error, which can be refined with increased accuracy by repeating the error estimation process. As a demonstration of the reliability of our approach, we apply it to a variety of benchmark problems characterized by partial differential equations. The results show that our error estimator is reliable, predictable, and beneficial, as it enhances the accuracy of the PINN-solution without adding to the training time. Furthermore, we extend our approach to solve two real-world problems, such as a Poisson equation with two unknowns and a stationary Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes k-omega turbulence model, thereby confirming its effectiveness in turbulent flow simulations. The obtained error estimates are comparable to the errors of the best available turbulence models used in the field. This research indicates that our approach is a valuable tool for validating numerical predictions from PINNs as well as other physics-informed machine learning methods. Its potential applications are wide-ranging, extending from engineering to the medical sciences for making informed inferences with uncertain data. The provided Python code enables the reproduction of the reported results and allows for the use of this error estimation method in new research contexts. The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources can rectify this issue. In this study, we explored how utilizing magnitude data in catalog matching by creating a dataset consisting of 40 individual catalogs containing a total of 740,000 objects. We implemented two different matching algorithms: Camaleao and Franca. Our analysis compared the performance of these algorithms based on astrometry alone versus when magnitudes were incorporated. When using the Camaleao algorithm, which considers a source's influence on its surroundings, incorporating magnitude data slightly improved the accuracy of matches. On the other hand, the Franca algorithm, which uses a peaking function to account for source influence, showed a more significant improvement of approximately 10% when magnitude data was included. To validate the effectiveness of these algorithms in real-world applications, we simulated two scenarios: one resembling the catalog of the Southern Sky Photon Counting Survey and another representing the Northern Sky Photon Counting Survey. Estimates based on these simulations suggest that incorporating magnitude data can lead to a 30% increase in the accuracy of matches for the catalog of the Southern Sky Photon Counting Survey and a 100% increase in the accuracy of matches for the catalog of the Northern Sky Photon Counting Survey. However, the actual gains may vary depending on the characteristics of future surveys. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the detection and navigation of all types of concept relationships within large ontologies. OntoPlot's novel hybrid structure incorporates an hierarchical tree view and an innovative interactive graph visualisation, utilising accelerated algorithms for path optimization to enhance overall performance. We illustrate the system's capabilities with two case studies involving substantial life science ontologies. These examples demonstrate OntoPlot's ability to aid in validating and visualising the results of automated mining and knowledge discovery processes. Moreover, we found that the system is well-suited for supporting in-depth systematized knowledge development, potentially enriching the development of ontologies in various knowledge domains. OntoPlot is open-source and freely available for use, with pre-assembled demo applications provided online. Additionally, accompanying videos depicting a comprehensive system walkthrough and the demonstration of both case studies can also be accessed online. A live demonstration of OntoPlot is scheduled for presentation at the ISWC'2020 conference. A related paper detailing the methodological framework and practical guidelines for OntoPlot is presented at the ISWC'2020 workshop known as SWPM. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle-consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after cross-domain conversion. As both approaches can train end-to-end models with unpaired data, we leverage their strengths to improve the speech-text mapping and shared representation, ultimately enhancing speech-to-text performance. Our method is versatile and can be applied to various speech processing tasks, including cross-variety settings. Empirical evaluations on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets demonstrate significant performance gains, with improvements of up to 10% observed in speech recognition accuracy. The corresponding source code is publicly available on GitHub. Moreover, we observe that the trained end-to-end models can serve as generalised speech-text aligners, providing new avenues for representation learning and transformation tasks. This work expands the scope of inter-domain loss and demonstrates the effectiveness of CycleGAN in tackling complex end-to-end ASR tasks. Furthermore, it is expected that this study will open doors for investigating novel applications of inter-domain loss and learning methods that entail transforming representations across different domains. The work also has potential to be extended to other areas, such as automatically generating images based on textual descriptions. CycleGAN, in this case, could be used to introduce complexity in the input by transforming perfect images into more nuanced ones. Conversely, it can preserve the style of the input domain. This capability to introduce randomness in the representation could, in turn, benefit various tasks involving image-to-text translation. Moreover, it enables a text-to-image translation model to introduce structure in the output by transforming random noise into coherent images based on the input description's style. The generation of random noise leading to realistic images is another area that can be explored. The work also delves into the feasibility of using end-to-end ASR models as tools for translating speech into other languages without requiring paired training data, a capability that has also been recently utilized in the case of automatic language identification. This study also examines the performance of the models when translating speech from English into Mandarin Chinese and Russian. It is expected that this research will contribute to advancing these translation capabilities and promote novel applications in translation. The work also has potential to be further expanded to other areas, such as automatic detection and classification of spoken languages. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. We have developed an innovative approach that utilizes advanced computer techniques to create a more realistic mental framework through active inference. This framework can be utilized for autonomous navigation in dynamic environments. We have successfully tested this theory on a six-legged robot to demonstrate its potential in driving autonomous navigation. Furthermore, our approach is versatile and can be easily adapted for use in various robots and diverse environments. We believe that this method not only facilitates autonomous naviation but also serves as a tool to evaluate the theoretical framework of active inference in intricate real-world situations. We have made our source code available for the benefit of the scientific community. It is our intention that this work stimulate the advancement of both theoretical frameworks and corresponding computer simulations, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of active inference. We have achieved significant reductions in entropy that are several orders of magnitude larger than those observed in previous theoretical studies employing active inference. Furthermore, our experimental findings indicate that uncertainty reduction is a substantial cost that can be as high as ten times the energy expenditure required for autonomous exploration. We have discovered two critical strategies that minimize the energy expenditure for uncertainty reduction: maintaining a relatively low level of mental complexity and using movements with sufficient variability to prevent the world state from becoming too predictable. Furthermore, our approach efficiently resolves the conflict between entropy growth due to exploration and entropy reduction through accurate world modeling, demonstrating that as the complexity of the mental framework increases, the variance of the state probabilities should decrease. We have demonstrated that the theoretical framework of active inference can generate efficient autonomous naviation policies in real-world environments, effectively validating the theoretical predictions in practical scenarios. We have observed similar behaviors in our experiments as those described in the theoretical context, including entropy spikes during exploration phases, a predominate standing behavior, and a rapid reduction in uncertainty when the robot achieves a relatively stable world state. These findings provide strong empirical support for the active inference framework. We have successfully replicated the theoretical predictions in our experiments, resulting in novel contributions to the scientific community. We plan to further evaluate the theoretical predictions of active inference in our ongoing works on autonomous multi-agent naviation and to promote the integration of theoretical and experimental approaches to advance both active inference simulations and autonomous navigation techniques. Our study of classical diatomic molecules at equilibrium demonstrates that the Soret effect is influenced by the internal freedom of high-temperature molecules. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we examined how temperature gradients affected diatomic molecules in both gas and liquid states, varying the temperature difference. Initially, we modeled molecules as non-rotating linear objects or as rotating diatoms to measure the Soret coefficient's dependence on their anisometricity. Subsequently, to isolate the effect of internal freedom, we represented diatomic molecules as two connected soft spheres connected by a harmonic spring and allowed either rotational or vibrational movements to vary the anisometry. By establishing thermal equilibrium and analyzing the Soret effect for different energy states, we identified a notable contribution of internal freedom to the Soret effect, particularly for systems with moderate anisometry. Moreover, we found that the Soret effect for vibrating molecules could be described by a simplified theoretical model, which was shown to be equivalent to the Helmholtz-Lagrange principle applied to the entire system. This model successfully accounted for the influence of internal mobility within the framework of the Stokes-Einstein-Zernike theory. Our research setting a foundation for understanding the Soret effect in various systems characterized by internal motions, including molecules, polymer brushes, and nanofluids. Ultimately, we hope that our work will facilitate a more comprehensive study of the Soret effect in systems with internal degrees of freedom. The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational complexity poses significant practical limitations to their deployment. This paper sets out to dispute the prevailing notion that larger models necessarily lead to better performance in Automated Essay Scoring. To this end, the study assesses the capabilities of multiple NLP models with fewer parameters that were fine-tuned on an AES dataset and demonstrates superior results can be achieved by combining these models' outputs, thereby reducing the total number of required parameters. The empirical findings also reveal that smaller models that were trained on noise-related data exhibit enhanced understanding of written content when compared to larger models lacking such training. Moreover, the study's results show the potential benefits of leveraging models developed specifically for AES evaluation and smaller, high-performing models that can be efficiently deployed on various mobile devices. Ultimately, the study aims to inspire further research in AES by smaller NLP models trained with noise-related data. One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical due to the high number of potential targets, we instead assign labels to box center points.  As a result, many supressed boxes are labeled as positives in the target domain.  We then propose re-ranking these boxes in a self-supervised manner to effectively eliminate false positives.  A novel loss function, referred to as the Box Re-Ranking loss, achieves this by reducing false positives that straddle domain boundaries while maintaining true positives.  A subsequent false positive score classifier relies on the precision-score autocorrelation of pedestrian boxes to effectively eliminate high-false-positive boxes.  Experiments conducted on multiple datasets highlight the effectiveness of our approach, leading to significant improvements over state-of-the-art domain adaptive pedestrian detection methods, with accuracy enhanced by up to 8.8 Mbps with FPs reduced by 25.6%. This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions like background noise, echo effects, and microphone distortion. A novel deep learning technique combines two processes: one transforms audio in a specific representation called the mel-spectrogram into a new, more desirable format, and another converts synthetically created mel-spectrograms into high-quality audio waves that are perceptually natural-sounding. Experimental results indicate that our approach surpasses established methods, which apply more conventional techniques such as removing noise and echo, as well as direct synthesis of mel-spectrograms followed by audio wave generation. Specifically, our method has been shown to achieve a significant improvement of 0.044 Sharpe and 0.288 PECOG compared to the best previous method, and its audio quality has been described as superior by human assessors. The method's effectiveness is due to the ability of extractive and generative techniques to address different aspects of the enhancement challenge. The implementation of this method is based on the JAX library, which provides scalable and efficient distributed training capabilities. The study includes a detailed analysis of the performance of various techniques for evaluating the quality of mel-spectrograms and audio waves generated by the method. Moreover, our method's potential for applications beyond low-quality music enhancement is also explored. The method's source code is publicly available. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our perceptual study revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underarm throws where the point of release occurs early, in contrast to late releases. Conversely, in the case of overarm throws, participants have a greater propensity to identify errors with a late point of release. Moreover, variations in the viewer's vantage point and the trajectory of the ball influence the overall perception of realism. These research findings can potentially contribute to the improvement of the authenticity of throwing animations in interactive applications such as virtual reality experiences or video games. Ultimately, this knowledge can aid animators in creating more realistic and engaging throwing motions. To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called Seq2DRNN has been designed, which leverages a tree-structured DRNN (Doubly-Recurrent Neural Networks) model originally proposed in 2017 for parallel analysis of syntax and text. Additionally, the proposed Seq2DRNN incorporates attention mechanisms inspired by attention-based NMT, while also retaining tree structure through constraints. As a result, the Seq2DRNN system utilizes O(n) computational complexity and O(h) memory, where n is the sentence length and h is the maximum height of the sentence's parsing structure. Experimental evaluations using English-Chinese and English-Japanese NMT tasks demonstrate that the Seq2DRNN system achieves superior results with significantly lower memory requirements compared to existing syntax-aware decoding methods. Furthermore, the system also produces more natural translations and exhibits better parsing performance in concurrent syntax and text analysis tasks. Ultimately, the proposed Seq2DRNN is considered an efficient and effective model for incorporating syntax-aware decoding in NMT. To address the limitations of existing syntax-based decoding methods, the Seq2DRNN system has been demonstrated to handle sequences of length n and tree height h, where h is greater than n, through the use of a top-down tree-structured decoding approach. As a result, the Seq2DRNN architecture can be viewed as a syntax-aware decoding extension for standard NMT systems, where the syntax-dependent part has a length of O(h), and the text-dependent part having length n. When combined, the system achieves an overall length of O(n + h). Importantly, the Seq2DRNN system has been found to handle sequences of length n and tree height h, where h is greater than n, indicating its ability to handle long sentences. Furthermore, the system has been found to determine the number of sentences and the tree structure more accurately than other syntax-based decoding methods. To verify these findings, the paper also presents a concurrent parsing and NMT evaluation that demonstrates the system's ability to produce more natural translations and better parsing results. The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account the diverse structures and energy patterns found at ice-grain surface binding sites. We developed the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP) to create a comprehensive database containing the full range of binding energies between molecules and an amorphous water surface model. BEEP employs highly automated quantum chemical methods to identify multiple binding sites on water clusters, along with varying degrees of hydrogen bonding, to determine the binding energies of molecules to these sites. Using a high-performance computing system, BEEP's evaluation platform can test over 80 different binding sites and energy patterns for any given molecule in under 80 hours. The BEEP database, which is discussed further in relation to current astrochemical binding energy values, highlights the significance of considering both binding sites and energy patterns when examining the complex interactions between molecules and ice surfaces. BEEP is now available online, enabling users to investigate the binding energies of custom molecules. All computed data and a read-only database can be accessed through the BEEP website at https://beep-astrophys.com/. A associated paper can be found at https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8205/AB8C9C. The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data due to the need to preserve the original class label. In order to overcome this constraint, we propose a concept called sibylvariance, which refers to the use of data transforms that maintain invariance, leading to the identification of sibylvariance-preserving transforms. These transforms are capable of converting any input data into unique categories, thus helping to amplify existing datasets. We provide theoretical justifications for the emergence of sibylvariance in machine learning models and demonstrate, through empirical testing, the positive impact of sibylvariance on enhancing the robustness of text classification models when confronted with unknown or adversarial inputs. We also showcase our method's effectiveness using Romanian-Hungarian news dataset and a well-known English sentiment analysis dataset. By engaging with the open-source community, we make our code and dataset annotations available for the development of sibylvariance-preserving transforms. We empirically demonstrate that sibylvariance-preserving transforms outperform conventional ones in certain scenarios, while the principles of invariance continue to yield consistent results across multiple benchmark tests. Importantly, the proposed method achieves better performance when faced with unknown or adversarial inputs. We attribute this outcome to the creation of a diverse set of training examples, which enables the model to effectively generalize across multiple tasks. Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing optimization-based approaches. A novel two-stage framework for meta-learning linear representations through least squares has been proposed, demonstrating the ability to exploit prior knowledge to acquire new tasks. Initially, a high-level prediction model is developed for task-dependent outcomes, followed by the optimization of a meta-level linear representation that is shared across similar tasks while minimizing prediction errors. This predictive model is optimized using least squares, and the representation is updated via convex optimization. Our study provides performance guarantees for this method, showing task-dependent and overall prediction accuracy bounded by specific margins. Experimental results on various synthetic datasets and a 3x3 sliding puzzle with multiple attributes are presented to validate the proposed framework. Furthermore, our approach outperforms an empirical meta-learning method based on gradient descent in empirical evaluations. Moreover, a related task of meta-adversarial learning has been proposed, and we have empirically confirmed its effectiveness in adapting to the adversarial environment. Interestingly, our approach was found to be unstable in some scenarios; for instance, when dealing with multiple identical tasks, the method can result in significant overconfidence. A meta-learning method based on elimination, specifically tailored for the mentioned scenario, was developed and evaluated. A comprehensive analysis, along with theoretical performance guarantees for these methods, has been provided, showing that the proposed algorithms outperform the baseline empirical meta-learning method in both empirical and analytical evaluations. This research addresses several key challenges in this domain. A comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between predictive performance, representation stability, and computational requirements for the proposed least squares method in comparison to an empirical meta-learning linears method based on gradient descent was conducted. Our study also explored the computational and predictive performance of this method in a setting with multiple similar tasks, and a method based on elimination was developed to mitigate the observed issues. Additionally, a meta-learning approach for adapting to the adversarial environment was proposed, and a comparative analysis of the methods was provided. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models and an established concept of actual causality, specifically emphasizing contrastive causation and default utility. The proposed definition demonstrates its capacity to address challenges in existing literature and highlights its significance in evaluating scenarios involving autonomous systems. The definition's usefulness isn't limited to discussing autonomous systems, as it provides a broader perspective on qualitative harm caused by non- autonomous systems as well. Additionally, this paper explores harmonious interpretations of qualitative harm, focusing on causal comparison and a utilitarian approach, while noting that other logical harmonies are feasible. Furthermore, the discussion emphasizes that qualitative harm should be treated separately from the more common notion of harm, which is based on harm-causing interventions, particularly in legal contexts. The proposed definition also leads to a new concept known as weak contrastive pre-eminence, connecting qualitative harm to emerging ideas in causality and law. The authors highlight the importance of qualifying what constitutes default utility in the context of qualitative harm and offer two potential strategies for doing so, which might involve integrating this concept into the definition of qualitative harm. The paper ultimately explores the relationship between qualitative harm, law, and autonomous systems, which requires careful consideration for applications. The analysis emphasizes that qualifying what constitutes default utility is particularly crucial when discussing proactive autonomous systems that act before their intended targets. The same analysis applies to other variants of autonomous systems, which share a common proactive characteristic with proactive autonomous systems. The existence of qualitative harm and its two harmonies raises fundamental questions about the best approach for addressing and regulating harm, particularly in the context of the law. The most direct strategy involves establishing the two harmonies into two separate legal principles, which could be further broken down into laws and guidelines. The possibility of using legal institutions to regulate qualitative harm exists, as the concept is linked to emerging technologies, such as autonomous systems. The ultimate goal is to create a new body of regulatory law related to qualitative harm. The definition of qualitative harm presented in this paper offers a valuable starting point for this endeavor, enabling qualitative harm to be effectively governed by law. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written text across different languages. The conventional approach involves two distinct steps: speech recognition and machine translation, which are initially trained and fine-tuned separately. However, this process is costly and inefficient, especially when there is a lack of supervision. To mitigate these issues, new methods have emerged that can learn speech-to-text patterns even from unlabelled data, effectively treating the two tasks as interconnected units. Notably, these methods can also generalize to languages never seen in training, including those with unique speech patterns, by focusing on learning speech characteristics. We explore various techniques that can unlock highly accurate zero-shot translation without the need for speech data annotation or extensive training. The experiments reveal that modifying existing translation models by discarding unrelated speech elements leads to significant advancements, achieving results comparable to those obtained with speech recognition data. Building upon this insight, we introduce a unified model that integrates speech recognition and machine translation, enabling it to learn relevant patterns from unlabelled data. We also conduct a thorough analysis to understand the underlying patterns in speech-to-text data and develop a novel loss function to optimize the translation of unlabelled data. The resulting model demonstrates superior performance, setting a new benchmark in zero-shot speech-to-text translation. Notably, our methods achieve better outcomes than those obtained by treating speech recognition as a supplementary task or combining speech recognition and machine translation into a single model, highlighting their efficiency and accuracy. The research is supported by public code repositories and data sets, enabling replication of the results. The research is further validated through comprehensive electrode analyses. Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions across individual devices. Although high-frequency measurement data are available, predictive models tailored for this time frame face challenges due to limited point-in-time information and high forecast uncertainty. This issue can be addressed by combining single models' forecasts with an additional meta-forecast, calculated from the weighted averages of individual outputs. This hybrid forecasting approach was investigated further by analyzing specific factors that influence forecast accuracy and variability, such as time of day, day of the week, and month, as well as unusual events like public holidays. Our study demonstrated the significance of meta-forecasting in low voltage forecasting and provided insights into the impact of daily load patterns and unusual events on forecast accuracy and variability. These findings contribute to the development of effective forecasting strategies for low voltage networks. Moreover, our research highlights the value of meta-forecasting in low voltage forecasting and illustrates its limited applicability in real-world contexts. Our study also explores the implications of daily load patterns and unusual events on forecast accuracy and variability. These findings can aid experts in designing low voltage forecasting systems. Finally, our research demonstrates the importance of probabilistic forecasting in low voltage, a aspect that is often neglected in real-world applications. Our study also showcases the utility of probabilistic forecasting for low voltage, a aspect that is often underestimated in real-world applications. For evaluation purposes, our team used 468 days of high-resolution measurement data from 7024 European low voltage nodes and comparison groups. Our main conclusions are the following: (1) meta-forecasting of operational energy consumption at 15-minute intervals using daily profiles significantly enhances accuracy, (2) the integration of meta-forecasting of operational energy consumption and peak load forecasts significantly enhances accuracy, (3) the main factors influencing the accuracy and variability of low voltage forecasts within a given time frame are daily profiles and unusual events, (4) the independence of comparison groups from one another is crucial for accurately modeling daily profiles and unusual events, (5) the proposed hybrid forecasting method outperforms current state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy and variability, (6) the proposed hybrid forecasting method outperforms current multi-step arithmetic models in terms of accuracy and variability. Our analysis also reveals that the proposed hybrid forecasting method does not surpass the current single-step least squares method in terms of accuracy and variability. We believe that the proposed hybrid forecasting method does not surpass the current single-step least squares method in terms of accuracy and variability.

The growth of machine learning algorithms has not entirely resolved the issues affecting performance, as numerous studies reveal that a significant portion of failed projects can attribute their demise to inadequate engagement between domain experts and machine learning teams. Consequently, knowing how to effectively integrate domain knowledge is essential for achieving optimal results, as several recent studies have demonstrated. This paper aims to provide an overview of methods used to incorporate domain knowledge, quantification of decision processes, and data representation. We will examine the challenges associated with incorporating domain knowledge and outline practical strategies for achieving successful integration. Furthermore, we will discuss the limitations of the current understanding in this area and suggest potential avenues for future investigation. This paper originates from a workshop on "Integration of Domain Knowledge in Machine Learning" held in 2020. We have incorporated the feedback gathered from the event and other sources, as well as recent advancements in the field. This paper is intended to serve as a comprehensive resource and entry point for researchers seeking to understand the role of domain knowledge integration, offering relevant background reading for approximately 2-3 hours. We have also compiled a list of 52 specific research projects proposed during the workshop for those interested in exploring this field. This overview covers various applications, including natural language processing, computer vision, tabular data, healthcare, science citation, bioinformatics, search marketing, and text search. We have identified promising research directions and potential contributors in these areas. This paper is part of a broader initiative to provide high-quality entry points and surveys for specific machine learning topics and subfields. We hope this overview will inspire readers to enhance their understanding of incorporating domain knowledge and to tackle the accompanying technical and methodological challenges. Detecting degenerative spine disorders requires detailed spinal curvature analysis.
However, manually marking each vertebra to construct a 3D spine profile is a labor-intensive task.
To address this challenge, researchers propose an efficient and accurate algorithm to localize and identify vertebrae in CT scans.
The proposed method involves spine rectification to establish a starting point for optimization, and an anatomically-constrained model to refine vertebrae alignment.
The method showcases high precision and fast processing speed, with a processing time of 2 seconds per image. The method achieved 100% identification accuracy for 99% of vertebrae and demonstrated robustness across various scanning positions and states. The study includes detailed analysis and evaluation of the method's performance. Additionally, the method has been applied to analyze spinal curvature in a study of 352 participants. In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the relationship between motor effort and joint torque, necessitating frequent parameter updates in feedback controller designs. We explore an alternative approach by using reinforcement learning double agents to model and exploit this effort-torque dynamic for all possible parameter settings, then employing this model to develop a reward function for feedback controllers. We compare the success of our proposed method against multiple variants of feedback linearization in quadruped locomotion scenarios, revealing that our reinforcement learning approach allows for more robust and adaptable locomotion, even when the robot's actual spring constant differs from its modeled value. Our research covers both plain and icy surfaces, demonstrating the potential of reinforcement learning in mitigating the challenges posed by actuator nonidealities in complex locomotion tasks. We publicly share our code and training data to facilitate future research. We also discuss potential ways to reduce the training time of the double agent, whose current requirements, while accessible via public code, still pose a significant hurdle. We outline areas for further optimization in future iterations.

We examine the issue of determining whether a given N-qubit quantum state exhibits significant properties of separability using a particular mathematical framework based on the principles of variational theory. This theoretical approach leads to a range of useful insights, including a generalised version of the sufficient conditions for separability, improved versions of existing metrics for measuring distance and mixedness in systems that are not fully pure, and new formulas for calculating specific quantities, such as the Chord and Bures distances in bilinear space. Furthermore, we derive precise standards for necessary and sufficient conditions for separability in terms of certain convex sets in bilinear space, and we develop an efficient algorithm for assessing the separability of quantum states in bilinear space. The theoretical method we devise is then tested on a variety of N-qubit states, particularly those corresponding to certain types of symmetry, such as U(SU(N)) states. Although our approach is specifically designed with quantum systems in mind, the method we develop is also applicable to more general mathematical contexts involving distance metrics on function spaces and the identification of radon planes in bilinear space. The method we develop avoids many of the computational difficulties associated with previously proposed algorithms for determining separability in quantum states, such as issues related to numerical instability. Rather than relying on solving complex equations, the method we develop involves a range of simpler geometric and algebraic operations in bilinear space. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by applying it to a range of N-qubit states, particularly fully entangled N-qubit states expressed as |N states. We also extend the method to a range of bipartite quantum systems, including those corresponding to certain types of U(SU(2)), U(SU(3)), and U(SU(4)) states. Prior research in a collisionless plasma setting has shown that there is no threshold for this mode of instability, which is contrary to what happens in a collision-dominated environment. In the case of a homogeneous background magnetic field, it has been found that electron temperature gradients can lead to island formation, but this tendency is reversed when the electron temperature gradient is inverted. Moreover, it has been observed that small-scale modes require significantly higher levels of electron temperature gradients than large-scale modes, which indicates that there is typically a cutoff point below which large-scale modes become less likely to occur. In comparison to other collisionless mechanisms of magnetic reconnection, it was found that small-scale modes are more resistant to changes in growth rate due to variations in electron temperature gradients, which highlights their potential significance in understanding element diffusion. In terms of practical application, it was suggested that the effects of microtearing modes could be modeled using a deterministic approach for large sets of island widths and spatial locations, and using a probabilistic approach for varying island widths and locations, which could provide a more comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon. In a collision-dominated setting, it was discovered that microtearing modes can also lead to island broadening and reduced maximum linear growth rates, which may also have implications for element diffusion. Lastly, it was noted that the characteristics of a type of mode known as the ETG mode in a collision-dominated setting are similar to those of a type of mode known as nonthermal mode in a collisionless setting, which suggests certain similarities and connections between these two types of modes across different types of plasma systems. In a collisionless setting, it was observed that the growth of mode occurs through a complex interplay of multiple electron fluid kinetics, which can be explained by solving the full set of electron Vlasov-Maxwell equations. In a collision-dominated setting, a simplified set of equations is sufficient to capture the essential dynamics of this mode of instability. In terms of computational complexity, it was noted that solving the full set of equations for the microtearing mode in a 3D simulation is computationally feasible even using relatively simple algorithms. We demonstrate SEM's effectiveness with state-of-the-art results on two prominent datasets: CUB-200-2011 and Stanford Online Marketplace. Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth, especially when it comes to occasion-based errors, where traditional methods using textural similarities often struggle with occasions like occlusions. Drawing on the dynamic programming principle, we propose an innovative algorithm that calculates cost with occasion. This approach starts by generating reference maps of horizontal and vertical epipolar planes, then uses a geometric-based cost metric which takes into consideration occasion. This cost metric is also occasion-aware, offering better results than traditional methods based on textural similarities. Furthermore, we develop an optimization process, using the eightquadrature method to determine optimal discrete displacement values. Experimental results demonstrate that our novel approach to constructing the matching cost, combined with our optimized quadrature method, significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in light field depth estimation. This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system and then employing double Wronskian solutions to yield a range of solutions for the reduced equations, resulting in a comprehensive overview of solutions for both classical and nonlocal Fokas-Lenells equations. Several solutions are illustrated through asymptotic analysis, notably, novel solutions are obtained for Fokas-Lenells equations linked to real discrete eigenvalues, previously unreported in analytical methods, and display behavior similar to (multi-)periodic waves or solitary waves with algebraic decay. Furthermore, by using Fokas-Lenells solutions to study the two-dimensional scattering problem for the nonlocal Fokas-Lenells equations, we find solutions for nonlocal Sasa-Satchler equations. This work also discusses the Fokas-Lenells equations in relation to the highly nonlinear regular periodic wave equation and the Fermi-Pasta-Lieuville system. Lastly, we attempt to extend the bilinear approach to a broader class of equations, including those integrating q-deformed eigenvalues. This approach is applied to study multi-component nonlinear equations in conjunction with their nonlocal versions. Several solutions are obtained, including periodic and algebraic decay type solutions for multiple-component nonlinear equations. Moreover, we use the bilinear method to study the nonlocal version of the Fokas-James equations, producing periodic and algebraic decay type solutions for multiple-component nonlocal systems. Interestingly, by studying nonlocal multiple-component equations, we find double-periodic scattering data for the nonlocal Sasa-Satchler equations, providing a new insight. This work is a first attempt to link the nonlocal multiple-component equations to two-dimensional scattering problems for multiple-component systems. It is hoped that this link may open a pathway for studying scattering problems for multiple-component systems in two dimensions, leading to new insights and understanding. A particularly intriguing aspect of this system arises from the fact that its solutions exhibit a periodic behavior, which in turn is linked to a periodic behavior of the multiple-component nonlinear equation of Fokas-Lenells type.
